in_favor.quote: This draft environmental impact statement is an excellent, well-thought product. It is thorough and easily understood. We have no comments on the five points.
in_favor.summary: The Ohio Department of Natural Resources praised the draft environmental impact statement as an excellent, thorough, and easily understood product, offering no comments on the five points. However, they urged the Department of Interior to promote mechanisms for ORV site selection that minimize adverse impact and irretrievable resource loss, and recommended periodic inspections of areas in use. They also suggested that a public land use plan could help facilitate site selections that account for unique natural areas, soil and vegetative conditions, and wildlife habitat.
in_favor.statementText:
WILLIAM B. NYE DIRECTOR
DEPARTMENT OF MATURAL RESOURCES
OHIO DEPARTMENTS BUILDING COLUMEUS 43215
August 9, 1972
United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240 Attn: G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director
Draft Environmental Impact RE: Statement for Implementation of Executive Order 11644-Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public
Lands-Kl4
Dear Director Hofe:
In response to your letter of June 1, 1972 forwarding the draft environmental impact statement for the above referenced project, a review was coordinated by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources. Comments were solicited from other State agencies under the auspices of the Office of the Governor, State Clearinghouse.
This draft environmental impact statement is an excellent, well-thought product. It is thorough and easily understood. We have no comments on the five points.
The Department of Interior should proceed with finalization of the statement. We would, however, urge you to promote mechanisms for site selection for Off-Road Vehicles use which would allow for the least adverse impact and irretrievable loss in the area being considered. In addition, qualified personnel should periodically inspect areas in use to assess the deterioration of existing land forms.
In light of the fact that ORV site selections must take into account the preservation of unique natural areas, special soil and vegetative conditions, wildlife habitat areas, etc., perhaps the implementation of a public land use plan would aid and/or facilitate these selections.

Director G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. August 9, 1972 Page Two
Thank you for the opportunity to review and comment on the impact statement. We look forward to receiving the final form and to cooperation in any way with the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation personnel associated with the State of Ohio in implementing this Executive Order.
Sincerely,
WILLIAM B. NYE Director
WBN/pjm

in_favor.statementText:
Executive Order 11644, though confined to regulation of off-road vehicles
on certain Department of the Interior and Department of Agriculture lands,
is compatible with objectives, activities and comprehensive planning
related to land management by the Kansas Forestry, Fish and Game Commission.
This Order addresses itself to problems common to Federal and State juris-
dictions. The Kansas Forestry, Fish and Game Commission has recognized
these problems at the state level and proposes to alter its regulations
to effect similar controls over its lands. Federal action will serve to

in_favor.role: Director, Recreation Vehicle Division, Trailer Coach Association
in_favor.quote: Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government.
in_favor.summary: Lee W. Moses, on behalf of the Trailer Coach Association, strongly supports a multi-use concept for all public lands, arguing that restricting access to preserve natural resources denies the public—particularly families and working people—the recreational opportunities they need. He criticizes the Draft Environmental Statement as overly influenced by 'hard core preservationists' and contends that off-road vehicle users are responsible conservationists, not destroyers of the environment. He offers numerous constructive suggestions for expanding and better managing public recreational lands while keeping them open to all users with minimal regulation.
in_favor.statementText:
3855 EAST LA PALMA AVENUE + ANAHEIM, CALIFORNIA 92806 (714) 630-1440 August 4, 1972
RE: INT DES 72-62
The Honorable Rogers C. Morton Secretary U. S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C.
Dear Sir:
Trailer Coach Association wishes to thank the Department for this opportunity to express our views on federal land use and recreational policies.
Trailer Coach Association was formed in 1936 and is the oldest association in the United States which represents the manufacturers of recreation vehicles. Recognizing the difference in marketing areas between those states east and west of the Rocky Mountains, Trailer Coach Association has endeavored to curtail its major sphere of operation to the 11 westernmost states and is extremely active in the promotion and protection of the industry in those states.
Additionally to deal with matters of national concern to the industry, Trailer Coach Association maintains a staffed office in the Washington, D. C. area. This office enables the industry to carry out expeditious liason with various departments of the federal government.
The term 'recreation vehicle' has been applied to many varied types of vehicles currently being used in the pursuit of outdoor recreation. However, the types of vehicles which are of direct concern to TCA are the recreational housing type vehicles which include Motor Homes, Travel Trailers, Camping Trailers, Truck Campers and Converted Vans (see Attachment #1 - Illustrated Definitions). There are currently in excess of four and a half million (4,500,000) of these types of vehicles in use in the United States which are used for varying periods of time during the year by over thirteen million (13,000,000) Americans for recreation, vacation and travel use. The industry is currently producing nearly one-half million (500,000) of these vehicles annually with a value which exceeds one and a half billion dollars ($1,500,000,000). If current trends continue, these figures will double within ten (10) years. These impressive figures are but a small part of the estimated one-hundred and five billion
. BOR [13"Codod"[11"]
100
#5-45860

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 2 August 4, 1972
dollars ($105,000,000,000) pumped into the national economy each year by the current leisure time/recreation boom which we are experiencing. The money spent in this country in spare time pursuits is in excess of the cost of national defense; it is more than we spend on the construction of new homes; it is greater than the aggregate income of all the country's farmers and exceeds the over-all value of this country's exports.
The current boom in outdoor recreation shows no signs of slowing down. Since there are currently in excess of 2,000 firms working on a four-day week, the establishment of five three-day holiday weekends each year and the fact that over forty million (40,000,000) workers enjoy a three week vacation each year, one can only anticipate continued increases. Early retirements too will contribute heavily to increased leisure time spending. It is currently estimated that over seventy-five percent (75%) of the people who are nine years of age or above indulge in some form of outdoor recreation. Unfortunately, due to a lack of urban recreation facilities and restrictive uses on rural land use, Americans continue to be faced with more and more time to do less and less.
Recreation vehicles are currently the only means by which families with small children and retired people may enjoy the pleasures of camping. Recreational camping vehicles offer the user sanitation facilities which are totally self-contained and provide a convenient way to carry their litter back home for proper disposal unlike the hiker who must find ways to dispose of waste materials in the out-of-doors without proper facilities.
Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government. The desire to preserve our "natural resources" by denying the use of land to the people who own and wish to make use of it is certainly not in the best interest of providing the needed opportunities for man to seek recreation and preserve their "human resources."
Over-use and conflict of interest have created a need for regulation of the use of federally-controlled public lands, as has become only too obvious by the preponderance of somewhat ill-conceived actions by extremest preservation groups. If regulation is to be fair, then certainly the prime objectives must be coordinated between various bureaus and departments charged with administrating the lands, equal consideration given to all recreational uses currently being pursued on those lands and an area by area determination must be made of the necessary regulation of individual sites.
The prime consideration must be to keep all lands open for all uses with minimum regulation unless there is a specific well-documented reason for establishing more restrictive regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 3 August 4, 1972
The need for an input from groups other than those interested in total preservation of our natural resources has recently given birth to several new organizations devoted to assisting the federal government in planning for the administration of land use and recreational policies. Among the most prominent of these new organizations is the "Outdoor Nation" (see Attachment #2). We are hopeful that this organization will provide your department with a realistic viewpoint and approach to solving some of the problems to which this statement is addressed.
Trailer Coach Association cannot help but feel that the definition of recreation vehicle as found in Presidential Order No. 11644 was never intended to include the vehicles as described above and in Attachment #1. However, the true off-road vehicles -- motorcycles, dune buggies, snow-mobiles, four-wheel drive, etc. are also of importance to the industry we represent. A recent study of the users of recreational camping vehicles in the State of California indicated that 40% of the vehicles surveyed were carrying or towing some type of off-road vehicle. We can only conclude that restrictions on the operation of these off-road vehicles will definitely effect the use and marketing of recreational camping vehicles and we, therefore, have a common interest in maintaining areas for their use.
We would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Department of Interior Task Force which developed the November 1971 study on Off-Road Recreation Vehicles. We feel that this is a true and objective look at the pros and cons of this legitimate form of outdoor recreation. On the other hand, we fail to understand the thinking of the Department as expressed in their Draft - Environmental Statement of May 26, 1972, which differs greatly from the ORRV Study. It would appear that the hard core preservationists must have had a hand in the drafting of the environmental statement.
Many unfortunate assertions have been made concerning the use and users of off-road vehicles by over-reactionary preservationist groups. Most of these extremists would have the nation believe that anyone who entered into the public domain on or in a mechanized vehicle was there for the sole purpose of damaging or destroying any or all things which came into his view. This most certainly is not the case. The users of recreation vehicles of all types are family people participating in family activities. They are conservationists interested in a clean, healthful environment and are concerned for the safety of themselves, their families and others while pursuing their preferred type of recreation. Through the use of public lands, people from all walks of life are brought together in a common interest, and healthy communication is often fostered between child and parent through their participation in activities which interest them mutually.

. The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 4
August 4, 1972
In the past year or so, many proposals have been made to not only restrict the use of public lands but to prohibit recreation vehicle use by classifying these areas as wilderness or primitive thereby denying use to some 98% of the national population. Since less than 2% of the nation's people are active hikers and backpackers, areas which restrict vehicle use become inaccessible to a very large majority. We have no quarrel with back-packing; however, the time required and the physical demands account for the relatively small number of people who are able to enjoy this type of activity. Surveys conclude that the majority of back-packers in the United States understandably are school teachers and students who have long summer vacations and are able to spend the long periods of time necessary to pursue this type of recreation. The average working man with two weeks annual vacation plus a few holiday weekends must restrict his recreational activities to those which may be reasonably pursued within a relatively short period of time.
It is interesting to note that the same groups who advocate increasing our country's wilderness areas and totally preserving our natural resources actively solicit and spend tax free funds to impair American commerce. These self-appointed guardians of the American public devote full time to lobbying and have filed lawsuits against nearly every large scale economically beneficial project which has been pursued by American industry during the past three to five years. Shocking examples of this unwarranted use of the country's judicial system are the halting of the Trans-Alaskan pipeline and the Florida Barge Canal. From where industry sits, it looks as if the government is "running scared" from a very vocal minority of the people.
Evidence of the preservationist impact on the United States economy is evidenced by the U. S. Chamber of Commerce's decision to take a stand against such groups, and to assume a more aggressive roll in shaping decisions being made not only by the courts, but by government agencies responsible for implementing environmental protection laws.
Areas which we feel worthy of exploration as a means of solving some of the problems created by the public's demand for outdoor recreation follow:
1. There are many tracts of government-owned land which at one time served as military reservations that are no longer in use which could be turned into recreation facilities to serve a portion of the close-in urban recreational needs.
2. The availability of low interest loans to recreational area development firms would stimulate development from the private sector.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 5 August 4, 1972
3. A problem currently being created by land closures is a higher concentration of use is being experienced by those areas which remain open which in turn auguments any problems that might be created by over-use. Therefore, very thorough consideration must be given to any closure of the public domain.
4. A reevaluation is in order of the types of recreation which are in one way or another subsidized by the government in relation to the numbers of people involved in various recreational pursuits.
5. The Bureau of Land Management should reevaluate their leasing practices of public lands for sheep and cattle grazing and mining operations. To prevent such unfair practices as "checkerboard leasing", current practices allow a lessee to lease sections of land which are diagonally adjacent to one another in a "checkerboard" pattern without paying for the lease rights on those sections of land which become entrapped by surrounding leaseholds. This practice allows leaseholders to monopolize 100% more land than they actually pay rental on and gives them the right to deny tresspass privileges to the general public.
6. An immediate and inexpensive solution to the problem of over-crowded existing recreation areas might be a rescheduling of vacation periods in the schools of our country. By requiring approximately 25% of the student bodies to vacation during each of four quarters annually, we would not only eliminate the summer vacation conjection but would make better use of our educational facilities as well.
7. A very effective program which was instituted by the government during the late 1930s under the banner of 'CCC' might be revitalized to assist in building new and rehabilitating our existing recreation facilities across the country while making use of the very large unemployed labor force which is currently available. Since through various welfare and unemployment compensation plans we, the taxpayers, support the unemployed while they are idle, it would make economical sense to accomplish some worthwhile end while supporting these people.
8. When conflicts occur between various groups interested in the use of a specific tract of land, we feel that the best solution is to call together the representatives from those interested groups and allow them to work out their differences in a democratic manner. The government body responsible for the operation and administration of the area in question should be called upon to moderate any arbitration of this type. Trailer Coach Association strongly believes in the theory of self-government and therefore feels that the people who are directly involved in the results of regulation are entitled to a say in the writing and implementation of those regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton
U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 6
August 4, 1972
9. Conflicts between user groups could be avoided to a large degree through proper education of the individuals involved and by encouraging users to understand the needs and motivations of other users. Through proper education by both government and organized user groups, policies of self-policing should be encouraged.
10. Under the present restrictions placed on wilderness and primitive areas, any "man-made" structures are prohibited. We suggest a reevaluation of these policies in view of the fact that the very people who demand expansion of our existing wilderness systems have a need for sanitary facilities, trash disposal and some degree of fire control in the existing areas.
11. A clean environment and balanced Ecosystem are among the top priorities involved in conservation and preservation of natural resources. We would suggest that the Department of the Interior take a close look at the sewage disposal facilities of any of the major cities in our country. It is appalling in this day of advanced technology that cities the size of San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago, New York, etc., etc., dump raw, untreated sewage into our rivers and oceans daily. It is naive indeed to think that we can solve our problems by continuing to pollute the areas in which we live while expending our financial resources to seek refuge away from those areas which we have polluted.
Again, we appreciate this opportunity to make our views known to your Department and trust that your consideration will be given to these remarks. We stand ready to assist in whatever manner which might be appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
Lee W. Moses, Director
Recreation Vehicle Division

conditional.summary: The Society of Exploration Geophysicists, through its President Carl H. Savit, argues that geological and geophysical survey vehicles should be exempted from the proposed ORV regulations, just as farm tractors, construction equipment, and forestry vehicles are exempted. The Society contends that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground impact and serve vital national interests related to energy and mineral resource discovery. They urge the Secretary of the Interior to amend his instructions to exclude such survey equipment from the recreational ORV regulatory framework.
conditional.statementText:
Dear Sir:
Members of the Society of Exploration Geophysicists have called to my attention Executive Order 11644 and your consequent memorandum of May 5, 1972 to the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish and Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources.
Our members are deeply concerned by the text of that memorandum which fails to take account of the special nature of off-road vehicles used in geological and geophysical surveys throughout the public lands of the United States. In particular, they feel that recognition of the exceptional nature of such vehicles should be included among the exceptions listed in the third paragraph of the subject memorandum. Vehicles for geophysical or geological surveying, when used exclusively for their designed purposes, should logically fall into the same broad category as farm tractors, self-propelled agricultural equipment, equipment for harvesting and transporting forest products, and earth moving and construction equipment when such vehicles are used for their designed purposes. It should be noted that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground loading consistent with their survey purposes and are therefore inherently far less likely to leave permanent imprints on the ground than are self-mobile construction and excavation devices or forest product transporters, vehicles which carry heavy loads and, of necessity, create large local ground loading.
Geological and geophysical surveys of the public lands are undertaken, in conformity with statutory requirements, for the purposes of discovering or assessing mineral, fuel, or thermal resources of the United States or for scientific and educational purposes. As such, the continuation of such surveys is of vital interest to the people of the United States in view of the present energy crisis and of the critical shortages of many of our mineral resources. To impose upon such surveys the requirement to conform to regulations designed for the control of recreational vehicles rather than to
11
* . · · · · · · ·

The Honorable the Secretary of the Interior June 30, 1972
Page 2
include such surveys along with agricultural, forestry, and construction operations would appear unjustified on any reasonable basis.
Our nearly 8000 members would be adversely and vitally affected in their activities on the public lands of the United States by being required to adhere to regulations designed for recreational activities. On behalf of our membership, I strongly urge that you amend your instructions to the Assistant Secretaries to except geological and geophysical survey equipment, while being used exclusively for their designed purposes, from the general category of off-road vehicle to which the proposed regulations will apply.
Sincerely,
Carl H. Savit
President

conditional.summary: Stewart R. Wallace, president of Mine Finders, Inc., expresses alarm that proposed ORV restrictions—particularly a four-month advance notice requirement for permits—would severely hamper mineral exploration activities that depend on flexible, unplanned off-road vehicle use. He argues there is a meaningful distinction between recreational 'joy-riding' and professional use of ORVs for making a living, and urges the Bureau to develop a licensing arrangement that allows exploration geologists to work without undue restriction. While he shares concern about environmental degradation from indiscriminate ORV use, he contends that the proposed regulations as written would jeopardize mineral discovery efforts critical to the nation's raw material supply.

MINE FINDERS, INC.
8700 WEST 14TH AVENUE LAKEWOOD, COLORADO 80215 (303) 233-0585
July 12, 1972
44
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Sir:
I am writing to express my concern for legislation or regulation which may come about as a result of executive order 11644 regarding the use of off-road vehicles — Draft Environmental Statement, Int DES 72 - 62, May 26, 1972, notice of which I understand appeared in the Federal Register June 2.
I am a professional geologist with two graduate degrees and have worked in the field for about 24 years. I was employed by the U.S. Geological Survey on both full-time and part-time bases from 1948 to 1955 and worked in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. For the last 17 years I have been a mining and exploration geologist and was fortunate enough, while in the employee of the Climax Molybdenum Company, to participate in two major mineral discoveries. For the last two and one-half years I have been working for a small company, of which I am the president, engaged in contract exploration in western North America for a major raw material company. We now have a staff of seven full-time geologists plus supporting personnel, and hope to add one or two more people during the next eighteen months.
As a geologist and one who enjoys and appreciates nature, I share your concern for the degradation of our remaining "wild lands" by the indiscriminate use or over use by off-road vehicles. On the other hand I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business. I am not familiar with all of the proposed regulations but understand that a four month advance notice would be required for the application of a permit for an off-road vehicle event. It is literally impossible for us to predict four months in advance a specific or, in many cases, even a general off-road vehicle usage. Thus, I am fearful that such restrictions rigidly enforced would greatly reduce our chances of success in making a mineral discovery and in properly locating it according to existing laws governing the location of mineral claims. I might add that mineral exploration is a particularly hazardous business at best and that the odds are great against making a significant find.

lfl
Since the end of World War II, the American mining companies (and others, too) have spent a great deal of time, effort and money here and abroad in the exploration for, and development of, new material resources. Now, for the first time in the last thirty years, the world has finally caught up with itself in that the supply of basic earth materials is sufficient to meet the immediate demand. This situation, however, will not long continue. If the U.S. is to maintain a competitive position (in any field) among the community of nations, it must have access to an assured supply of raw materials at reasonable prices. I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
I do not know what ethical or moral problems there may be in denying use to some while allowing others freedom from such restrictions. I do contend, however, that there is a real difference between simple "joy-riding" and travel for the purpose of making a living. I also maintain that the exploration geologist does perform useful and necessary work, not only for himself and his company, but for the country.
Sincerely yours,
Stewart R. Wallace
Situan IR (1 milenne.

conditional.quote: We concur with the general approach outlined by the Department for regulating ORV use, and urge that the specific regulations developed by Interior's land managing agencies to designate lands for ORV use contain stringent provisions for: (1) analyzing the environmental impact of the specific types of ORV use contemplated on an area-by-area basis prior to opening any lands; (2) controlling the type and intensity of ORV use in lands opened; (3) monitoring the effects of such use; and, (4) if significant damage to environmental values is occurring, taking prompt corrective measures, including restrictions or prohibition of further ORV use.
conditional.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency concurred with the Department of Interior's general approach to regulating ORV use but urged that specific regulations include stringent provisions for environmental impact analysis, use controls, monitoring, and prompt corrective measures including restrictions or prohibition if significant damage occurs. EPA deferred its detailed comments pending review of proposed regulations from the land managing bureaus and the National Park Service. Overall, EPA's stance was conditionally supportive, endorsing the framework while pressing for robust environmental safeguards in implementation.

Dear Mr. Watt:
The Environmental Protection Agency has reviewed the draft environmental impact statement for the Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands prepared by the Department of Interior and dated May 26, 1972. We concur with the general approach outlined by the Department for regulating ORV use, and urge that the specific regulations developed by Interior's land managing agencies to designate lands for ORV use contain stringent provisions for: (1) analyzing the environmental impact of the specific types of ORV use contemplated on an area-by-area basis prior to opening any lands; (2) controlling the type and intensity of ORV use in lands opened; (3) monitoring the effects of such use; and, (4) if significant damage to environmental values is occurring, taking prompt corrective measures, including restrictions or prohibition of further ORV use.
We are advised that the official comment period for this environmental impact statement has been extended to cover the period allowed for review of the regulations proposed by the Bureaus of Land Management, Reclamation and Sport Fisheries and Wildlife and the National Park Service. Therefore, we are deferring transmittal of our detailed comments on this draft impact statement until after we have had an opportunity to review the proposed regulations.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this statement. We look forward to reviewing the pending regulations on ORV use on public lands and the subsequent operating regulations.
Sincerely yours,

conditional.summary: The Illinois Department of Conservation conditionally supports the ORV framework but expresses serious concern that the Draft Environmental Statement downplays environmental harm and that expansion of ORV use will damage natural resources, particularly on smaller state properties near federal lands. They insist that firm limitations must be imposed, warning that registration fees and other funds will be inadequate to cover environmental repairs, facility costs, and administration, and that enforcement is the most serious practical problem. They commend Interior for taking initiative but urge that demographic pressures on Midwestern states be factored into any technical assistance or promotion of ORV facilities.
conditional.statementText:
State of Illinois
DEPARTMENT OF CONSERVATION
Springfield 62706
RICHARD B OGILVIE
HENRY N. BARKHAUSEN DIRECTOR
August 8, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Director Watt:
It is with pleasure the Illinois Department of Conservation responds to your invitation to review the draft "Environmental Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-the-Road Recreation Vehicles".
In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
We do, however, have several comments regarding the Statement which I am attaching to this letter.
Sincerely,
Henry N. Barkhausen Director
.0

The Illinois Department of Conservation in general has felt that recreational opportunities which are not particularly dependent on natural resources should more appropriately be provided by local government rather than state or federal government. Our feelings have been based more with consideration to state owned lands of this Department than in the context of the federal properties. We feel that, in general, the types of recreational experiences provided to the public should proceed from a strong natural resource orientation to a less strong natural resource orientation as one proceeds from the federal to local levels of government.
Our feelings are that the imposition of off-the-road vehicles on public lands has been more by default than by design. The tremendous increase, however, in production and use of off-the-road vehicles has brought us to a point in time where it will be very difficult to step back and prohibit use of these vehicles in all cases even though there are many instances where they seem to exhibit a disharmonious factor with major objectives and uses of lands involved, particularly those uses which are more traditional. We may be exhibiting the polarization in viewpoints here, representing the more resource-oriented opinions, as discussed in the Task Force Study; however, it is difficult for us, with 11 million people to serve in Illinois, to adequately view the extent of the problem in the much less populated states of the west. At the same time we have a 250,000 acre federal forest within our state, and we are aware of the tremendous pressure placed by the motorcycle industry for utilization of the federal lands in Indiana and their desire to move into Illinois.
In spite of this, we have a feeling that use of off-the-road recreational vehicles on some public lands is an accepted recreational activity. We view very apprehensively, however, the likelihood that pressure for use, and expansion of 'territory' will cause a legal or illegal use to be imposed upon state lands which may be adjacent to these larger federal properties in our midwestern states.
Implied in these comments is our feeling that the intensity of pressure will be applied more toward states like Illinois than toward the federal government because our properties are so much smaller, relatively, and because we have such dense concentrations of people.
TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROPOSED
In light of the above general comments and as a result of the proposal to provide technical assistance to a variety of agencies including state governments, it is desired that these demographic factors be considered in order, that promotion for the development of areas and facilities does not overburden state and local resources. The recent task force study promulgated by the Conservation Foundation proposed a recreation extension service, which if operated at the state level, would serve to bring unique factors such as those mentioned, into proper focus.

Comments from the Illinois Department of Conservation
on
Draft Environmental Statement
Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles
on the Public Lands
Submitted to: Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
August 8, 1972

The use criteria proposed appear to be very adequate. It is recommended, however, that whenever trails or areas are proposed that, wherever possible, controlled access be a prerequisite to the establishment of these areas. Because it is anticipated that guidelines for use of ORV's on federal properties will serve as guidelines to the states, it seems important that ramifications be considered because of expected greater intensity of use with greater numbers of people on smaller properties.
DESCRIPTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT & ENRIVONMENTAL IMPACTS
Much like the more restrictive conditions proposed to prevail on National Park Service lands, this is also desired when considering state lands and the smaller units of federal properties such as many of the Corps of Engineers reservoirs. Low pool stages of many federal reservoirs provide an additional possibility for minimum environmental damage except when concentrations of wildlife are present.
The fact that determination has not been made on what peak use will be, nor the extent to which the demand will continue to increase, and because of the lack of adequate research data on environmental degradation, it is our desire that limits be placed upon the extension of facilities available for use by ORV's. In the words of the Draft Environmental Statement, "No areas are really inaccessible anymore". It is anticipated that as we allow new areas and new types of uses to be allowed that even more severely harmful uses may be requested and/or experienced in the future.
Perhaps our most critical comment regarding the Draft Environmental Statement is that because we feel we are in the ORV business by default, that the Statement is designed to reduce adverse public relations effects by providing an abundance of positive reactions to CRV use. It is our feeling that ORV use in almost every situation is going to cause a deleterious effect on the environment. In our own activities in Illinois regarding use of state properties by snowmobiles, all terrain vehicles, metercycles, etc., we question seriously whether we are adequately exhibiting the responsibility we have in the proper stewardship of public lands. We question this as well in the federal context.
Again, quoting from your Statement, "Growth of public interest in ORV use has outstripped easy control of controversial impacts". You follow this statement saying, "The current thrust will be to alleviate this controversy by providing space for users and space for non-users and protection of the natural legacies several Interior bureaus are charged with". We feel this is a very dangerous practice which will result in naive public interest (pressure) or economic interests at the expense of the environment, causing an expansion of the system which will only serve to further damage existing natural resources. Limitations must be imposed. It is anticipated that funds derived from registration fees, etc. will be insufficient to provide adequate repairs for environmental damage, capital expenditures necessary to provide desired facilities,

and monies needed for administration and management: Our own experience has shown that enforcement necessary to control of ORV usage is the most serious of the problems, this in spite of the fact that our Department has even purchased snowmobiles for enforcement and maintenance purposes.
It is our feeling that enforcement problems would be reduced if areas rather than trails were provided.
ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED ACTION
Alternatives to the Draft Environmental Statement are perhaps the key to the necessity for the Environmental Statement. We agree the proposed alternatives are absolutely unsatisfactory. Therefore, the best thing expected to happen is that environmental concerns be studied with resultant action which will have the least environmental damage.
The State of Illinois, as the result of the initiative by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, anticipates the application of the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement to a review of our own properties as they may be affected by ORV use. We commend the Department of Interior for again setting the tone for proper management of public lands.

United States Department of the Interior
NATIONAL PARK SERVICE . WASHINGTON, D.C. 20240
マ8年

Memorandum
To:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Through: Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Notes &
From:
Assistant Director, Cooperative Activities
Subject: Draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation
of Executive Order 11644
We are pleased to send you our comments on the subject draft environmental statement in accordance with former Director Douglas Hofe Jr.'s memorandum of June 1.
However, before commenting on the draft statement, we offer the following comments on the Secretary of the Interior's memorandum of May 5 containing guidelines for use by Interior bureaus in preparing regulations to implement Executive Order 11644.
1. Page 3, b.(1), lines 6, 7 and 8: Thirty-six CFR 2.34[e] provides that a person under licensing age may operate an off-road vehicle (ORV) within a unit of the National Park System if he is supervised by a licensed operator of 21 years of age or more. A licensed operator may supervise only one unlicensed operator.
2. Page 3, b.(1)(a): The meaning of "reckless and careless manner" should be made as clear as possible in any proposed regulations. The National Park Service has attempted to do this in 36 CFR 4.14.
The following comments pertain to the draft environmental statement:
1. We suggest that comments or the draft statement also be solicited from the Advisory Council for Historic Preservation.
2. Page 9, line 9: Add "The Service is currently enforcing regulations pertaining to ORVs which appear in CFR Title 36."

3. Page 11: The section entitled <u>The Environmental Impact of the Proposed Action</u> would be more effective if the positive and negative consequences were segregated.
4. Page 12, 2nd paragraph, 2nd and 3rd sentences: We believe that these two sentences should be modified to read "Many areas are accessible and available to public use every season of the year and all hours of the day."
5. Page 12, 3rd paragraph: We suggest evidence be submitted to support the claim that ORVs "can strengthen family ties."
6. Page 13, line 1: We suggest that "ORV" be inserted between "by" and "user" for further clarification.
7. Page 16, last paragraph: This paragraph lists beneficial effects of ORV use by recreationists and by land managers. We question the value of ORV use for protection of forests from fire. Where wild land fire from natural causes is recognized as a natural ecological process, there is no advantage in allowing ORV use under the guise of fire protection. Back country fires may be approached more rapidly and effectively with helicopters.
8. Page 24: The section entitled Any Adverse Effects Which Cannot Be Avoided Should The Proposal Be Implemented is so general that it lacks substance. It should be strengthened by listing and discussing specific negative effects.
9. Page 26, VIII, A): The text should recognize that National Park System lands are protected from uncontrolled ORV use by existing legislation, policies and regulations, and therefore, would be affected little or not at all by the proposed action. Also, for the sake of balance and completeness, positive economics and social benefits, as well as negative effects, should be identified and discussed.
10. Page 29, VIII C): This section also should identify and discuss possible economic and social benefits.
In addition to offering the above specific comments, we wish to express our concern about lack of attention to protection of historic (including archeological and paleontological) resources. We believe that Section 2(b) of Executive Order 11593 of May 13, 1971, must be observed in contemplating use of ORVs on federally-owned lands. Section 2(b) requires that certain cautionary steps be taken to assure that no historic resources worthy of preservation and nomination to the National Register of Historic

Places will be inadvertently damaged or destroyed. We believe that the subject statement should indicate whether compliance with E. O. 11593 will be assured during implementation of E. O. 11644.
Also, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 (P.L. 89-665) requires certain procedures prior to any Federal action that might affect a property listed in the National Register of Historic Places. We believe that the subject statement should indicate whether compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act will be assured during implementation of E. O. 11644.
We appreciate having an opportunity to review the subject draft environmental statement, and we offer you our comments in a spirit of assisting you in complying with requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
Thereor Q. Swern

I have recently had the opportunity to review your letter of May 5, 1972, instructing your assistant secretaries of Public Land Management, Fish and Wild Life and Parks, and Water and Power of departmental policy on off-road vehicle use on federal lands.
I have great concern that in implementing the President's Executive Order 11644, dated February 8, 1972, that consideration of local and state government needs will be ignored by your administrators. I feel that unless the needs and desires of the local people are given proper consideration, that eventually Congress will step in and prescribe off-road management practices for all federal land managing agencies.
I look forward to you advising your staff of this important need.
Sincerely,

conditional.summary: The Oregon Environmental Council generally commends the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation's impact statement on ORV use, praising its fairness and the restrictions placed on National Parks. However, they raise two main objections: the statement lacks enforceable noise standards (recommending a maximum of 73 decibels at 50 feet), and they oppose the 'monitor after the fact' approach to determining ORV compatibility with land resources, insisting that studies be conducted before ORV use is permitted in any area.
conditional.statementText:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
We wish to commend the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation for its fair and well-developed impact statement dealing with the Off Road Vehicles (ORV) problem. With a few exceptions the statement reflects the concerns we as conservationists share toward the use of the ORV.
We are particularly pleased with the policy established for ORV use in the National Parks. We are impressed by the restrictions and would encourage the BOR to place this type of control on all lands. However, we realize the ORV is here to stay and no matter how strongly we object, the ORV users have a right to use the public lands. They have a right to use them, but not destroy them. We hope the Department of the Interior controls can prevent any destruction.
There are two areas, however, that we must object to and encourage revisions in the policy. The first is the treatment of noise. The statement recognizes that there is a real problem, but makes no effort to minimize the levels. The most stringent statement concerning noise is found on page 5. "An ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The problem here is that there is no indication as to what is considered excessive so enforcement would be extremely difficult.
The problem of noisy ORVs, particularly snowmobiles, is regarded as one of the greatest problems with the vehicles. The Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission says, in its publication "Snowmobiling in Washington State" that "Probably the greatest concern relating to snowmobiles is noise encroachment in a naturally quiet environment." Here is where ORV users encroach upon the rights of other recreation users. How noisy are these machines? The level of the snowmobile is about 112 decibels at the operator's ear. That is over standards set up under Walsh-Healy

Letter to Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. July 6, 1972 Page 2
18
for a 30-minute per day period. At 50 feet the noise level is about 86 decibels, which is just below the maximum for an eight hour period. Not too many non-users will suffer hearing loss from these machines but the noise levels at which they operate certainly indicates they could do a rather thorough job of destroying the peace and quiet of an outdoor area.
Why are these machines not quieter? A Conservation Foundation publication by Malcolm F. Baldwin entitled "The Off-Road Vehicle and Environmental Quality" attributes the reason to what the American buyer wants. Industry representatives say they could be made half as noisy but they would not sell. The Oregon Environmental Council recommends that BOR establish stringent noise restrictions in order to force the ORV industry into using a quieter machine. We suggest a maximum level of 73 decibels at 50 feet. This will not alleviate the problem by any means but it will help control it and possibly cut down the antagonism between ORV users and other more traditional recreation users.
Our second main objection to the statement is found on pp. 12-13. Reference is made to the negative environmental impact on the areas. Mention is made of the difficulty of determining the levels of use compatible with the resource. The method of determination is to monitor effects of ORV use on the lands to discover this data. We find this unacceptable. Extensive studies should be made of the areas before ORV use is allowed. If the monitor method is implemented, once it is found that the ORV is non-compatible with the resource, it will be too late. This determination must be made before ORV use is allowed.
Page 7 of the report discusses public review of the area policies before implementation. This would be a good time to conduct these studies to determine if use is compatible with the area. We commend the BOR for allowing public review and we encourage them to follow through with this proposal.
The Oregon Environmental Council is very concerned with the ORV problem and the potential damage they can cause to the environment. Generally we approve of the impact statement but encourage that there be:
. More stringent noise restrictions on the vehicles; and
. Better review before allowing the vehicles into an area.
Sincerely,
(Larry Williams
Executive Director

conditional.statementText:
Alaska Conservation Society
Box 80192 College, Alaska 99701
July 6, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
US Department of the Interior
C Street Between 18th and 19th
Washington, D. C. 20240
Subject: Comments on Interior DES 72-62 RE: Draft Environmental Impact Statement: "Proposed Departmental Implementation of E. O. 11644 Pertaining to Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands".
Dear Sir:
The Alaska Conservation Society appreciates the spirit and philosophy behind E. O. 11644 establishing the basis for departmental control of off-road vehicle use on all of our public lands. Because of the vast proportion of Alaska's lands within the public domain, and because of the present and potential damage to the tundra and boreal forest ecosystems, and their wildlife resources, we are anxious to see that strong regulations are promulgated.
The Draft Environmental Impact Statement prepared by your Bureau applies to all Interior Agencies, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, National Park Service and the Bureau of Reclamation. Because of the importance of these agencies in the management of Alaska's public lands, we offer the following comments for your review and consideration.

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Two
1. The draft environmental impact statement appears to be generally poorly written and fragmentary. The mention of various "impacts", both environmental and economic, and both positive and negative, is poorly developed and little or no attempt is made to relate these impacts to one another quantitatively. The discussion of the economic impacts of ORV is useless, as well as fragmentary throughout the entire document. The concept that ORV use could aid in strengthening family relationships, mentioned several times in the statement, is undocumented and, in truth, use of ORV by young people may contribute to the destruction of the American family that has paralleled the evolution of the automobile.
2. The Preamble to E.O. 11644 refers specifically to "recreational" vehicles. The subsequent statements refer to off-road vehicles without the qualifier "recreational". The regualtions should apply to all vehicles, including official use by governmental agencies, etc. Throughout Alaska, much of the damage done by ORV is the direct result of mineral and petroleum exploration, government-sponsored surveys, forestry activities and construction equipment. It is essential that these uses be adequately regulated, in addition to recreational uses. We recognize that the use of ORV for emergency fire or law enforcement and other such purposes may be needed, however, the increasing use of aircraft in these cases may soon preclude much of the ORV use.
3. Since the issuance of E.O. 11644, considerable confusion has arisen concerning whether lands will be classified as "open unless otherwise designated" or "closed unless otherwise designated". The statement partially clarifies this problem by stating that Wilderness and Primitive Areas are closed, and that trails and areas will be established in National Parks, Monuments, Natural Areas, and National Wildlife Refuges and Ranges only if the Bureau head so decides.
However, the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Reclamation lands appear open to access unless closed (except for Bureau of Land Management Primitive Areas). The

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Three
The statement is made in Memorandum K-14 that "Areas and trails shall not be located in areas possessing unique natural, wildlife, historic or recreational values unless the Bureau head determines that these unique values will not be adversely affected". This statement is not referred to in the outlining of the Bureau of Land Management's responsibilities in DES 72-62, thus leaving the criteria for Bureau of Land Management classification vague.
4. Although various criteria are mentioned by which Bureaus will establish open and closed areas, no mention is made of the unique Alaskan tundra and Boreal forest permafrost regime. In summer, ORV travel on permafrost-underlain areas can be severely destructive, as permafrost, once thawed, may never reform. Travel over a deep winter snowbed is less destructive, although compression of the snow layer and thin vegetative mat may result in damage to the plant covering. Although research into this possible damage is still continuing, it may be possible to open some areas in winter, and close them the remainder of the year. This technique has proven somewhat effective on the North Slope of Alaska.
I realize that the above comments are, by no means, a comprehensive criticism of DES 72-62. However, I hope our suggestions will result in an improved, stronger statement and policy for use of ORV on our public lands.
Sincerely,
ALASKA CONSERVATION SOCIETY
Ernst Mueller President

conditional.statementText:
State of Wisconsin \ DEPARTMENT. OF NATURAL RESOURCES
L. P. Voigt Secretary
July 10, 1972
BOX 450 MADISON, WISCONSIN 53701
IN REPLY REFER TO: 1600
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation US Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Re: Draft Environmental Impact Statement (Int. DES 72-62)
We have completed reviewing the draft environmental impact statement for the proposed "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to the Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands" -- Int. DES 72-62.
This statement appears to represent a reasonable appraisal of off-road vehicles and their potential impact on public (federal) lands. However, we submit the following comments for your consideration.
The use criteria and the operating criteria are desirable but they are general and more detailed standards should be developed to permit effective enforcement. Comments on adverse effects of off-road vehicles should also contain some documentation as to source of reference. Because of the broad scope of the proposed program and the diverse public lands involved the actual environmental impact of the proposed action on Executive Order 11644 will be difficult to determine. As pointed cut in the draft environmental impact statement, the most difficult ranamment assessment will be the determination of use levels which will be compatible with the resource base and which will still provide the type of recreation sought by the user group. While the monitoring of effects is desirable entreme caution should be used in the original decision to permit vehicles on the various types of public lands.
The physical and biological impacts are well presented in the proposal. The human impacts have been fairly well presented. However, our Eureau of Correctal Recreation believes that the snowmobile in Wisconsin is carrying a greater share of the off-road vehicle impact at the present time. In the area of human impacts there will continue to be tremendous conflict between motorized and non-motorized interests.
Some of the problems identified in the draft statement will apply to both motorized and non-motorized users of public land (i.e. littering, signing for public information, erosion, etc.)

2.
Point 2 of the Assistant Secretary's program policy states that technical assistance will be provided to all Interior bureaus, other federal agencies, states and their local governments, and the private sector in coordinating planning and programming for the development of areas and facilities for the use of off-road vehicles. This is the only place in the program proposal where the private sector is mentioned. We feel that more attention must be given to the private sector in planning for these vehicles. Off-road vehicle programs on private lands can have a significant impact (both beneficial and adverse) on public lands. Perhaps a companion program can be developed to assist the private sector in coping with off-road vehicles.
Point 3 discusses public information. This section should be broadened to include commercial facilities.
The draft statement does not include a discussion on inventory and demand. This is an important part of the broad program policy and should be considered in the final statement. The proposal indicates that each bureau of the Department of the Interior will be charged with locating areas that can stand the development of off-road vehicle facilities and then conceivably these bureaus could proceed with independent development. Executive Order 11644 requires development of a well-coordinated and planned program at the Assistant Secretary's office to get away from a piece-meal approach to public land development.
A statement is made on page 21 that additional resources will be needed to designate areas, develop facilities, post signs and conduct enforcement. This is an important part of program planning but the impact statement does not contain information on how these critical needs will be met.
Because of the growing interest and concern relating to off-road vehicle use public agencies will be required to concentrate more effort on the private sector for satisfying the demand of the more environmentally damaging recreational activities. The multiple use concept of land use has certain advantages where there is a tremendous amount of public land available and where various activities can be segregated for optimum use. In areas where public land is at a premium, the private sector may be the logical place for certain recreational activities.
The off-road vehicles is undoubtedly a permanent addition to the recreational industry. We agree that the opening or closing of all Interior Department lands to off-road vehicle use would be an undesirable solution to the current problem. We support the program policy whereby the Assistant Secretary of the Department of the Interior would be responsible for reviewing and coordinating off-road vehicle use activities on Interior lands.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this draft environmental impact statement.
Very truly yours,
Bureau of Environmental Impact

We support the program policy whereby the Assistant Secretary of the Department of the Interior would be responsible for reviewing and coordinating off-road vehicle use activities on Interior lands.

conditional.quote: We are in general agreement with the objectives of the statement which would restrict the use of off-road vehicles on lands administered by the Department to ensure that such use, where permitted, would be compatible with other uses, and would not result in significant adverse environmental impact or cause irreversible damage to existing ecological balances.
conditional.summary: The FCC generally agrees with the objectives of the draft environmental statement restricting ORV use on public lands to prevent environmental damage. However, the Commission expresses concern that the regulations adequately provide for access by common carriers and Commission licensees who maintain communications facilities on public lands, ensuring that vital communication circuits can be constructed, operated, and maintained at all times. The FCC also requests clarification that governmental inspection and investigatory operations involving off-road vehicles will be explicitly exempted from the proposed restrictions.
conditional.statementText:
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION WASHINGTON, D.C: 20554
IN REPLY REFER TO:
9400
Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary, United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
This concerns the draft environmental statement prepared by the Department of the Interior's Bureau of Outdoor Recreation and dated May 26, 1972. The statement proposes regulations for use of motorized off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The Commission wishes to avail itself of the opportunity extended on June 2, 1972 (37 F.R. 11078) to comment on the draft environmental statement. We are in general agreement with the objectives of the statement which would restrict the use of off-road vehicles on lands administered by the Department to ensure that such use, where permitted, would be compatible with other uses, and would not result in significant adverse environmental impact or cause irreversible damage to existing ecological balances.
The proposed regulations would implement Executive Order 11644 which appears to have been prompted primarily because of the rapidly increasing use of off-road vehicles such as minibikes and snowmobiles for recreational purposes. However, the restrictions appear broad enough to be applicable as well to motorized vehicles used for business or other non-recreational purposes. Accordingly, we are concerned that provision be made so that common carriers and others who have wire, cable or radio communications facilities on public lands pursuant to land-use permits may have reasonable access to such facilities, to whatever extent may be necessary or desirable, in connection with the construction, operation and maintenance of such communications facilities. In this connection, we note that any vehicle whose use was expressly authorized by an agency head of the Department under a permit, lease, license, or contract would be exempt from the proposed use restrictions on off-road vehicles. However, it is not apparent whether existing or future authorizations for use of Department lands for

communication requirements by common carriers and Commission licensees would include authority for use of off-road vehicles necessarily incidental to construction, operation, and maintenance of the necessary communication facilities.
As you are aware, communication facilities on or traversing public lands often provide vital public and national defense communication circuits. Continuity of such service is dependent upon immediate access to the lines and other facilities at all times. Further, spurious emissions from radio transmitters could cause destructive electrical interference to communication requirements of others, including harm to common carrier circuits which the Commission is charged with protecting from such interference. It is also possible that such interference could pose risks to safety of life and property.
The foregoing public interest considerations are merely illustrative of those with which the Commission may be concerned and are not intended to encompass all such considerations which we may properly consider in discharging our statutory responsibilities.
Such responsibilities are discharged, in part, via inspections and investigations by Commission employees and other governmental agents in the field, often involving the off-road use of motorized vehicles. It would appear that such operations would be exempt from the proposed restrictions in light of the provision excepting law enforcement vehicles. We believe it imperative that it be made clear that such governmental inspection and investigatory operations will be exempted.
In short, the Commission wishes to stress the necessity for ensuring that whatever regulations are finally promulgated restricting off-road uses of vehicles, adequate provision be made to ensure that vital communication requirements are capable of being duly satisfied at all times.
This letter was adopted by the Commission on July 6, 1972. Commissioner Nicholas Johnson concurring in results; Commissioner Benjamin Hooks absent.
BY DIRECTION OF THE COMMISSION
11.1
Chairman

The International Association of Geophysical Contractors is deeply concerned with the probable impact of your May 5, 1972 Memorandum to the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, for Fish and Wildlife and for Parks and Water and Power Resources as concerns implementation of Executive Order 11644.
The Draft of the Environmental Statement by the Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation expended most of his wordage specifically at damages of all varieties which may and now are being consed by motocycles and snowmobiles. Finally on Page 25 he states
"The Department's proposed action makes provision for the demands of other rightful users of the public lands;"
Our culture is dynamic largely because of the technological advantages attained because of reasonably available energy. Approximately a third of the land and water surface of the United States is controlled by your Department. For years geological and geophysical investigations impart for education purposes but primarily for the economic discovery of hydrocarbons, uranium and other metals and waters both drinkable and superheated have been conducted on public lands and waters under your Department's regulations. These operations have been in harmony with other rightful users. The discoveries and development of our mineral resources is a National Necessity.

24
In the third paragraph of your Memorandum you exempted
"any registered motorboat; any military, fire, emergency, or law enforcement vehicle; farm type tractors and other selfpropelled agricultural equipment when used exclusively for agricultural purposes; any self-propelled equipment for harvesting and transportation of forest products or for earth moving or construction while being used for these purposes;"
We now urge that you also exempt geological and geophysical equipment when used for their designed purposes so that there will not be misunderstandings in the future.

conditional.quote: We definitely support recent presidential action directing federal agencies to establish policies regarding ORV use on their public lands.
conditional.summary: The Kentucky Program Development Office expresses conditional support for federal ORV regulation, endorsing the presidential directive to establish ORV policies on public lands while also supporting exclusion of ORV use from wilderness, primitive areas, national parks, and wildlife refuges. They suggest opening certain lands to ORV use on a demonstration basis under close supervision until more questions about environmental effects are resolved, and recommend parental guidance and manufacturer cooperation as complementary measures.
conditional.statementText:
Kentucky
Program Development Office
The Capitol
Frankfort, Kentucky 40601
Wendell H. Ford Governor
July 31, 1972
2.3 Y
Mr. James G. Matt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Reference: Implementation of Presidential
Executive Order 11644 (K14)
Dear Mr. Watt:
It is apparent that Kentuckians are contributing to the national popularity of comparison and subsequent use of off-road vehicles (ORV). For comparison, our state licensing records reveal a four-fold increase in ORV licensing for use on public roadways since 1960, from 6,944 to 29,451. To license an ORV for such use the owner-operator must be at least 16 years of age. We have no indication of the number of vehicles not licensed. There is no evidence that their popularity may be leveling off.
ORV use in Kentucky State Parks is generally permitted on park roads open to automobile and camper traffic, within established safety regulations. ORV use in Kentucky State Forests is generally discouraged. The City of Louisville, Kentucky Park Board recently rescinded an earlier decision permitting ORV use in certain designated park areas because of serious destruction of the natural environment. The State Attorney General's Office has ruled that public park roads are in effect public roads, and therefore, state licensing requirements for ORV operation must be enforced. The operator under 16 years of age is placed at a certain disadvantage.
We definitely support recent presidential action directing federal agencies to establish policies regarding ORV use on their public lands. The increased popularity of the ORV accompanied by apparent pressure for a place to ride certainly warrants this action. By definition, ORV use must legitimately be given a position among outdoor recreation activities and must be considered in terms of total demand.
We further support the policy that ORV use not be permitted on wilderness or primitive areas, and we encourage the federal agency heads to recommend a similar policy for the national parks and national wildlife refuges and game areas. Since our federal govern-

335
Letter to Mr. Watt Page Two July 31, 1972
ment already owns approximately 30 percent of all the land in the United States, and an even greater percentage in the Western United States, it would seem that sufficient land for ORV use could be located so as to not encroach upon parks and wildlife areas.
In the interim, until many of the questions can be resolved regarding the effects of ORV use on public lands, we suggest that consideration be given to opening certain lands to ORV use on a demonstration basis under close supervision and management. We also suggest that government leaders seek the cooperation of manufacturers concerning the operating features of the ORV. However, there is really no substitute for parental guidance and restraint in the teenager's selection of an ORV, with individual as well as the public interest in mind.
Thank you for the opportunity to review the subject environmental statement. We certainly want to be kept up-to-date on the policies established regarding ORV use on federal lands. If further state coordination is desired this office will be pleased to provide assistance.
Sincerely yours,
L. W. True
Administrator
