conditional.role: Manager, Bruneau Dunes State Park, Idaho
conditional.quote: I strongly feel that some major guidelines, in addition to those stated in the draft, are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use.
conditional.summary: Bryan W. Rowder, Manager of Bruneau Dunes State Park, supports the draft's goals but argues that stronger guidelines are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use. He recommends excluding ORVs from designated Wilderness, Primitive, National Park, Wildlife Refuge, and Game Range areas; capping total ORV-designated land at 0.5% of each state's public land; requiring organized groups with agency supervision for trail use outside designated tracts; and imposing a minimum 15% federal tax on ORV equipment to fund development, maintenance, and enforcement.
conditional.statementText:
Dear Sir:
I have reviewed your draft environmental statement on executive order 11644 pertaining to use of ORV on public lands. Along with other public land managers who have dealt closely with ORV users. I recognize that you have carefully defined the problems in regard to existing and potential ORV impacts. However, I strongly feel that some major guidelines, in addition to those stated in the draft, are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use. I have four basic recommendations:
1. The statement on page 4, section iv, smould be changed to read, "treas and trails shall not be located in officially designated Wilderness areas, Primitive areas, National Parks and Monuments, National Wildlife Refuges, and Game Ranges."
2. The total public land area designated for ORV use should not exceed 0.5% of the total public land area of each state. Why? Here are three main reasons: 1) ORV sales are increasing at a fast rate. To delay making strong restrictions is to promote more sales and later cause an economic hardship to the expanded industry. 2) Irreversible land damage will occur. 3) The effects of CRV use negates the effects and raises the costs of tax-supported conservation programs.
3. The areas designated for intensive CRV use should be in tracts not less than ten square miles, with good natural or man-made boundaries. Trails outside of the tracts can be designated for CAV use. Such trails may be used only by organized groups of ten or more people who have registered with the land manager and who are accompanied by an agency representative on the trail who acts as guide, interpreter, and enforcer.
4. To finance the development, maintenance, and manpower necessary for these projects, a federal tax should be imposed on all DRV and related equipment. The minimum tax on retail value should be 15,00
Sincerely,
Bryan W. Rowder, henager Bruneau Dines State Fork

mentions.quote: I strongly feel that some major guidelines, in addition to those stated in the draft, are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use.
mentions.basis: supports ORV regulation but calls for stronger guidelines including strict area limits and federal tax on ORV equipment

conditional.quote: We question whether ORV should be used at any time or place where they would cause damage and disturbance of land, wildlife or vegetative resources.
conditional.summary: The Division of Wildlife (Denver, Colorado) conditionally supports ORV management but raises serious concerns about allowing any damage to land, wildlife, or vegetative resources, questioning whether ORVs should be permitted anywhere they cause such harm. They critique the draft statement's use of vague or permissive language (e.g., 'excessive' damage, 'minimized' impacts) and argue that bonding and fee mechanisms are inadequate substitutes for preventing irreplaceable resource loss. They recommend stronger coordination with state wildlife agencies, clearer definitions, and that the final statement include a controlled-use alternative.
conditional.statementText:
DIVISION OF WILDLIFE
Harry R. Woodward, Director 6060 Broadway
Denver, Colorado 80216 • 825-1192
August 10, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
We have reviewed the May 26, 1972 statement entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on the public lands" prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation. We have made some general observations and several specific comments.
The statement reiterates and possibly reinforces the policies and procedures established by Executive Order 11644, use of off-road vehicles on the public lands. Unfortunately, the Executive Order is directed to the Secretary of Interior alone; we believe the Order should be expanded to include the Secretary of Agriculture and possibly other appropriate land management agencies. We further feel that coordination could best be accomplished by the Department of Natural Resources. We also believe that comments from national conservation organizations should be solicited.
SPECIFIC COMMENTS
Page 3 - (2) I question whether all lands, both open and closed for use, should be designated. Why not just those open, this would lead to less signing, mapping and administration. Signing all lands could cause visual pollution.
The several states have laws which allow them to control the harassment of wildlife.
98

Mr. James G. Watt August 10, 1972 page 2.
Page 4  (iii) Determine the effect of the use of areas and trails of ORV on private lands adjacent to public lands.
Page 5  (Operating Criteria) A specific explanation of the meaning of "than conditions warrant" is needed.
We question whether ORV should be used at any time or place where they would cause damage and disturbance of land, wildlife or vegetative resources.
(d) Allows damage and qualifies the damage by inserting the word "excessive" which is purely judgemental.
Page 6  (2) We still question the wisdom of allowing even minimal damage. Assuming that minimum damage will be allowed we would like to see wildlife specifically mentioned.
Bonding a permittee so as to insure adequate moneys for restoration and rehabilitation of trails and areas used is an extremely questionable procedure: 1. There could be an irreplaceable loss to the resource,
2. The cost of restoration and rehabilitation would be measured monetarily with no consideration given to elapsed time for restoration,
3. No consideration for the destruction of a quality environment,
4. Estimate of costs would necessarily be judgemental, and 5. Administrative procedures would be cumbersome, i.e. how long would a permittees bond or deposit be held, would it be deposited and draw interest, would the interest be collected by the permittee or the federal government, etc.
We feel that it would be extremely difficult to assess an appropriate fee as authorized under the provisions of the Land and Water Conservation Fund Act. How much would be charged? Would the fee be charged before or after the rally or contest? Would the money collected be used for restoration in the area destroyed or would it go into a general fund and be spent in another area?
Continued citation of other executive orders, organic acts and laws without describing their purpose is not extremely enlightening. Perhaps attachment to the environmental statement of all the executive orders and rules and regulations cited would be beneficial.
The method proposed by the Bureau of Land Management for the administration of ORV use is incisive, comprehensive and appears to be a good solution.

Page 11  (U. S. Bureau of Reclamation) Who determines which regulations are appropriate?, the Bureau of Reclamation or the federal or non-federal agency, or a combination?
Page 12  "ORV do limited damage to the human environment, etc."
Possibly "limited" should be defined; preferably ORV should be limited to areas where no damage would be caused.
Page 13  (Physical Impact) Statement that damage could be "minimized" should read the damage could be "eliminated."
Page 16  We agree with the philosophy of prohibiting ORV in certain wildlife areas. Hopefully, this can be accomplished in close coordination with the state wildlife agencies.
There should be a definition of "established roadways."
Page 17 - (Human Impacts) Snowmobiling in the Great Lakes States probably cannot be compared with snowmobiling in the Western States.
We doubt whether there is a direct correlation between the use of ORV and economic enhancement.
Page 18 - We also doubt that in areas where ORV are prohibited, a negative impact will result.
The paragraph on ORV experience is purely conjecture. As you describe the exhilarating feeling you should also describe the feeling of sheer terror - in other words, feelings are highly individualized. Perhaps the incidence of snowmobile-auto accidents should be related. Crossing of highways is highly hazardous.
Page 19 - We agree noise levels must be reduced and standards rigidly enforced.
We agree that the proper procedure is to specify designated areas of use for ORV vehicles.
The Section on Human Impacts sounds like it was written by a PR man for ORV, not that we totally disagree with most of the statements; the thrust is one of promotion rather than attraction.

Page 23  Who will provide the technical assistance to all Interior Bureaus, and other federal agencies, etc.
Page 24  Land, water, air, wildlife, etc., need not always be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Page 28  We are not certain that the Department of Interior should be relied upon by private enterprise to support the economy of an area.
Page 30  More emphasis should be placed upon the interaction at the interface of the public lands with the non-public lands.
The draft environmental statement should contain the alternative of controlled use within the statement.
Sincerely,
Harry R. Woodward
Director

Spicer, writing on behalf of Florida's Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations, supports strong controls on off-road vehicles and recommends prohibiting driving off established roads except on a few small designated tracts deemed suitable by the Department of Interior. He notes that Florida does not require a driver's license for off-road vehicle operation, suggesting a federal permit system with fees for enforcement and land renovation would be more appropriate. conditional.statementText:
Dear Mr. Douglas:
Functioning as the state planning and development clearinghouse contemplated in U. S. Office of Management and Budget Circular A-95, we have reviewed the following draft environmental impact statement prepared by U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Ourdoor Recreation:
Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public Lands (K-14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
During the course of our reivew, we have referred the environmental impact statement to the following agencies, which we have identified as interested in the environmental effects of the project or in developing or enforcing standards relating to these effects: Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund; Department of Community Affairs; Game and Fresh Water Fish Commission; Department of Legal Affairs; Department of Natural Resources; Department of Pollution Control; Department of State - Division of Archives, History, and Records Management, Department of Transportation - Division of Transportation Planning and Programming; Central and Southern Florida Flood Control District and the Environmental Information Center.
Agencies were requested to review the statement and comment on the adequacy of treatment of environmental matters of their concern, additional alternatives which should be considered, and project modifications or special control measures to reduce or avoid adverse environmental effects. Agencies comments follow: The Department of Community Affairs suggests that alternate B in the statement be adopted and offers other comments which should be considered. See attached letter. The Department of Legal Affairs suggests that a test program to control off-road vehicles be instituted on a limited bas s; the Department offers comments on several other portions of the statement which should be considered. See attached letter. Letters endorsing the proposal or offering no adverse comments on the proposal and statement from the following agencies are attached: Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund; Game and Fresh Water Fish Commission; Department of Natural Resources; Department of State - Division of Archives History, and Records

Mr. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Page 2 August 14, 1972
Management; and Department of Transportation - Division of Transportation Planning and Programming. No response was received from the Central and Southern Florida Flood Control District. The final environmental impact statement should adequately consider each point of concern contained in the attached letters from the Department of Community Affairs and Department of Legal Affairs.
This statement was discussed at a conference held by the staff of the Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations on July 14. See attached conference agenda and attendance list. It was pointed out at the conference that, whereas item b(i) on page 5 of the statement states that a person must have a state driver's license or learner's permit to operate an off-road vehicle on Interior Lands, the State of Florida does not require a driver's license to operate a vehicle off public roads. Therefore, it may be more appropriate to require a federal permit to operate an off-road vehicle on federal lands. Further, the Department may wish to consider charging a fee for such a permit: revenues derived could be used for enforcement and land renovation. We believe strong controls on off-road vehicles to be much needed and recommend that driving of any vehicles off established roads be prohibited, except on a few small tracts of land which may be determined suitable and designated for off-road vehicle use by the Department of Interior. Our concern about off-road vehicles is due to the severe ecological damage caused by off-road vehicle in recent years in South Florida. Effects of off-road vehicles on our land is distinguishable on nearly any recent low altitude aerial photograph taken in the Big Cypress Swamp or Everglades region of the State.
Please append a copy of this letter, with attachments, to the final environmental impact statement submitted to the Council on Environmental Quality. This will assure the Council of our compliance with guidelines implementing the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (PL 91-190).
We request to be forwarded one copy of the final environmental statement submitted to the Council on Environmental Quality, and, in the letter of transmittal, refer to the SPDC number assigned this statement.
Sincerely,
Don L. Spicer
Chief
Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations

conditional.quote: In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
conditional.summary: Henry N. Barkhausen, Director of the Illinois Department of Conservation, commends the Department of the Interior for the comprehensive Environmental Statement and ORRV Task Force Study, but expresses serious concerns about ORV use on public lands. He argues that ORV use has been imposed by default rather than design, that the statement is overly promotional of ORV use at the expense of environmental stewardship, and that enforcement and resource degradation problems are severe. He calls for strict limitations on ORV area expansion, controlled access, and careful consideration of how federal guidelines will pressure smaller state properties with denser populations.
conditional.statementText:
State of Illinois
DEPARTMENT OF CONSERVATION
Springfield 62706
RICHARD B OGILVIE
HENRY N. BARKHAUSEN DIRECTOR
August 8, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Director Watt:
It is with pleasure the Illinois Department of Conservation responds to your invitation to review the draft "Environmental Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-the-Road Recreation Vehicles".
In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
We do, however, have several comments regarding the Statement which I am attaching to this letter.
Sincerely,
Henry N. Barkhausen Director
.0

The Illinois Department of Conservation in general has felt that recreational opportunities which are not particularly dependent on natural resources should more appropriately be provided by local government rather than state or federal government. Our feelings have been based more with consideration to state owned lands of this Department than in the context of the federal properties. We feel that, in general, the types of recreational experiences provided to the public should proceed from a strong natural resource orientation to a less strong natural resource orientation as one proceeds from the federal to local levels of government.
Our feelings are that the imposition of off-the-road vehicles on public lands has been more by default than by design. The tremendous increase, however, in production and use of off-the-road vehicles has brought us to a point in time where it will be very difficult to step back and prohibit use of these vehicles in all cases even though there are many instances where they seem to exhibit a disharmonious factor with major objectives and uses of lands involved, particularly those uses which are more traditional. We may be exhibiting the polarization in viewpoints here, representing the more resource-oriented opinions, as discussed in the Task Force Study; however, it is difficult for us, with 11 million people to serve in Illinois, to adequately view the extent of the problem in the much less populated states of the west. At the same time we have a 250,000 acre federal forest within our state, and we are aware of the tremendous pressure placed by the motorcycle industry for utilization of the federal lands in Indiana and their desire to move into Illinois.
In spite of this, we have a feeling that use of off-the-road recreational vehicles on some public lands is an accepted recreational activity. We view very apprehensively, however, the likelihood that pressure for use, and expansion of 'territory' will cause a legal or illegal use to be imposed upon state lands which may be adjacent to these larger federal properties in our midwestern states.
Implied in these comments is our feeling that the intensity of pressure will be applied more toward states like Illinois than toward the federal government because our properties are so much smaller, relatively, and because we have such dense concentrations of people.
TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROPOSED
In light of the above general comments and as a result of the proposal to provide technical assistance to a variety of agencies including state governments, it is desired that these demographic factors be considered in order, that promotion for the development of areas and facilities does not overburden state and local resources. The recent task force study promulgated by the Conservation Foundation proposed a recreation extension service, which if operated at the state level, would serve to bring unique factors such as those mentioned, into proper focus.

Comments from the Illinois Department of Conservation
on
Draft Environmental Statement
Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles
on the Public Lands
Submitted to: Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
August 8, 1972

The use criteria proposed appear to be very adequate. It is recommended, however, that whenever trails or areas are proposed that, wherever possible, controlled access be a prerequisite to the establishment of these areas. Because it is anticipated that guidelines for use of ORV's on federal properties will serve as guidelines to the states, it seems important that ramifications be considered because of expected greater intensity of use with greater numbers of people on smaller properties.
DESCRIPTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT & ENRIVONMENTAL IMPACTS
Much like the more restrictive conditions proposed to prevail on National Park Service lands, this is also desired when considering state lands and the smaller units of federal properties such as many of the Corps of Engineers reservoirs. Low pool stages of many federal reservoirs provide an additional possibility for minimum environmental damage except when concentrations of wildlife are present.
The fact that determination has not been made on what peak use will be, nor the extent to which the demand will continue to increase, and because of the lack of adequate research data on environmental degradation, it is our desire that limits be placed upon the extension of facilities available for use by ORV's. In the words of the Draft Environmental Statement, "No areas are really inaccessible anymore". It is anticipated that as we allow new areas and new types of uses to be allowed that even more severely harmful uses may be requested and/or experienced in the future.
Perhaps our most critical comment regarding the Draft Environmental Statement is that because we feel we are in the ORV business by default, that the Statement is designed to reduce adverse public relations effects by providing an abundance of positive reactions to CRV use. It is our feeling that ORV use in almost every situation is going to cause a deleterious effect on the environment. In our own activities in Illinois regarding use of state properties by snowmobiles, all terrain vehicles, metercycles, etc., we question seriously whether we are adequately exhibiting the responsibility we have in the proper stewardship of public lands. We question this as well in the federal context.
Again, quoting from your Statement, "Growth of public interest in ORV use has outstripped easy control of controversial impacts". You follow this statement saying, "The current thrust will be to alleviate this controversy by providing space for users and space for non-users and protection of the natural legacies several Interior bureaus are charged with". We feel this is a very dangerous practice which will result in naive public interest (pressure) or economic interests at the expense of the environment, causing an expansion of the system which will only serve to further damage existing natural resources. Limitations must be imposed. It is anticipated that funds derived from registration fees, etc. will be insufficient to provide adequate repairs for environmental damage, capital expenditures necessary to provide desired facilities,

and monies needed for administration and management: Our own experience has shown that enforcement necessary to control of ORV usage is the most serious of the problems, this in spite of the fact that our Department has even purchased snowmobiles for enforcement and maintenance purposes.
It is our feeling that enforcement problems would be reduced if areas rather than trails were provided.
ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED ACTION
Alternatives to the Draft Environmental Statement are perhaps the key to the necessity for the Environmental Statement. We agree the proposed alternatives are absolutely unsatisfactory. Therefore, the best thing expected to happen is that environmental concerns be studied with resultant action which will have the least environmental damage.
The State of Illinois, as the result of the initiative by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, anticipates the application of the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement to a review of our own properties as they may be affected by ORV use. We commend the Department of Interior for again setting the tone for proper management of public lands.

conditional.quote: Our plea, therefore, is for designating most areas "open," then managing the use based on resource capability and on increased capacity resulting from proper design, maintenance, and other management practices.
conditional.summary: Harmston, writing on behalf of the Utah Department of Natural Resources, agrees with the EIS's identification of ORV impacts but argues that most public lands should be designated 'open' and then managed according to resource capability and improved management practices rather than defaulted to closure. He acknowledges that intensified management will require additional resources but warns that failing to do so would underutilize public lands and neglect a legitimate public need. He also recommends that states be required to play a role in ORV regulation on public lands, citing Utah's own comprehensive ORV Act as a model.
conditional.statementText:
Dear Mr. Watt:
This is in response to a request from your office, which we received on June 19, 1972, for comments on a draft environmental statement concerning use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
We duplicated the information sent us and distributed it to agencies representing a variety of resource and user interests. A meeting with representatives from each of these agencies was held July 11, 1972 to discuss the statement and their respective comments. Some agencies unable to attend the meeting are sending us their comments. We hope to summarize this information and send it to you by the last week in July. We will have many specific comments to make at that time; but would like to give you our general impression of the environmental statement now.
We agree with the E.I.S. in terms of the existing and potential impacts identified in relation to use of ORV's on public lands. We note, however, that many existing and traditional uses of these lands do similar, if not worse damage, if not properly managed. Our plea, therefore, is for designating most areas "open," then managing the use based on resource capability and on increased capacity resulting from proper design, maintenance, and other management practices.
We recognize that intensified management will require additional manpower, training, and funding. To do less, however, will be to under utilize our resources and to fail to meet a justifiable public need.
The State of Utah has recently passed a comprehensive Off-Road Vehicle Act which addresses itself to many of the problems mentioned in the Executive Order and in the environmental impact statement. Our experience to date leads us to recommend that you require state involvement in ORV regulation on public lands. Copies of our regulations will be sent with our more detailed comments.

conditional.summary: Robert L. Shevin, as Florida's Attorney General, argues that the draft EIS inadequately evaluates the alternative of prohibiting ORV use entirely and fails to quantify the economic effects of such a prohibition. He contends that given the acknowledged irreversible environmental damage and insufficient data on ORV impacts, it would be more prudent to initiate a limited test program rather than implement controlled ORV use across all public lands. During any such test program, ORV use should be restricted to established roadways, and the public lands' role as a retreat from urban noise and annoyance should be carefully protected.
conditional.statementText:
TALLAHASSUE, PLOUIDA, 3290-1
August 7, 1972
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
State Planning and Development Clearinghouse
Department of Administration
725 South Bronough Street
Tallahassee, Florida 32304
Re: U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Outdoor Recreation: Draft Environmental Impact Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands (K14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
Dear Mr. Still:
The following are comments on the draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The general approach to the regulation of off-road vehicles on
public lands, as delineated in the proposed Impact Statement, appears
to be adequate and comprehensive, assuming that one agrees with the\nunderlying policy.
The President's Executive Order 11644 and the Memorandum from Interior Secretary Morton to various assistant secretaries appear to assume that off-road vehicles will be permitted to use public lands off established roadways. The entire draft statement addresses itself to minimizing the damage or conflict caused by the use of these vehicles off established roadways. It assumes that there should be allowed certain damage or conflict with the present activities that exist on these lands.
As a result of this policy choice, the draft statement attempts to make a case for the use of such vehicles, rather than fully evaluating the alternative of prohibiting such use. For example, on page 28 of the draft there is a statement that prohibiting

completely the use of these off-road vehicles on public lands would result in "effects on economic sectors which are presently influenced by current demand for and production of off-road vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near bepartment lands where off-road vehicle use takes place."

The would seem that the more important consideration here should be the tagnitude of impact on the economic sector as opposed to the rare presence of an effect. The amount of the economic effect is not ordinanted in the draft, and so one cannot evaluate the significance of any negative economic effect. On page 29 of the draft statement, there is a statement that
closing all Department of Interior lands to ORY use would constitute an action inconsistent with the Department's responsibility to maintain certain of its lands for the enjoyment and inspiration of the general public. It would, likewise, not be consistent with the Department's mandate to encourage the broadest possible mix of compatible multiple uses on certain of its lands— multiple uses which include recreation among the primary potentials and ORV use being a primary sounce of enjoyment to significant numbers of recreationists.
The draft does not discuss the bases for these conclusions. A policy or maintaining certain lands for the enjoyment and inspir tion of the general public hardly requires the use of areas off established roadways by off-road vehicles. Certainly, the Department does not allow all desired uses of its lands which may be sujoye le to certain members of the public. The necessity of evaluating competing uses of the land and determining acceptable uses must often come before the Department. The proposal to permit off-road vehicle use of public lands would seem to be one of those instances requiring an evaluation of competing and conflicting uses. The draft statement does not adequately treat this fundamental question.
In regard to the alternative of allowing off-road vehicle use of public lands, it seems highly questionable from comments in the draft statement that such use is a wise one. At page 12 of the draft, it is stated that whether operated properly or improperly, ORV can cause irreversible and irretrievable harm to man and the environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates that 0 W use will have an adverse effect on wildlife. The adverse effects of encessive noise from ORV on humans and wildlife are outlined at page 19.

Page 3
Part V of the draft statement, at page 24, states that
Even though the net effect of implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memoraneum would be a reduction in the adverse impact on human and natural values, there are certain continued unavoidable adverse effects.
* * *
Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Noise levels will be discomforting to some users of public lands.
Historical and archeological structures may be changed or destroyed by ORV use.
These conclusions are reiterated at page 26 in part VII, of the draft entitled "Tracversible and Irretrievable Commitments of Resources Which Would be Involved in the Proposel Action Should It be Implemented".
In addition to the above concerns and effects, the draft statement observes, at page 13, that there is less than satisfactory data available in regard to the impact of ORV on the lands in question. Therefore, I would suggest that instead of instituting a program of controlled ORV use throughout the Nation's public lands system, it would be more prudent to initiate a test program on a very limited basis. Such a program would facilitate monitoring and data collection, would not require the commitment and expenditure of large sums of money for additional policy and enforcement (see page 21 of draft statement), and would enhance the ability of the Department of Interior to fully evaluate ORV use on public lands. During the operation of such a test program, ORV use of public lands should be limited to established readways.
With the increase in the metropolitan style of living and all the attendant noise and pressure associated with that life, it seems that the public lands are playing an increasing role in providing

Page 4
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
the public with a retreat from the type of noise and annoyance associated with ORV. We should be reluctant to facilitate the intrusion onto those lands by urban sources of noise and annoyance, and so should scrutinize carefully any proposal for CRV use of public lands.
Sincerely
ROBERT L. SHEVIN Attorney General

conditional.quote: EDF supports the controlled use of off-road vehicles (ORV) on public lands in order to protect its resources.
conditional.summary: The Environmental Defense Fund conditionally supports controlled ORV use on public lands, emphasizing that public recreational use must be secondary to protecting wildlife resources and ecological integrity. EDF calls for careful determination of use levels, including regulation of ORV events and rallies, as well as attention to noise, traffic, and litter impacts. They also urge continued bureau supervision of open lands and meaningful public participation before designating areas as open or closed to ORVs.
conditional.statementText:
ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND
1712 -1910 N STREET, N.W., WASHINGTON, D.C. 20036/202 833-1485
July 6, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Sir:
The Department of the Interior has circulated for comment a draft impact statement on proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands. As a national membership organization of scientists, lawyers and concerned citizens, the Environmental Defense Fund takes this opportunity to submit our remarks.
EDF supports the controlled use of off-road vehicles (ORV) on public lands in order to protect its resources. We recognize the Department's responsibility in managing the use so as not to create an adverse environmental impact or cause irreparable damage to existing ecology. We feel, however, that public use is secondary to protecting and perpetuating wildlife resources. Although the growth of public interest in ORV makes its own controversial impact, primary concern should still be the environment.
EDF feels that the determination of use levels, including recreational benefits, is crucial to the environmental impact of the proposed action. Specifically, the determination of where and how often, if at all, ORV events and rallies should be conducted. It seems that the adverse effects of such events would be damaging to the public as well as to the land itself, unless properly regulated. In order for ORV recreational use to be "safe" for the environment, responsible determination should be made as to the physical impact on susceptible land forms. Also, noise control and the problem of increased traffic and litter are primary areas of our concern.
In implementing Executive Order 11644, those ORV activities and uses which may cause irreparable harm to ecological balances must be fully evaluated. The Department's draft impact statement carefully delineates the situations it anticipates facing with respect to ORV control and use. However, if public lands are to be "open" to off-

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Page Two July 6, 1972
road vehicles, then continued supervision of these lands by the various bureaus is essential. We also hope that public participation is encouraged and solicited before declaring a land "open" or "closed" to the public.
The Environmental Defense Fund appreciates this opportunity to submit our comments for your consideration.
Respectfully submitted,
23
Roberta Danzansky
Administrative Assistant

conditional.quote: these non-recreational uses must be addressed to provide strict control if E011644 is to have any meaning in Alaska
conditional.summary: The Fairbanks Environmental Center argues that the draft EIS is too vague regarding BLM land management responsibilities and fails to adequately address non-recreational ORV uses (such as military, commercial, and government activities) that are particularly damaging to Alaska's fragile tundra and permafrost ecosystems. They call for strict controls on all ORV uses—recreational and non-recreational alike—and insist that no ORV use should be allowed in existing or future Alaskan national parks and monuments. They also request that the revised statement more accurately reflect Alaska's unique ecological conditions and clarify the 'open until closed' versus 'closed until opened' question for BLM lands.
conditional.statementText:
MEMORANDUM 
July 6, 1972
TO: Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, United States
Department of the Interior
FROM: J.A. "Jim" Hunter, President, Fairbanks Environmental Center, Inc.
SUBJECT: Comments on "Department of Interior Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands" and the BOR "Draft Environmental Statement"
The Fairbanks Environmental Center, Inc. is a membership organization "dedicated to protection of the quality of the Alaskan environment through education and action." It is a community organization which addresses itself primarily to environmental problems and concerns of interior and arctic Alaska.
I wish to be brief and helpful in these remarks. I feel that the draft statement omits too many problems which are peculiar to the vast Public Domain lands in Alaska which are particularly subject to ecological and other damages by both recreational and non-recreational uses of ORVs.
It is not possible from your draft to determine whether public lands—especailly those within BLM management—are open to uprestricted CRV use until administratively closed, or the reverse situation. The Center wishes to ask you to revise your statement to reflect this lack of clarity in EOl1644. We also wish to call your attention to the time necessary for public input prior to the actual promulgation of regulations governing the use of ORVs in certain areas of BLM lands.
In Alaska we also have considerable use and/or potential use of ORVs by military personnel for non-military use. We have large tracts of lands under U.S. Forest Service management for commercial timber. We have learned that our interior forests are of interest to the U.S.F.S., and that they will be opened to lumbering. U.S.F.S. use of ORVs could be intensive

Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page 2
in our interior. We fail to see by your draft how E0116 will be interpreted to control this non-recreational use. Our fragile tundra and its associated eco-systems on these public lands are very easily damaged.
We also suggest that your draft drop all discussion of economic impacts. You have done little or nothing to quantify and interrelate these with the environmental impacts which such assessments are to deal with.
We find your statements suggesting ORV use may strengthen family relationships to be absurd in the extreme and without any evidence. In this part of Alaska the very opposite effect in the use of ORVs--particularly the snowmobile--is likely to be closer to the truth.
As suggested earlier, we are particularly concerned with non-recreational uses of ORVs as you treat them in your draft. In Alaska, construction off highways, private and government surveys, and mineral and petroleum explorations as well as subsistence hunting and fishing, firefighting, and law enforcement are current and/or potential uses for ORVs.
We must impress upon you that 1) these non-recreational uses must be addressed to provide strict control if E011644 is to have any meaning in Alaska, and 2) that the use of aircraft here in Alaska is extensive, including for work such as law enforcement, seismic surveys and firefighting (ORVs cannot and should not replace the aircraft for such tasks here, and your draft should reflect this.).
We also very strongly feel that no ORV use should be administratively--or in any other way--allowed, encouraged or even suggested in our existing Alaskan national park, national monurents, or future national parks.
SUMMARY: To summarize, the scope of your draft confines itself too much in tis exclusion of non-recreational ORVs, and it is too vague as to BLM responsibilities as regards "open until closed" or vice versa. It also fails to define policy regarding public input for this particular BLM administrative responsibility.

Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page 3
We also wish a revised statement to more accurately reflect the particular Alaskan tundra-boreal forest systems which characterize the vast Public Domain lands of Alaska. ORV damage to these due to our unique permafrost condition can be severe, regardless of whether caused by recreational or non-recreational use, and by commercial, non-commercial, government or private ORV use. Strict control and enforcement procedures must be clearly defined in your discussion of E011644.
I sincerely hope that these comments will be useful in helping the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation revise and improve its environmental impact draft statement.
JH:jh

conditional.summary: David W. King, as New Mexico's State Planning Officer, conditionally supports ORV use on public lands, provided that strict restrictions and enforcement mechanisms are put in place to prevent indiscriminate abuse of natural resources. He recommends that all lands be designated either closed or open with restrictions, with no areas left entirely unrestricted, and that noise levels be regulated with specific decibel limits and penalties for violators. He also emphasizes the need for inventorying lands suitable for ORV use and protecting historical and archaeological sites from ORV damage.
conditional.statementText:
SANTA FE
DFFICE OF DIRECTOR
July ]2, ]972
Mr. Thomas Watts, Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
United States Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watts:
We were pleased to review the draft environmental statement of off-road vehicles. The need for this statement is evident due to the increased interest in this type of recreational activity.
We have carefully studied the proposed statement. We are highly concerned with the use of off-road vehicles on open lands since a large portion of New Mexico consists of these type of lands.
We hope our comments and recommendations will benefit your planning process. Thank you for providing this information to us.
Sircerely,
David W. Kirg
State Planning Officer
DWK:CLM:eg
1. 45

OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES
The need for an environmental statement involving off-road vehicular use has been essential with the widespread use and evident interest across the country. An established policy to protect natural resources and users of public lands will help eliminate further problems that could have had early solutions.
The proposal as described in the environmental statement of off-road vehicles (ORV) appears to indicate positive direction for this type of mechanized use on public lands. Coordination of involved land use agencies toward implementing consistent and comprehensive ORV policies is a key factor in establishing a compatible program. Highest priorities must be given to minimize abuse of natural resources and conflicts with other public land users. Policies should allow use only with the enforcement of rules and regulations.
If we are to accept ORVs on public lands, we must face the responsibilities of protection and safety of all public land users. An effective policing procedure must be implemented. Control must be organized and established to eliminate conflicts and avoid abuse. The "Operating Criteria" are excellent; however, these regulations will need enforcement to penalize violators of designated ORV lands. We endorse stringent penalties of ORV abusers—these abusers only jeopardize ORV use for nonviolators.
In order to achieve the stated purpose of Executive Order 11644, several components must be implemented. A review of existing restrictions and rules regulating ORV use on public lands would be highly feasible.

Additionally, lands compatible to ORV use could be easily identified

through this type of inventory. All lands should be designated as CLOSED TO ORVs or OPEN MITH RESTRICTIONS ON ORVs. Some lands may not be suitable and others may be opened for limited ORV use. No lands should be open without restrictions. Future research may indicate revision in our present conception of a particular land use. To designate an area without restriction would open the land to unlimited ORV abuse. Lands open to ORVs with restrictions would allow an area to be closed when use impairs environmental values.
In reference to the "adverse effects which cannot be avoided should the proposal be implemented", we believe that some of the stated adverse effects can be avoided. For example, most non-ORV user groups would not resent concentration of ORVs in certain areas if the areas were located in places where conflicts would not occur. The proposed inventory of existing potential ORV lands could supply information of lands that are separated from non-ORV user groups. Most objection to ORV land use lies in the indiscriminate vehicle noise levels and abuse to land. Secondly, noise levels do not necessarily have to be discomforting to users of public lands. Noise levels coupled with land damage by ORVs need drastic and immediate action to retain any semblance of a quality daily existence for living plants and animals. A noise level allowable could be specified by the establishment of an acceptable decibel reading. Violators should be fined or penalized. Continued violations would cause loss of license to operate an ORV. Lastly, historical and archeological structures need not be destroyed by ORV use. These sites could be inventoried and designated as areas "off-limits" to ORVs. Further study of additional adverse effects may be necessary prior to opening lands to ORVs with controls.
1/5 In summary, we are not opposed to ORV land use; however, some

restrictions must be established to avoid indiscriminate abuse of public lands. Certain areas must be identified and maintained for ORV use without conflict to other public land users. The need of these types of areas cannot be overlooked. If demand and interest indicates the need for an ORV area, the site should be provided where feasible. Prior to designation of such an area, thorough examination of all related factors and conflicts must be completed. With this type of planning, land use provisions of off-road recreational vehicles can be established to the satisfaction of the majority of public land users.
45

STATE OF NORTH CAROLINA
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATION
GOVERNOR
W. L. TURNER
W. L. TURNER
DIRECTOR
STATE PLANNING DIVISION
RONALD F. SCOTT
STATE PLANNING OFFICER
REPLY TO:
CLEARINGHOUSE AND INFORMATION CENTER 116 WEST JONES STREET RALEIGH, N. C. 27603 (919) 829-4375
July 13, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U. S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Re: Draft Environmental Statement for the Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to the Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands - File No. 80-72
We have completed our review of the subject draft environmental statement, which was transmitted by your letter of June 1, 1972.
On the basis of our review and the comments of other State agency representatives who have reviewed the statement, we have no comments relative to the assessment of environmental effects of the proposed action, and consider the statement adequate.
The North Carolina Recreation Task Force, an inter-agency committee which provides policy direction for recreation planning and establishes priorities for the allocation of Land and Water Conservation Fund grants, has adopted the following goal as stated in "Goals of North Carolina Outdoor Recreation Planning," published May 5, 1970: "In order that public funds be used efficiently, it is the goal of the State that all levels of government work cooperatively and without duplication to meet North Carolina outdoor recreation needs identified in the Plan (State Comprehensive Cutdoor Recreation Plan). To this end, this Plan, and its subsequent ammendments, will be used as a basis for evaluating, assigning priorities, and endorsing projects of Federal, State and local Government."

In keeping with this goal, we submit for your consideration the following recommendations for implementation of Executive Order 11644:
1. Heads of the various land managing bureaus and agencies within the Department of the Interior should contact and coordinate with the applicable regional office of the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation in developing regulations regarding ORV use.
2. Heads of these bureaus and agencies, in developing regulations governing the use of ORV on lands within their jurisdictions, should coordinate with the applicable Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP) for the purpose of: 
a. Assuring that such regulations are in compliance with the SCORP.
b. Providing input data (location, size, etc.) concerning "open" areas for inclusion in the SCORP inventory and information system.
c. Affording SCORP planners the opportunity to help formulate regulations and establish criteria for the use of ORV. It is felt that this would mutually improve the "state of the art" at Federal, State and local levels regarding the techniques and methods for determining and understanding the impact of ORV.
d. Maximizing the satisfaction of recreation needs identified in the SCORP.
Sincerely yours,
- Bhalliers
RANDOLPH HENDRICKS
Planning Coordinator

conditional.quote: The one aspect of the proposal which both the State and Wyoming based federal administrators point to as the key to success is that the proposal must be based on the philosophy that all areas will be considered open to use until circumstances and conditions develop which would merit specific action to the contrary.
conditional.summary: Governor Hathaway expresses Wyoming's strong concern about the proposed ORV regulations, emphasizing that the key to success is an 'open until closed' philosophy where all areas are presumed open to ORV use unless specific conditions warrant closure. He argues this approach has worked well in Wyoming and provides the flexibility needed for successful administration across diverse regions. Given that nearly 50% of Wyoming's land is federally owned, he stresses the state's substantial interest in ensuring the proposal supports major economic activities like mineral exploration, agriculture, hunting, and fishing.
conditional.statementText:
WYOMING. EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT CHEYENNE
STANLEY K. HATHAWAY
GOVERNOR
July 20, 1972
The Honorable Rogers C.B. Morton Secretary of the Interior U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
The State of Wyoming is quite concerned regarding the proposed rules and regulations to be established by the Department of the Interior concerning the use of off-road vehicles.
Federal consideration and thinking on this proposal was first officially brought to our attention at a recent Wyoming and federal Recreation Action Team meeting and subsequently when the State was given the opportunity to review the Draft Environmental Statement on the subject.
The one aspect of the proposal which both the State and Wyoming based federal administrators point to as the key to success is that the proposal must be based on the philosophy that all areas will be considered open to use until circumstances and conditions develop which would merit specific action to the contrary. This open until closed philosophy has successfully been used in Wyoming for pears and by its continuance we feel that enough flexibility will be built into the proposal to allow for successful administration in Wyoming as well as the highly populated areas east of the Mississippi and on the west coast.
As you know, almost 50 per cent of the surface land of this state is owned by the federal government, and this land will obviously be directly affected by this proposal. Major activities such as mineral exploration, agriculture, hunting and fishing and all general outdoor recreational activities directly and substantially

The Honorable Rogers C.B. Morton Page 2
July 20, 1972
affect Wyoming's economy and our way of life. Thus, we feel we have a substantial interest in the initiation and success of this proposal.
Thank you for your consideration of this matter.
With best wishes, I am
Sincerely yours,
MISYL

conditional.role: Interior Department bureau, cooperating agency reviewer
conditional.quote: We have reviewed the subject draft statement. Enclosed are our comments which indicate areas in which additional clarification or information would aid in assessing the impacts of the proposed action on the environment.
conditional.summary: The Bureau of Land Management reviewed the draft environmental impact statement and offered detailed comments requesting additional clarification and information on several fronts. BLM noted that the statement focused too narrowly on recreational ORV use, called for clearer criteria and definitions, and requested more accurate description of BLM's own proposed planning-based approach to ORV management. The agency also provided numerous specific editorial and substantive suggestions to improve the accuracy and completeness of the document's environmental analysis sections.
conditional.statementText:
We have reviewed the subject draft statement. Enclosed are our comments which indicate areas in which additional clarification or information would aid in assessing the impacts of the proposed action on the environment.
he laye
Enclosure

General Comments
The statement generally focuses in the impacts of recreational use of ORVs on the public lands. The statement should recognize that ORVs have an impact whether they are associated with the recreational or other authorized uses. The impacts of failing to administer ORV uses uniformly should be discussed.
There is a diverse variety of environmental impacts which can occur as a result of the various types of ORV (dune buggy vs. snomobile), and the terrain (desert vs. tundra). Additional discussion of the impacts of the various types of ORV and their impact on different type of terrains would be helpful.
The "use" and "operating criteria" identified in the statement appear to be a reiteration of the criteria identified in Secretary's memo to implement Executive Order 11644. They are very general in nature. The statement is not clear whether these are the only criteria Interior agencies will use to identify use and operation of ORV or whether the various agencies will develop more specific criteria to implement the Executive Order. If this section is meant merely to quote the Secretary's memo, that should be clarified.
The statement should clarify the interim status of all Interior lands prior to designation of ORV use areas. Will they be open or closed to ORV use? What effect will this have on the human environment?

Specific Comments
I. Description of the Proposal.
If the .criteria for "use" and "operation" provide a guide for more specific criteria to be developed by each Interior agency the following is suggested:
Page 4. a). The heading indicates criteria for official use may by different from that of the public. Establishment of "double standard" can raise questions as to its appropriateness. Search and rescue, firefighting, or other types of administrative duties may require exceptions. Official use should generally comform with the constraints placed on the public.
(iv). "Areas and trails shall not be located on officially designated Wilderness Areas or Primitive Areas." Should the exclusive language of this section be modified to provide for administrative determination with full public input?
Page 6. (iv). Should running lights, etc., be allowed as an alternative to taillights? Dune buggies, for instance, do not use taillights since they cannot be seen by other vehicles. At night they are marked by a light carried atop a fiberglass staff.
"All applications for permits for such ORV events shall be submitted no less than four months, or a lesser amount of time ..." The four months acts as a constraint on advance notice. In many cases, six months or more prior to an event, may be desirable.
If the criteria for "use" and "operation" are the only criteria to be used by Interior agencies to regulate ORV use a more definite description of terms such as, "minimize", "excessive", "unique", etc., should be provided.
11. Description of the Environment.
The discussion of the implementation of EO.11644 seems out of place. It's the BLM alternative in approaching management of ORVs. The statement is not an accurate description of the proposed BLM regulations as now drafted.
Addiscussion of the BLM proposal should include the following information: "BLM through its planning system will identify areas for ORY use and the stipulations which will guide such use. Through the planning system all resource values will be identified. Areas which present an opportunity for ORV use as well as those in need of protection from ORV will be identified.

The public will be presented this information. They will be requested to provide additional information on resources or environmental values requiring protection as well as the needs and opportunities for ORV use. BLM will then analyze the information provided by the public, information it has previously identified, and conflicts which exist between resource uses and identify areas to be closed and stipulations governing ORV use which will insure maintenance of environmental quality.
In the case of commercial use of ORVs, the statement should indicate:
"Commercial use e.g., races, rallies, etc., of the public land will
be allowed only on those areas designated as suitable for ORV use
by the planning system and an environmental analysis which indicates
there will be no serious degradation of the environment. The\nenvironmental analysis will be used to indicate the need for
stipulations to protect both the public and environmental values
during the event".
Page 11, first sentence. "Low vegetative production potential" should not be a controlling factor in ORV trail selection. Properly laid-out and managed trails can be successful in timber or other vegetated areas. In fact, heavy vegetation often helps confine the vehicles to the trails and good vegetative potentials can help heal environmental wounds.
III. Environmental Impacts of the Proposed Action.
Page 12, last sentence, paragraph 2, appears to conflict with first sentence, paragraph 5. In one sentence, it is stated that properly operated ORVs do limited damage; in the other sentence, it states that even when properly operated, impacts may be great and, in many instances, irretrievable. The last sentence of the paragraph could be re-worded as follows: "In most areas, ever where properly operated and managed, ORVs are capable of serious damage..." The third paragraph should also be re-worded to read: "In all areas ..." rather than "In some areas ...".
Paragraph 4. Would this paragraph be more appropriate in Section VII?
The following sentences describe mitigating measures which would appear to be more appropriate in Section IV.
Page 13. Paragraph 3  last two sentences.
Page 15. Paragraph 2  last two sentences.
Page 16. Paragraph 2  last sentence.
Page 18. Paragraph 3  last sentence.
Page 19. Paragraph 2  last sentence.

Page 20. All of paragraph 2 and paragraph 3, last sentence.
Page 21. Paragraph 1  last sentence.
Page 13 A) Physical Impacts. The discussion provided appears to contradict the last sentence in paragraph 1 on page 12. The following re-wording would eliminate this contradiction: First paragraph, third sentence "Prohibition ... would prevent further impact...". Paragraph 2, fourth line, change "impaction" to "compaction".
Page 14. Line 3 from the bottom. Change "increase" to "vary". 
Page 15. Paragraph three, third and fourth sentences suggest the following: "A few animals will be killed by ORV use. Some will be temporarily driven from their natural habitat and others will adjust to the presence of the vehicles".
Page 16. Line 3. Change "accomodate" to "tolerate".
Third paragraph, last sentence. Discusses the advantages of increased fire-spotters and fire fighters as a result of ORV use. It should be noted that increased incidence of fire caused by the ORV users may be much more hazardous and costly than the benefits provided by the increased number of fires detected and extinguished.
Page 18. Line 2. Change "negative" to "adverse".
Page 20. Line 5. Could be re-worded as follows: "Increased ORV accidents, litter, and sanitation...".
Paragraph 2, the discussion of designation and signing techniques identifies a multitude of problems. Notifications of restrictions of use requires authority for enforcement. Signs, a basic tool of notification, create a visual impact which cannot be minimized. Guidance is needed. Standardization of signs, with a readily identifiable format, will help the user making it possible to use smaller individual signs.
Page 21. Third line from the bottom, change "of" to "to".
V. Any Adverse Effects Which Cannot be Avoided should the Proposal be Implemented.
The adverse effects of the BLM's lack of authority or manpower to efficiently and effectively implement the Executive Order should be identified and discussed.

VIII. Alternatives to the Proposed Action.
The effects the various alternatives will have on the incidence of fire could be discussed. For example, no action can be expected to result in an increase in fires from campfires and sparks from overtaxed exhaust systems, requiring increased fire protection; closing all Interior lands will result in a reduced incidence of fire; and opening all Interior lands could be expected to result in a corresponding increase, similar to no action, in the incidence of fires.
Page 30, paragraph 4, first sentence. Will fewer trespass problems result from opening lands to ORV? Less ORV trespass may result, but there will probably be an increase of related activities such as illegal occupancy, antiquity trespass, etc.

conditional.quote: Responses from review in this office and our field offices indicated general concurrence relative to adequacy of the subject statement. We suggest, however, that further consideration be given to Subsection III of the operating criteria pertaining to noise control.
conditional.summary: The Bureau of Reclamation generally concurred with the adequacy of the Draft Environmental Statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644. However, it recommended that Subsection III of the operating criteria on noise control be strengthened by replacing the vague phrase 'unusual or excessive noise' with more definitive provisions to ensure reasonably uniform application.

United States Department of the Interior
BUREAU OF RECLAMATION 
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20240
IN REPLY 420 REFER TO: 120.1
JUL7 1572
Memorandum
To:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
From:
Commissioner, Bureau of Reclamation
Subject: Draft Environmental Statement for the Proposed
Implementation of Executive Order 11644
Responsive to your memorandum of June 1, 1972, the subject statement has been distributed in accordance with the Secretary's notice of availability dated May 26, 1972.
Responses from review in this office and our field offices indicated general concurrence relative to adequacy of the subject statement. conditional.quote: The State Planning Office strongly feels that off-road vehicle restrictions should not only apply to federal lands, but certainly to State lands as well.
conditional.summary: The New Mexico State Planning Office, having coordinated review with multiple state agencies, found the draft environmental statement well-prepared and adequate in presenting ORV impacts. They strongly support implementing restrictions on off-road vehicles and believe those restrictions should apply not only to federal lands but to state lands as well. They also emphasize that the regulations must be strictly enforced.
conditional.statementText:
STATE PLANNING OFFICE
SANTA FE
OFFICE OF DIRECTOR
August 9, 1972
Mr. Thomas Watts, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20204
Dear Mr. Watts:
In reference to your draft environmental statement of off-road vehicles, I have coordinated a careful study of this document with the Department of Game and Fish, the State Park and Recreation Commission, the State Land Office, and the Division of Recreation and Historic Preservation of the State Planning Office, and have the following comment to offer.
It is felt that your statement is well prepared and adequately presents the impact of off-road vehicles on recreation, wildlife, and preservation. It is further felt that certain restrictions must be implemented on all off-road vehicles, as well as the various terrains involved, to minimize the indiscriminate abuse of public lands; and moreover, that these regulations be strictly enforced.
The State Planning Office strongly feels that off-road vehicle restrictions should not only apply to federal lands, but certainly to State lands as well. For your additional information, actions that the State of New Mexico has taken concerning off-road vehicle travel is enclosed.
Thank you for allowing us to review your draft statement. If I may be of additional service on this or any other matter please feel free to contact me anytime.
Sincerely,
David W. King
State Planning Office
DWK/CK/nt

conditional.entity: AMA-Motorcycle Industry Council Combined Committee on Land Use
conditional.quote: This statement by the Task Force reflects very accurately the feeling of the American Motorcycle Association, and of the AMA-Motorcycle Industry Council Combined Committee on Land Use.
conditional.summary: The AMA-MIC Combined Committee on Land Use is referenced within the AMA's letter as sharing the view that a comprehensive, scientifically-based land classification system is needed to ensure fair and equitable ORV use on public lands. The committee is actively working to hire a professional ecologist to develop clear guidelines for land use, acknowledging that some public land may be lost to ORV use but expressing willingness to cooperate. Their position is conditional — supporting ORV access where scientifically justified, while accepting reasonable restrictions based on evidence.
conditional.statementText: This statement by the Task Force reflects very accurately the feeling of the American Motorcycle Association, and of the AMA-Motorcycle Industry Council Combined Committee on Land Use. This committee, composed of delegates from the AMA and the MIC, presently is reviewing resumes by professional ecologists. The group has resolved to hire one of these gentlemen for the purpose of establishing guidelines in a very comprehensive and clear textbook fashion. Through such a set of guidelines we hope to establish fair and equitable use of the land, knowing full well that some public land will be lost to the use of off-road recreational vehicles, yet with the feeling that our effort to cooperate will be returned by those with other interests.
