conditional.quote: Arctic firmly supports the position of the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) as set forth in the comments submitted on behalf of the ISIA by Patton, Boggs, Blow, Berill, Brand & May, as counsel for the ISIA.
conditional.summary: Arctic Enterprises, Inc., the largest U.S. snowmobile manufacturer, endorses the ISIA's comments and argues that different types of ORRVs must be classified and regulated individually rather than as a single class. They contend that snowmobiles are environmentally distinct from other ORRVs because they travel over snow covering dormant vegetation in winter, causing minimal lasting damage, and therefore more areas should be open to snowmobiling in winter than to other ORRVs in other seasons. They also call for the development of uniform, meaningful safety performance standards for snowmobiles in cooperation with the industry.
conditional.statementText:
June 28, 1972
Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
Re: Notice of Availability of Draft
Environmental Statement (Int Des 72-58)
Gentlemen:
The following comments are submitted on behalf of Arctic Enterprises, Inc., (Arctic) in response to the Notice of Availability of Draft Environmental Statement (Int Des 72-58) published in the Federal Register, Volume 37, No. 107 on June 2, 1972.
Arctic is the largest manufacturer of snowmobiles in the United States and second worldwide only to Bombardier, Ltd., the Canadian manufacturer of the Ski Doo and Motor Ski snowmobiles. Arctic also produces a line of mini-bikes, another type of off-road recreational vehicle (ORRV). Arctic produced over 110,000 snowmobiles during the 1972-73 snowmobile season.
Arctic firmly supports the position of the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) as set forth in the comments submitted on behalf of the ISIA by Patton, Boggs, Blow, Berill, Brand & May, as counsel for the ISIA. There are however, a few points that we believe need to be stressed.
Arctic believes that the various types of ORRV's <u>must</u> be classified and considered on an individual basis due to their differences in use, effects on other users of a particular area and the effects on the environment itself. A snowmobile travels over the temporary medium of snow. Underlying the snow is the <u>frozen</u>, dorment vegetation and ground. In contrast, other ORRV's travel over and can easily adversely affect the soft spongy ground, as in the Spring, and the growing plant life. In addition, during the winter months the areas are free of migratory birds and the hibernating animals.

Department of the Interior Page #2
June 28, 1972
Some ORRV's greatly damage the vegetation over which they travel and this damage is readily apparent to the eye while in most instances one cannot spot in summer the paths snowmobiles took the previous winter. While snowmobiles change the appearance of the landscape by leaving tracks in the snow, there is not sound evidence that there is any permanent adverse affects on the underlying vegetation. Snowmobilers have damaged seedlings and small shrubs, but we believe this is a matter that can be handled through education and restricting snowmobiles from those areas that are susceptible to such damage.
Arctic does not advocate the summer use of snowmobiles, since the vehicle is not designed for such use. If snowmobiles are fitted with wheels or otherwise modified for use on mediums other than on ice or snow, it is our position that they <u>must</u> be classified during those months of use with the other ORRV's that are similarly used and have similar effects.
Additionally, snowmobiles are used in the winter months when the competition for the use of any land area is at a minimum. Consequently, more areas should be open for snowmobiling in the winter than for an ORRV use during the other season.
Snowmobiles are not alone in the need for classification of ORRV's. Campers, for instance, should be allowed in certain areas where motorcycles and dunebuggies are prohibited for obvious reasons.
In order to insure safe use of snowmobiles on public lands, uniform safety performance standards must be developed and enforced. The current state standards are underdeveloped and inconsistent one with the other. The Department of Interior is the logical agency to work with the industry to develop meaningful standards since it will understand the vehicle, the conditions of its use and will be charged with the responsibility of controlling the enforcement of the snowmobile use and required safety equipment. The safety and machine operating requirements in the Draft Environmental Statement, are rudimentary and must be greatly expanded upon to insure safe operation on public lands.
8

To summarize, our position, all ORRV's cannot and must not be grouped together as a class. To do so would be to contravene the intent and the words of Executive Order 11644 and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963.
Very truly yours,
ARCTIC ENTERPRISES, INC.
Roger P. Worth Legal Counsel

mentions.quote: Arctic firmly supports the position of the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) as set forth in the comments submitted on behalf of the ISIA by Patton, Boggs, Blow, Berill, Brand & May, as counsel for the ISIA.
mentions.basis: Supports ISIA position; objects to grouping all ORRVs together; demands individual classification of vehicle types

conditional.quote: We would again, as we have before, join in the ORRV Report recommendation for a comprehensive inventory and classification of the public lands and the extension of the police power to all those lands.
conditional.summary: The California Outdoor Recreation League strongly criticized the Draft Environmental Statement for contradicting the earlier ORRV Task Force Report, which had recognized off-road vehicle use as a legitimate recreational activity and acknowledged the lack of sufficient data to justify restrictions. The League argued that the DES unfairly singled out recreational ORV users while exempting logging trucks and other off-road vehicles, and that it failed to provide any retention of off-road vehicular activity as a matter of elementary fairness. Conditionally, they supported a comprehensive inventory and classification of public lands with extension of police power to all those lands, so that responsible users would not be penalized for the actions of an outlaw minority.
conditional.statementText:
CALIFORNIA OUTDOOR RECREATION LEAGUE, Inc.
Non-Profit - Statewide
The United Voice For Active Outdoor Recreationists
4264 EAST FLORENCE AVENUE BELL, CALIFORNIA 90201 AREA CODE 213 - 773-6260 AREA CODE 213 - 585-0581
June 22, 1972
Department of the Interior Office of the Secretary Washington, D.C. 20240
Gentlemen:
We have the letter of June 14 from Deputy Assistant Secretary Lyons together with enclosures, and we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Draft Environmental Statement (DES) proposed for Departmental implementation of Executive Order 11644.
We have reviewed the Off-Road Recreation Vehicle Task Force Study Report of March 15, 1972 (ORRV), and we find that the differences between that thorough study, for which we would compliment the Department and those who prepared it, and the DES difficult to reconcile.
The entire thrust of the ORRV Report is that the off-road vehicle user has a right to use and enjoy the public lands of this nation; the Report specifically recognizes the great lack of factual information (pp 42 et seq & 69, and Recommendation 8, p. 73); it specifically recommends that off-road vehicle use be recognized as an accepted recreational use and that existing use areas be kept open to the public "... where environmental balance is not at issue." (Recommendation 3, p. 70)
We would compliment the Department on this position that, in view of the need for additional study, governmental regulation should not rush blindly into the vacuum of its own ignorance with restrictions for which there is no evidence of need. We think that this is in accord with a fundamental tenet of this nation's legal system: we do not presume ever anyone's guilt.
The promise to the ear, though, was apparently only to be broken to the hope, for what was so doubtful in March evidently had become certain by May when the DES was issued. The DES could easily have been prepared without any assistance from the ORRV Report; in fact only one of the ORRV Report recommendations is included in the DES (#5), and that one is a purely restrictive one.
In March the problems with off-road vehicles were not "...as widespread or
Responsible People Working for Multiple Use of Public Lands

Department of the Interior, 6-22-72, p. ?
serious as previously thought." (ORRV 43); in May, the off-road whicle users were "...frequently in conflict with wise land and resource management practices." (DES 1) But for the fact that both the ORRV Report and the DES bore the same signature, one would almost be forced to the conclusion that this is another instance of the bureaugracy grown so large that the left hand can no longer assist in washing the right.
We note the parade of the conclusions throughout this DES as they assume themselves: "...no area of the public lands is free from potential damage..."

(13) "...use of machines...may rut slopes..." "Use of machines...

can affect..." (14) "Indiscriminate use of IRV...can have severe...
\neffects...." "...plant communities...can suffer...." "All wildlife is affected to some degree...." (15) The doubts of March are the suppositions of May.
On the other hand the "economic boom" noted by the ORRV Report (51)
"...both in the general market and in individual sections of rural America"\nin March had diminished by May to the "minor economic effects" of
controlled ORV use. (DES 17) The flowers of March plainly died in May;
the rites of Spring were brief this year.
This confusion that is so evident in the Department's turning its back on its own study less than two months after that ten-month-long study was completed is characterized, we believe, by the current term "future shock" which, though it may be excused by the arrogation of the Congressional function to the Presidential Office, is even more evident in the Secretarial directive of implementation of May 5, 1972. The Secretarial Memorandum, incorporated into this DES, adopts a definition of off-road vehicle totally at variance with the one prescribed by the Executive Order. The Presidential Proclamation made no exemption for logging trucks or construction equipment or farm tractors. Earth, in this instance, survived May, for the Secretaria, Memorandum copts the ORRV Report definition, without, however, Executive authority for doing so.
The President commands that you regulate all off-road vehicular use; you propose to requeste only off-road recreational vehicle use. The recreational vehicle user that but note his objection to this discrimination and wonder, perhaps, where in the rabbit warrens of official Washington sits this man who thinks that a motorcycle does more ecological damage than a logging truck.
We would suggest that a resolution of this difficulty, and most of the others that the implementation of Executive Order 11644 is certain to provoke, is to be found quite imply in supplying a definition of the word "road", for we are at a total loss in trying to understand how anyone can intelligently discuss "off-road" without first locating that which one shall not be permitted to get "off".

For those of us who are attempting to rise to the task of communicating in words, and to understand our lawgivers, this is the first essential.
4
Permit us, therefore, to suggest such a definition: "A road is a continuous strip of land, presently or formerly used, and suitable for use, by a vehicle."
Once this giant leap for mankind is taken, then we think your Department and its agencies can come forward with the regulations required by the Executive Order for any land use "off" the roads. It will not, of course, resolve all conflicts, but it will surely narrow them for intelligent evaluation.
We do not think even that is going to be an easy task within the assigned time limits, and especially is this so since this DES nowhere makes any provision, as the ORRV Report did, for any retention of Off-road vehicular activity, and the necessity for that is, we think, a matter of elementary fairness. The people of this land own and are entitled to use their public lands, and unless that thought is given the consideration which it deserves, your Department will be assisting in the process of transforming Executive Order 11644 into the Wilderness Act of 1972, without, mind you, even the courtesy of Congressional consultation.
We would again, as we have before, join in the ORRV Report recommendation for a comprehensive inventory and classification of the public lands and the extension of the police power to all those lands. Otherwise we, the conserving user of our public lands, must forever be called to account for, and restricted in our rights because of, the actions of the outlaw minority, the course again so patently and blindly followed by this Draft Environmental Statement.
Very truly yours,
(Mrs) Hildamae Voght Executive Secretary

mentions.quote: We would again, as we have before, join in the ORRV Report recommendation for a comprehensive inventory and classification of the public lands and the extension of the police power to all those lands.
mentions.basis: Objects to DES as more restrictive than ORRV Task Force Study; supports ORV use rights with proper land classification

conditional.quote: Such a balance can only be achieved by a detailed classification of ORRV's, ORRV uses and land resource categories together with a realistic appraisal of demonstrable and significant adverse environmental impacts resulting from specific ORRV uses on specific types of lands.
conditional.summary: The International Snowmobile Industry Association argues that the Draft Environmental Statement fails to adequately differentiate between types of ORRVs and land resource categories, and that snowmobiles in particular have a minimal environmental impact compared to other off-road vehicles. The Association supports a balanced regulatory approach that promotes recreational use while protecting the environment, but strongly opposes reversing BLM's historical 'open except where prohibited' policy, arguing it would unjustifiably restrict recreational access pending completion of a lengthy land classification process. They call for detailed classification of vehicles, uses, and land types, with regulatory approaches tailored to the specific characteristics of each bureau's lands.
conditional.statementText:
The following comments are submitted, on behalf of *
the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) in response to the Notice of Availability of Draft Environmental Statement [Int Des 72-58] published in Federal Register Vol. 37, No. 107 on June 2, 1972.
Virtually all major manufacturers of snowmobiles and related products. In this capacity, the Association has been actively interested in the development of federal policies affecting Off-Road Recreational Vehicles (ORRVs) and in addition to its consideration of the above referenced Draft Statement, has carefully reviewed and considered the Department's OERV Task Force Study released in April of 1972. Since the Task Force Study is an important background document for the Draft Statement, the comments set forth below are directed to such Study as well as to the Draft Statement itself.
* See attached membership list.
12

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Two .
At the outset, we should like to emphasize the fact that neither the National Environmental Policy Act nor Executive Order 11644 in any way supersedes or supplants the Secretary's responsibility, under the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963 to assure adequate outdoor recreation resources and to take prompt action "to conserve, develop and utilize, such resources for the benefit of the American people."
with this factor in mind, and since ORRV use is recognized as a significant and beneficial outdoor recreational acticity, it is clear that, in promulgating regulations in implementation of the Executive Order, the Department must strike an appropriate balance between its stewardship responsibility under the Order and its general obligation to develop and utilize its land resources in such a manner as to promote broad public recreational use.
Such a balance can only be achieved by a detailed classification of ORRV's, ORRV uses and land resource categories together with a realistic appraisal of demonstrable and significant adverse environmental impacts resulting from specific ORRV uses on specific types of lands. The Draft Statement totally fails to isolate and identify any specific demonstrable environmental impact of ORRV use. It is clear that further study is required and that, properly done, this project will be of significant duration. Thus careful planning is necessary to assure that recreational opportunities are not unduly restricted pending completion of the final classification.
Against this general background, the Association's specific comments are as follows:

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Three
I. Adequate Differentiation Between Classes
of ORRVs and ORRV Uses -
We are surprised and disappointed to note that neither the Draft Statement (and the proposed regulations discussed therein) nor the Task Force Study's recommendations make any reference to any intention to give consideration to varying types of ORRVs and ORRV uses in establishing the final regulations under the Executive Order. We fail to see how any regulatory program can properly balance the need for minimization of adverse environmental impact against the need to promote recreational use without carefully classifying the possible impacts of the varying types of ORRV use and tailoring the regulatory approach to take into account the specific requirements of each type of vehicle.*
This failure to differentiate between ORRV classifications would be especially discriminatory and unjustified in respect to its impact on opportunities for snowmobile use since the snowmobile's impact on the environment, as compared to that of other ORRV types, is insignificant.
Snowmobile operation takes place in the winter when the land is dormant and well covered by a protective blanket of snow and the snowmobile is designed to be supported on wide skis and a flexible track of sufficient width to provide flotation on the snow. Because of this design, the snowmobile exerts a pressure
* The failure to take such factors into account would result, for example, in the absurd conclusion that snowmobile and trail bike use must be permitted in all camping areas where vehicular "campers" are allowed.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Four
of only .40 to .50 p.s.i. on the ground beneath it (as compared to the approximate 2.75 p.s.i. exerted by an average man standing and the approximate 10 p.s.i. exerted by an average man riding a motorcycle).
Because of these factors snowmobiles, during the winter period in which they are designed to be used, can be operated without significant risk of environmental harm except in certain limited areas which are especially delicate or especially susceptible to environmental harm.* The foregoing statement does not hold true for all ORRV classifications and there is no doubt that, in the winter snowmobiles can properly be used, without environmental risk, in many areas which should. clearly be closed to use by other types of ORRV's during other seasons of the year (e.g. trail bikes on grasslands in the early spring). Failure to distinguish between the environmental impact of snowmobile use and that of other ORRV uses will result in the unavailability of important Outdoor Recreational Resources for snowmobile use even though there is no relevant environmental basis for such unavailability. Such a result is not only manifestly unfair but is also in direct contravention of the Outdoor Recreation Act's mandate to "utilize" these resources "for the benefit of the American people."
* 
Reference is made to the Report on the Ecological Impact of Snowmobiles on Public Lands prepared by the Editors of Popular Science Magazine. Copies are being forwarded under separate cover.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Five
II. Adequate Differentiation Between Types of Land Resources Under Department of Interior Jurisdiction -
Historically, there have been definite distinctions in the characteristics of lands managed by the separate Bureaus within the Department of Interior. In response to those distinctions, each of the Bureaus has developed a regulatory approach which is tailored to the peculiar requirements of the lands under its jurisdiction. Consider, for example, the following historical approaches.
A. The Park Service (NPS) -
NPS is charged under its enabling statutes with the administration of National Parks, National Monuments and National Historic Sites. These land areas were added to the national park system by specific congressional action based on their unique scenic, natural, historical or archeological characteristics and, in general, receive high density use by the public. With respect to these areas, the enabling legislation emphasizes the Park Service's responsibility for conservation and protection of unique natural values and the Park Service has adequate staff resources for the fulfillment of this responsibility.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Six
NPS is also charged with the administration of "recreational areas" which, like the land areas referenced above, are designated by specific Congressional enactment, generally have somewhat unique natural characteristics and receive high density public use. Unlike the areas noted above, the primary purpose of recreational areas is that of public recreation.
Based on its experience in administering the above described areas and in light of the Congressional emphasis on the stewardship function and the high density use which is common in such areas, NPS has determined that ORRV use can best be regulated by confining such use to specifically designated areas. In light of the Park Service's substantial personnel resources, this regulatory approach has apparently been enforceable. This "prohibited except where specifically permitted" regulatory approach would apparently be carried forward by the regulations under the Executive Order. In light of the unique characteristics of the land areas involved, the Congressional emphasis on preservation, the high density use and the existence of adequate enforcement personnel, the Association agrees that, with respect to the lands described above, the aforementioned regulatory approach is appropriate. It should be emphasized, however, that with regard to recreational areas, their primary purpose is recreation and thus great emphasis should be placed on the establishment of trails and designated areas wherever significant

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Seven
and irreversible environmental impact would not result. With respect to the parks, national monuments and national historic sites, we note that the encouragement of enjoyment by recreational users is a congressionally established goal which should be actively pursued wherever compatible with the steward-ship or environmental preservation functions of the NPS with respect to such lands.
B. Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife (BSFW) -
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BSFW is responsible for the management of some 30 million acres of public land and is charged with the primary responsibility of the protection and perpetuation of wildlife resources. Historically, BSFW has followed a fairly restrictive use policy similar to that of the National Park Service described above. The Association is in agreement as to the applicability of the "prohibited except where specifically permitted" regulatory approach when applied to BSFW lands. However, it is again emphasized that the Secretary does have a responsibility for promoting recreational use of this land to the extent that such use will not adversely affect environmental values. Accordingly, BSFW should be encouraged to actively review its land areas with a view towards designation of ORRV areas and trails wherever possible under the aforesaid criterion.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eight
C. Bureau of Land Management
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BLM is responsible for the management of approximately 452 million acres of public land. In general, the BLM lands do not possess the unique scenic, natural, historic or archeological characteristics present in the NPS lands nor do they generally function as important wildlife conservation centers as is the case with the BSFW lands. Public use of BLM lands is generally low density in nature and BLM has limited personnel available for the purpose of enforcing any regulation of ORRV use. Based on these factors. the historical BLM policy with respect to ORRV use has been to permit such use in all areas except those which are closed to such use for a specific reason. The Department's proposed implementation of the Executive Order would apparently reverse this policy and would provide for the confining of ORRV use to areas and trails designated as open to such use. Even in such open areas, ORRV use would be subject to certain controls.
while the Association does not disagree with the goal of imposing reasonable restrictions on ORRV use in any area of the BLM lands, it does strongly disagree with the Department's apparent intention to reverse BLM's historical approach with respect to the classification of lands. For the reasons set forth below, such reversal is not only unwise from an environmental

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Nine
point of view but is also in direct contravention of the Secretary's responsibilities under the 1963 Outdoor Recreation Act. In our opinion, such reversal of policy would have the following aspects:
Indefinite and Unjustified Limitation of Available Outdoor Recreation Resources Pending Completion of Classification - BLM, as noted above, is responsible for the management of over 452 million acres of public land which land is widely dispersed and of highly diverse characteristics. Given existing staff resources, it would be expected that the envisaged classification of all BLM lands into that which is open for use and that which is closed to use will be a project of at least several years in duration. Since no significant amount of public lands has yet been classified as opened to ORRV use, the effect of the proposed sudden reversal in policy will be to close all BLM lands to ORRV use until the above-referenced classification scheme is completed. Thus, the proposed scheme of regulation would presume that ORRV use - a beneficial recreational activity - is environmentally objectionable until the contrary is proven. It is submitted that such policy is not reasonably calculated to promote and develop recreational resources for the American people. To the contrary, it seems more reasonably calculated to have the opposite result. The appropriateness

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Ten
of such a policy is clearly questionable in light of the manifest Congressional intention set forth in the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963. There is no justification for this contravention of Congressional policy either by reference to the characteristics of BLM lands or by any demonstration of environmental damages which have resulted from the historical implementation of the present open use policy.
2. Concentration of ORRV Use Within the

Specifically Defined Areas  As noted above, ORRV use
on BLM lands is now widely dispersed and it is clear that
such low density use tends to have a less significant\nenvironmental impact than high density use in designated
areas. The effect of the reversal in policy referenced
above would be, especially in the earlier years of the
policy's implementation, to concentrate ORRV use in such
areas as have been specifically classified as open. Thus,
with respect to BLM lands, the proposed reversal in policy
would not protect the environment but, by concentration of
ORRV use in certain areas, would tend to heighten any impact
which such use might have.
3. Placing of Impossible Burdens Upon BLM

Enforcement Personnel  As indicated above, BLM has limited staff resources and, even assuming that such staff is adequate to evaluate and classify all of the 452 million

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eleven
acres of public domain land under BLM jurisdiction, it is ludicrous to expect that staff to post and deny public access to all of such lands except those that are specifically classified as open. If, on the other hand, BLM is permitted to follow its existing policy of focusing on the specific areas where adverse environmental impact is likely to occur and devoting its resources towards the exclusion of ORRV users from those specified areas, there is at least some hope of achieving an effective scheme of regulation which will be adhered to by the users.
Compared to these apparent and significant adverse impacts of reversal of existing BLM policy, the only advantage of such reversal of which we are aware is that of achieving uniform policy for all lands under Interior jurisdiction. Such uniformity is a mere matter of administrative convenience. It is not dictated either by the Executive Order or by any other Interior enabling statute. Elimination of the positive environmental and recreational benefits of the existing regulatory approach as a mere matter of administrative convenience is clearly inappropriate and we would therefore suggest that the Department reconsider its apparent intention to deviate from ELM's existing land management policy with respect to ORRV use.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Twelve
D. Bureau of Reclamation Lands - The Bureau of Reclamation Lands are similar in characteristic to those under the management of BLM. Historically, the Bureau of Reclamation has followed an "open except where prohibited" policy similar to that of BLM. For the reasons discussed above with respect to the BLM lands we believe that the existing regulatory approach of the Bureau of Reclamation should be preserved and that departure from this historic approach would have adverse impacts both from the environmental point of view and the point of view of available outdoor recreational resources.
Based on the foregoing, it is our opinion that the Draft Environmental Impact Statement and the proposed regulations discussed therein give inadequate attention to the varying characteristics of the lands administered by the several Bureaus. This approach appears to be in direct contravention of the Task Force Study's recommendations that, in developing the new regulations consideration be given to existing regulations and specific land classifications. It is our opinion that the significantly divergent characteristics of the several land categories require significant variations in regulatory approach. These factors should be taken into account in finalizing the regulations in implementation of the Executive Order.

JULY 7, 1972
My name is John W. Grandy, IV. I am Administrative Assistant for Wildlife at the National Parks and Conservation Association.

I appreciate the invitation of this Committee to submit the views of the NPCA on this important matter.
The National Parks and Conservation Association is the leading conservation organization concerned primarily with the protection of the National Park System, but also with other major environmental and conservation subjects such as wildlife and forestry.
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the draft environmental impact statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
while the statement seems adequate in most places, alternatives to the proposed actions are insufficiently discussed.

The Secretary's memorandum (Page 3, paragraphs (a)(4) and (a)(5))
gives criteria for use of vehicles by area classifications such
as wilderness. The impact statement, however, considers all
areas as a group when considering alternatives.
27 Costs and benefits of the vehicle use pattern assigned, and alternative patterns, should be considered with reference to each area for which regulations (guidelines) are considered in (a)(4)

and (a)(5).
By adequately evaluating areas such as National Parks in relation to their legal status, their primary purposes, and all alternative sets of vehicle regulations, we believe that you will satisfy the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act. In addition, analyses will likely bring clearly to focus the extent of prohibitive regulations necessary on recreation areas, natural areas, or historic areas of the National Parks; wildlife refuges; and Bureau of Land Management lands.
The concept of multiple-use, cited as the major rationale for not closing all Interior lands to ORV use (Page 29 of draft, statement), has never been applied to national park areas either by the Congress or the adminstering agencies. Many of the recreational pursuits provided on other public lands are thus excluded from the parks. Hence, we at NPCA are certain that analyses such as we suggested will indicate that off-road vehicles should be prohibited on natural areas of the National Park System.

conditional.summary: The Commonwealth of Virginia Commission of Outdoor Recreation expressed concern that the environmental impacts of off-road vehicles are not fully understood, and criticized the draft EIS for making vague or undocumented claims about impacts. conditional.statementText:
Dear Mr. Watt:
We have been giving serious consideration to the many public land management problems which must be solved because of the growing popularity of recreational use of off-road vehicles. • believe the impact of these vehicles on the environment is not fully understood at this time. The draft environmental statement enclosed with Mr. Hofe's letter of June 1, 1972, reinforces our feelings, particularly in those sections that outline the damages which may be done.
In commenting on the statement we would suggest that it repeatedly points out possible impacts without stating that one thing or another will happen. For example, to say "there is reason to believe that family relationships are strengthened by these activities," is hardly a documented statement of favorable impact upon the environment. Another we note for your consideration is that, "use of over-snow vehicles for fishing purposes may result in some water pollution from the litter and waste left on the ice." We have every reason to believe pollution will occur.
A fatal weakness of the statement is that it pertains to all types of off-road vehicles, even those at this time not invented. We would suggest an impact statement should be made regarding each type vehicle in its most common use environment.

In closing, we suggest that great care should be taken not to allow use where the impact is not fully understood or where the local land manager believes no harm will be done. An example of the type of permitted use that concerns us is the opening of selected roads in Acadia National Park to over the snow vehicles. While it is probably true that little or no damage will be done to the roads so used, we would be concerned about the harrassment of wildlife of the park. During the winter months land animals are under great stress in finding food and shelter and great rafts of migratory waterfowl numbering in the thousands of birds nest and feed off shore if not disturbed.
Thank you for asking for our comments.
Sincerely,
Rob R. Blackmore
Director

conditional.role: Chief, Planning Division, Wyoming Recreation Commission
conditional.quote: The first recommendation we would like to make in connection with the above mentioned draft is that procedures be established to insure that any rules and regulations adopted in connection with this subject have sufficient built-in flexibility to allow for administration on the state and local level, thus enabling their adjustment to the existing situations.
conditional.summary: McNiff, writing on behalf of the Wyoming Recreation Commission, argues that national ORV regulations must be flexible enough to accommodate state and local conditions, warning that Wyoming does not face the same problems as heavily populated areas and that imposing uniform rules could create problems where none currently exist. He recommends an 'open until closed' policy rather than a 'closed until open' approach, and stresses that Wyoming's agencies actively encourage ORV use. He also raises concerns about inconsistent federal guidance, the need to address non-recreational ORVs (e.g., mineral exploration), and the importance of a clear definition of 'road.'
conditional.statementText:
INTER-OFFICE MEMO
DATE
 June 29, 1972
Paul H. Westedt - Director
FROM. Peter J. McNiff - Chief, Planning Division
SUBJECT DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT, PROPOSED
EXECUTIVE ORDER 11644 PERTAINING TO USE OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES ON THE
PUBLIC LANDS
COPIES TO: Dr. Clynn Phillips; P. J. McNiff; RF.
The first recommendation we would like to make in connection with the above mentioned draft is that procedures be established to insure that any rules and regulations adopted in connection with this subject have sufficient built-in flexibility to allow for administration on the state and local level, thus enabling their adjustment to the existing situations.
The theme that must be stressed by Wyoming in connection with this type of topic dealing with standardized land use and administration is that problems and potentials in Wyoming cannot be dealt with the same as problems and potentials found east of the Mississippi or on the West coast. (On page 9 of the Department of the Interior Task Force Study of Off-Road Recreation Vehicles, it states that Task Force Staff members selected thirteen (13) states for personal visits to gather much needed information for the report. All 13 of these states were east of the Mississippi River.)
There is a tendency in all national observations of this type to lump the United States into one category and administer all areas in accordance with rules and regulations adopted to solve problems found in heavily populated areas. If this is done, Wyoming, not having the problems to be treated by this type of administrative procedure, may see the creation of a bad situation where none previously existed.
When viewing and analyzing a standardizing administrative proposal, we first look to see if a problem exists in Wyoming which would be serviced by the proposal. We find Wyoming is not experiencing a great off-road vehicle problem, on the contrary, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission, the Wyoming Recreation Commission, the Department of Economic Planning and Development, the Wyoming Agriculture Department, and many of the federal agencies encourage off-road vehicle use in connection with their various interests and activities. In the few cases where problems have been spotted, they have been solved by existing authority on both the
The second recommendation relates to the above but more specifically to the Wyoming situation. If rules and regulations on this subject are to be successful in Wyoming, they must be based on the principle that all the areasunder administration are open to use with only those areas already closed or where problems develop, closed to use. Both the open and the closed areas must be continually studied with respect to use and non-use and a review process established whereby their respective status can be changed if merited.

We were very disturbed when we learned at the recent Governor Hathaway Recreation Action Team meeting that the National Forest Service had apparently received instructions from Washington that the open until closed philosophy was fine, but that the Bureau of Land Management had been told by Washington to work for a closed until open policy. This dichotomy of federal guidance is strange in itself, but frightening when the Bureau of Land Management and presumably the National Park Service is contemplating a course of action on the Washington level contrary to the suggestions of their local representatives, the Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan, and of sister federal agencies.
The following are general overall observations of the draft, etc., and hopefully will serve as a review of areas of concern with respect to the final product of this proposal.
There appears to be a difference in the titles between the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement which might be of some significance, i.e., the Task Force Study is entitled off-road Recreational vehicles and the Draft Environmental Statement indicates that all off-road vehicles, i.e., those used for agriculture and accdemic purposes, terrain mapping, administrative inspection, mineral prospecting, etc., are represented and included within the statement but not within the Task Force Study. In any case, there should be an addendum to the Statement concerning the effect of the proposal on these important non-recreation off-road vehicles. In connection with this, a study of the various conflict in laws involving the proposal and the established prospecting and mineral exploration laws, etc., should be carefully analyzed and effectively dealt with.
The definition of a road will also be of primary importance to the success of this proposal. With over 50 percent of Wyoming in federal ownership and potential roads involving everything from the dimmest game trail to Interstate Highways, it takes little imagination to think up problems of administration if the definition of a road is left nebulous.
Attached hereto please find a copy of the Draft upon which comments, suggested wordings, etc., have been made. .

conditional.summary: New Hampshire State Planning concurs with the proposed management policy of closing some public lands to ORVs and opening others with controls, while emphasizing the need for monitoring and flexible management. They question the wisdom of issuing permits for ORV races, rallies, and meets on public lands, suggesting such intensive use is better handled by the private sector. They also raise concerns about the vagueness of noise criteria and note they cannot fully endorse Interior's policy until they have reviewed the Department of Agriculture's statement covering the White Mountain National Forest.
conditional.statementText:
Members of my staff have reviewed the draft environmental statement, prepared by the Department of Interior, entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11544 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands."
We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
The designation of areas closed to ORV use based on physical and biological impacts makes a great deal of sense. Predictions of impacts are not in themselves sufficient. Monitoring of designated use areas must be provided for, and management must be sufficiently flexible to allow changes based on the results of monitoring.
We question the wisdom of issuing permits for the use of public lands as sites for ORV races, rallies, meets, etc. Such intensive use can be better provided by the private sector.
The issue of excessive noise poses some difficult problems. First, there is the definitional problem. No attempt is made to specify what decibel level is considered to be acceptable. Second, the Operating Criteria include a clause that "...an ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The environmental impact of that management policy states in part that "...most motorized ORV are noisy in excess of acceptable levels." Logic demands, therefore, that most motorized ORV shall not be permitted on Interior lands. Obviously, the criterion of "excessive noise" is too vague to be of any use.
Since the State of New Hampshire will be affected greatly by policies yet to be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture through its large White Mountain Muticaul Forest, we cannot at this time be certain that we fully endorse the policy and projected impact set forth by Interior. This can better be ascertained after we have had an opportunity to review Agriculture's 102 Statement.
We wish to emphasize that New Hampshire feels a need to evaluate any specific plans for designating use and non-use areas on Federal lands within the State. The evaluation of a national policy involving lands of great diversity is necessary but not sufficient for an adequate environmental assessment.

mentions.basis: supports general ORV management policy but questions permits for organized ORV events and raises noise criteria concerns

conditional.role: Deputy Assistant Secretary for Environmental Affairs, Department of Commerce
conditional.quote: We would call your attention to 16 USC 478 which provides for access to public lands for the purpose of prospecting. The restriction of ORV's to designated areas could not apply in this case.
conditional.summary: Galler, writing on behalf of the Department of Commerce, offers conditional support for the draft EIS while suggesting specific textual amendments. He recommends clarifying which resources are affected and to what degree, and importantly flags that 16 USC 478 guarantees access to public lands for prospecting purposes, meaning ORV restrictions to designated areas cannot apply to prospectors—though environmental, health, and safety information should still be made available to them.
conditional.statementText:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
The draft environmental impact statement for "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands" which accompanied your letter of June 1, 1972, has been received by the Department of Commerce for review and comment.
The Department of Commerce has reviewed the draft environmental statement and has the following comments to offer for your consideration.
Summary Paragraph 2 line 4 - We suggest that you amend the sentence that begins "The directive establishes policies..." to read "The memorandum . . ."
Page 12 line 3 and 4 - In stating "Further, many resource interests will be affected" the implication derived is one of wide ranging affects. We suggest that you delineate those resources affected and to what degree of affectation this directive will have. We would call your attention to 16 USC 478 which provides for access to public lands for the purpose of prospecting. The restriction of ORV's to designated areas could not apply in this case. However, environmental, health and safety concerns should be made available to the prospector.
We hope these comments will be helpful to you in the preparation of the final statement.
Sincerely,
Sidney P. Galler

conditional.role: Environmental Protection Coordinator, Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Game and Fish Division
conditional.quote: This agency believes that the statement is adequate in describing the nultiplicity of problems inherent with off-road vehicular use on our public lands.
conditional.summary: Claude E. Hastings, on behalf of Georgia's Game and Fish Division, found the draft environmental statement adequate in describing the problems of off-road vehicle use on public lands. He conditionally supported the proposed regulations but insisted that any ORV rules promulgated by federal secretaries should require concurrence from Georgia's Director of the Division of Game and Fish, since wildlife resources belong to the state. He also recommended specific protections for streams, trout habitats, and wildlife areas where ORV use would cause significant adverse effects.

This agency is interested in the above application and wishes to make the following comments:
The Department of Natural Resources, Division of Game and Fish for the State of Georgia would like to make the following comments relative to this environmental statement.
This agency believes that the statement is adequate in describing the nultiplicity of problems inherent with off-road vehicular use on our public lands. We recognize the conflicts of interest which can occur due to these vehicles. Since the fish and wildlife resources on all public lands belong to the State and the State is charged with the responsibility of the protection, management and perpetuation of the fisheries and wildlife resources, it is our judgement that off-road vehicle regulations promulgated by the Secretary of the Interior or the Secretary of Agriculture should have the concurrence of the Director of the Division of Game and Fish, Department of Natural Resources.

218
Department of the Interior Implementation of Executive Order 11644 72-06-22-18
It is recommended that extreme caution be used to preserve public lands for beauty, solitude, remote values and wildlife habitat. These are what are presently making these lands valuable.
On Page 4 of the Environmental Impact Statement under "a) Use Criteria (except for official use): " "(i) Areas and trails shall be located to minimize damage to soil, water, vegetation or other resources of the public lands." should be changed to include streams and their tributaries. This is especially important on trout streams to control silt pollution and all soil disturbances that would result in disruptions to the stream bottom habitats.
We are certainly in agreement with (ii) which states, "Areas and trails shall be located to minimize harrassment of wildlife or significant disruption of wildlife habitats."
On Page 14, the sentence, "Use of machines in stream beds can affect the spawning, migrating, and feeding habits of fish and other aquatic life" is true and we would not wish to see the use of off-road vehicles permitted in stream beds. Where certain off-road vehicle trails cross streams, the vehicles should cross the streams on bridges rather than disrupting the stream beds, which causes silt pollution with its adverse effects on fisheries habitat.
On Page 16, the statement, "Certain animals will not be able to accommodate the opening of their habitat to off-road vehicle traffic and accompanying human activities" is quite true. In those instances where it is recognized that the use of off-road vehicles will have a significantly adverse effect upon certain wildlife resources, such use should be prohibited.

Dear Mr. Watt:
We are writing in regard to Mr. Hofe's request for comments on the Draft Environmental Statement for the proposed implementation of executive order 11644 pertaining to the use of off the road vehicles on public lands. We wish to point out that the State of Indiana is currently involved in an off the road vehicle study through which we hope to assess demand for this activity, determine its environmental as well as human effects, and determine if there is compatibility between the use of this activity and the management philosophies that cover areas under our jurisdiction. Therefore, our comments at this time are of a limited nature since the results of our study have not been completed.
The Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Department of Interior is to be congratulated for the work that has been done in the development of this Statement. However, we feel the Statement is of a general nature regarding the impact of off the road vehicles. The very difficult areas with regard to this outdoor recreation activity have not been defined by this Statement, but have been left to the individual Bureaus of the Department of Interior to solve. The questions of how to effectively manage this activity and in which areas the activity is to take place must be answered if this activity is to be acceptable.
With regard to specific areas of the Statement, under operating criteria, a number of terms appear to need further definition such as defining "excessive damage or disturbance of the land, wildlife or vegetative resources" in Section D and "unusual or excessive noise" in Section V. Under Section IV, we question whether ORV's should be allowed to run from dusk to dawn because of the noise factor and also from a safety

conditional.quote: We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
conditional.summary: Hancock concurs that the proposed ORV management policy—closing some public lands and opening others with controls—is consistent with responsible stewardship of natural resources and recreation interests. However, she raises several concerns: the noise criterion is too vague, issuing permits for ORV races and events is unwise (better left to the private sector), and monitoring must be built into any designation system. She also notes that New Hampshire cannot fully endorse the policy until the Department of Agriculture issues its own statement covering the White Mountain National Forest, and that any specific designation plans for federal lands within New Hampshire must be open to state evaluation.

INTER-DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION
JUL 6 572
FROM Mary Louise Hancock, Director
DATE June 29, 1972
AT (DAFICE) State Planning
SUBJECT Draft Environmental Statement, Department of Interior, regarding the Use of Qff - Road Vehicles
To Alexander M. Taft, Director Comprehensive Planning
Members of my staff have reviewed the draft environmental statement, prepared by the Department of Interior, entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11544 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands."
We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
The designation of areas closed to ORV use based on physical and biological impacts makes a great deal of sense. Predictions of impacts are not in themselves sufficient. Monitoring of designated use areas must be provided for, and management must be sufficiently flexible to allow changes based on the results of monitoring.
We question the wisdom of issuing permits for the use of public lands as sites for ORV races, rallies, meets, etc. Such intensive use can be better provided by the private sector.
The issue of excessive noise poses some difficult problems. First, there is the definitional problem. No attempt is made to specify what decibel level is considered to be acceptable. Second, the Operating Criteria include a clause that "...an ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The environmental impact of that management policy states in part that "...most motorized ORV are noisy in excess of acceptable levels." Logic demands, therefore, that most motorized ORV shall not be permitted on Interior lands. Obviously, the criterion of "excessive noise" is too vague to be of any use.
Since the State of New Hampshire will be affected greatly by policies yet to be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture through its large White Mountain Muticaul Forest, we cannot at this time be certain that we fully endorse the policy and projected impact set forth by Interior. This can better be ascertained after we have had an opportunity to review Agriculture's 102 Statement.
We wish to emphasize that New Hampshire feels a need to evaluate any specific plans for designating use and non-use areas on Federal lands within the State. The evaluation of a national policy involving lands of great diversity is necessary but not sufficient for an adequate environmental assessment.
MLH: Imd

conditional.quote: Commissioner Nicholas Johnson concurring in results; Commissioner Benjamin Hooks absent.
conditional.summary: Commissioner Nicholas Johnson concurred in the results of the FCC's letter to the Secretary of the Interior, which generally supported the ORV regulations but stressed the need to ensure that communications carriers and government inspectors retain adequate access to public lands for construction, maintenance, and inspection of communications facilities. conditional.statementText:
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION WASHINGTON, D.C: 20554
IN REPLY REFER TO:
9400
Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary, United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
This concerns the draft environmental statement prepared by the Department of the Interior's Bureau of Outdoor Recreation and dated May 26, 1972. The statement proposes regulations for use of motorized off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The Commission wishes to avail itself of the opportunity extended on June 2, 1972 (37 F.R. 11078) to comment on the draft environmental statement. We are in general agreement with the objectives of the statement which would restrict the use of off-road vehicles on lands administered by the Department to ensure that such use, where permitted, would be compatible with other uses, and would not result in significant adverse environmental impact or cause irreversible damage to existing ecological balances.
The proposed regulations would implement Executive Order 11644 which appears to have been prompted primarily because of the rapidly increasing use of off-road vehicles such as minibikes and snowmobiles for recreational purposes. However, the restrictions appear broad enough to be applicable as well to motorized vehicles used for business or other non-recreational purposes. Accordingly, we are concerned that provision be made so that common carriers and others who have wire, cable or radio communications facilities on public lands pursuant to land-use permits may have reasonable access to such facilities, to whatever extent may be necessary or desirable, in connection with the construction, operation and maintenance of such communications facilities. In this connection, we note that any vehicle whose use was expressly authorized by an agency head of the Department under a permit, lease, license, or contract would be exempt from the proposed use restrictions on off-road vehicles. However, it is not apparent whether existing or future authorizations for use of Department lands for

communication requirements by common carriers and Commission licensees would include authority for use of off-road vehicles necessarily incidental to construction, operation, and maintenance of the necessary communication facilities.
As you are aware, communication facilities on or traversing public lands often provide vital public and national defense communication circuits. Continuity of such service is dependent upon immediate access to the lines and other facilities at all times. Further, spurious emissions from radio transmitters could cause destructive electrical interference to communication requirements of others, including harm to common carrier circuits which the Commission is charged with protecting from such interference. It is also possible that such interference could pose risks to safety of life and property.
The foregoing public interest considerations are merely illustrative of those with which the Commission may be concerned and are not intended to encompass all such considerations which we may properly consider in discharging our statutory responsibilities.
Such responsibilities are discharged, in part, via inspections and investigations by Commission employees and other governmental agents in the field, often involving the off-road use of motorized vehicles. It would appear that such operations would be exempt from the proposed restrictions in light of the provision excepting law enforcement vehicles. We believe it imperative that it be made clear that such governmental inspection and investigatory operations will be exempted.
In short, the Commission wishes to stress the necessity for ensuring that whatever regulations are finally promulgated restricting off-road uses of vehicles, adequate provision be made to ensure that vital communication requirements are capable of being duly satisfied at all times.
This letter was adopted by the Commission on July 6, 1972. Commissioner Nicholas Johnson concurring in results; Commissioner Benjamin Hooks absent.
BY DIRECTION OF THE COMMISSION
11.1
Chairman

Gentlemen:
This letter is in protest of Executive Order 11644 which would severly limit the use of off-the-road vehicles on public lands. conditional.quote: Enclosed herewith are the comments of the Sierra Club on the draft environmental impact statement for the Department of the Interior's implementation of Executive Order 11644 concerning the use of off road vehicles on public lands.
conditional.summary: Michael McCloskey, on behalf of the Sierra Club, submitted detailed comments arguing that ORV use should be presumed harmful and all public lands should be closed to ORVs by default, with areas opened only after studies confirm acceptable impact levels. The Sierra Club called for stronger protections including licensing of operators, carrying capacity limits, rationing of use through permits, and strict restrictions near wilderness, wildlife, and desert areas. While accepting that some controlled ORV use may be permitted under Executive Order 11644, the Club insisted that resource protection and the interests of all the public must take priority over ORV user groups.

conditional.summary: The Sierra Club argues that ORV use should be heavily restricted on public lands, with all areas presumed closed unless proven safe through objective study. They call for licensing of operators, carrying capacity limits, prohibition of organized ORV events in closed areas, and stronger protections for wildlife and desert ecosystems. They support the principle that public land administrators must prioritize resource protection over accommodating ORV user groups.
conditional.statementText:
SIERRA CLUB
Mills Tower, San Francisco 94104
1050 Mills Tower
220 Bosh Street
by Ansel Adams in This Is the American Farth
July 14, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Director Hofe:
Enclosed herewith are the comments of the Sierra Club on the draft environmental impact statement for the Department of the Interior's implementation of Executive Order 11644 concerning the use of off road vehicles on public lands.
We appreciate having had this opportunity to submit comments on this important environmental matter.
Yours truly,
Michael McCloskey
Executive Director
Enclosure. MM:1kn

Sierra Club Comments on the
Draft Environmental Impact Statement
For Department of Interior Implementation Of
Presidential Order 11644
Concerning the Use of Off Road Vehicles on Public Lands
General Comments
(1) ORV areas should be located near urban areas where possible and not allowed in more remote lands of a wilderness or semi-wilderness character. Most ORV users are interested in testing their machines and not in access to scenic areas. These areas, however, should not be immediately adjacent to homes where a citizen's right to privacy, peace, and quiet would be threatened. ORV areas distant from urban areas would create traffic congestion with accompanying air pollution. Control would be easier to maintain closer to urban centers.
(2) No mention is made of the amount of land that will be closed to ORV vs. that which will be open. This will probably turn out to be the most critical issue when the program is implemented. The statement should recognize this problem and state that the interests of all of the people will be placed above those of the ORV operators when those interests are in conflict. The primary charge of public land administrators is to protect resources first and to accommodate various users of the land second.
(3) Since our public lands are not limitless, regulation beyond the zoning emphasized in the statement will be needed. If ORV areas are over-used and are receiving unacceptable damage, the solution should not be to open up more areas to their use. Consideration must be given to rationing their use. This could be done by issuing permits to individual ORV operators and restricting the frequency of their use. This is being considered for wilderness areas now and there is no reason why other users of public lands should not be similarly restricted. Before any ORV area is opened up an attempt to determine its carrying capacity should be made in order to limit damage. The carrying capacity should not be

exceeded under any circumstance.
Specific Comments
<u>Page 5, b-i.</u> The Sierra Club strongly supports the statement requiring operators of ORVs to be licensed. Since a lot of ORV damage to the environment is caused by unsupervised, under age operators, strong regulations regarding under age operators must be made and enforced. The adult supervisor should be held legally responsible for any damage caused by under age operators under his supervision.
<u>b-i (d)</u>. <u>Excessive</u> damage should be changed to something like <u>permanent</u> and noticeable damage. Damage by ORV should be controlled far short of being excessive.
<u>b-iii</u>. The Sierra Club strongly supports this good provision requiring proper muffler and spark arrestor equipment on all vehicles and that this equipment be in good working order and in constant operation.
<u>Page 6 (iv)</u>. Organized off road vehicle events must not be allowed <u>under any</u> <u>circumstance</u> in any areas normally closed to ORVs. Bonds must be put up by people conducting such events. Provision must also be made to rehabilitate and restore areas impacted by these events.
Page 10, lines 10-11. This states that lands will remain open to public use unless closed for a specific reason. This should not apply to ORVs because of their unquestioned damage. All BLM lands should be closed to ORV and then opened up on a parcel by parcel basis after a study has been shown that the leval of ORV damage will be acceptable. This should be true of all federally owned land, not just BLM land.
Page 11, lines 1-5. The terms used to identify ORV areas are qualitative.

Objective criteria are needed or at least a system for arriving at objective criteria. If the decision to open or close an area becomes merely subjective, then we can expect decisions to be made only on the basis of pressure and not on what is best to protect the resources. Furthermore, determination of ORV carrying capacity must be made for all areas open for their use and limited to such levels as the environment can handle without significant environmental damage.

Page 12, lines 8-11. ORVs do cause damage in most areas with substantial use. Repeated use by large numbers (in excess of the carrying capacity) causes excessive damage in nearly all types of terrain and vegetation.
Furthermore, ORVs are not primarily used for access to remote areas when all use is considered collectively. Very few ORV operators are interested in access as much as they are in testing out their machine. ORVs are used for sport and not for an appreciation of the aesthetic and cultural qualities of the public lands. If ORVs were used merely for access we would have minimal conflict with them.
Page 13, line 1. Emphasis is placed upon the benefits to user groups. This statement should acknowledge that the public lands belong to everyone, not just user groups. The public lands of the nation need to be managed so that the resources are managed in the best interests of all the people -- present and future generations -- and not just for the user groups who happen to be on the scene at this point in time.
<u>Page 13</u>. The discussion of soil erosion in the last paragraph should include wind erosion of desert soils. Under normal conditions much of the desert surface is covered by desert pavement — a covering of pebble to boulder size rocks, the smaller material having been carried away by wind erosion. ORV wheels break up this thin crust exposing the finer soil beneath to further wind erosion. The problem is especially severe where cross country races are held in the desert. Participants take off in waves, sometimes one-mile-across lines, axle to axle, cutting a huge swath of destruction across the desert.
Page 14, paragraph 2. Snowmobiles do more than create a litter problem.

Studies are increasingly demonstrating significant environmental impact on vegetation from snowmobiles as the result of twig breakage and snow compaction. Also, the snowmobile is used as a vehicle to chase a number of species of wildlife, which all too frequently causes severe exhaustion and sometimes death. Harassment

129
of wildlife of any sort must not be allowed.
Page 14, last paragraph. The dust problem is especially bad in the desert and should be mentioned in this statement.
Page 15, last paragraph. The California Department of Fish and Game has set up quali guzzlers in many areas of the California desert and some game birds are entirely dependent on this source of water. Cross country motorcycle races have been routed right by some of these. Vandalism in areas accessible only by ORVs has also been a critical problem with quali guzzlers.
The Desert Bighorn Sheep is known to disappear in areas of heavy human use.

This species should receive a higher priority in management decisions than ORVs.
Page 16, paragraph 2. It should be emphasized here that ORV use should be considered harmful to wildlife until proven otherwise. All areas should be considered closed until it is shown that ORVs would have an acceptable impact upon wildlife.
Page 16, paragraph 3. The only ORV users who might need access to game management purposes are the game and land managers themselves. If it is determined that an area should be closed to ORVs, then hunters should walk or ride horses. It should be very clear that an area normally closed to ORVs will not be opened to hunters on ORVs merely because of a surplus of game.
Page 17, line 11. This mentions revenues from sales of motorcycles. It should be recognized that not all motorcycles are used as ORVs. Only those that are used as ORVs should be included in the statement.
Page 17, lines 15-16. Winter access to small towns via snowmobiles can be on snow covered roads and need not be cross country.
Page 18, line 11. The case for strengthened family relationships caused by ORV use should be proven. Saying there is reason to believe this is true is not enough. The reasons should be spelled out.

Page 19, last paragraph. The signs of ORV use are very offensive to non-users. This remark should remain in the statement and receive more emphasis.
Page 21, paragraph 2. It is true implementation will be costly. The statement should place more emphasis upon this fact and groups like the Sierra Club can help in acquiring the necessary funds to effectively control ORVs.
Page 22, line 6. This recognizes a land ethic itself. This is very important and should be greatly emphasized by the use of a separate heading and a greatly expanded text.
This same paragraph again only refers to users of public lands and does not mention that all of the people own the public lands. Their best interests need to be considered.
Page 24, line 10. Urban dwellers will be especially resentful if ORV areas are established within hearing range of homes.
Page 26, lines 6-8. This sentence implies that decisions will be semi-permanent. If ORV areas are shown to suffer unacceptable damage they should be closed. It should not be implied that any ORV area will not be closed at a future date if necessary.
Page 26, lines 9-12. The problems mentioned in this paragraph would be minimized if all areas were considered closed and then opened to ORVs only after a careful study shows damage would be acceptable.
Page 29, line 4. "Inspiration" is hardly the word to use when discussing the benefits of ORV benefits. It should be deleted.

mentions.quote: The operation of CRV's should be presumed to be detrimental to all areas and should accordingly be prohibited on all public lands unless proven otherwise by competent, is partial investigators.
mentions.basis: supports strong ORV restrictions with presumption of harm; conditions any ORV use on proven safety by impartial investigators

conditional.quote: Therefore, special controlled areas should be designated for OPV use in order to make OPV use compatible with other uses of public lands.
conditional.summary: The South Dakota State Planning Agency conditionally supports ORV regulation, agreeing that unregulated ORV use creates a nuisance but that recreation participants should be allowed to fulfill their desire for ORV experiences. However, they insist that special controlled areas must be designated for ORV use to protect other recreationists, grazing, wildlife, and vegetation. They also provide specific technical comments on the draft statement, recommending stronger and clearer language around restrictions, soil protections, exhaust emissions, and noise impacts.
conditional.statementText:
SOUTH DAKOTA
OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR
STATE PLANNING AGENCY
PIERRE
RICHARD F. KNEIP GOVERNOR
DR. LYNN MUCHMORE DIRECTOR
July 19, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas hofe, Jr., Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation United States Department of the Interior Washington, DC 20240
Dear Sir:
Thank you for giving the State of South Dakota the opportunity to respond to your draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 which pertains to the use of off-road vehicles on public lancs.
In general, we agree that unregulated off-road vehicle traffic on public and private lands creates a nuisance and that ignoring the popularity of such vehicles is not an approach which should be taken. Also, we believe that recreation participants desiring such an experience should be allowed to fulfill that need. However, a fulfillment of their desires should not take place at the expense of other recreationists who feel a need for a quieter, more isolated type of experience without interruption by noise, etc. In addition, we are cognizant of the fact that harmful effects on grazing, wildlife preceding and vegetation can be intensified by disruption due to OPV traffic. Therefore, special controlled areas should be designated for OPV use in order to make OPV use compatible with other uses of public lands.
The following are brief references to specific statements found in your draft with comments directed toward clarifying problem areas and delineating points implied but not necessarily spelled out:
Secretary Authorities and Responsibilities
1. Page 3-#2  Scientific areas should be added to the categories listed.
2. Page 3-#2  Loological balance should be added to the categories listed.
3. Page 3-#2  The phrase is used: "special soil or vegetation or vegetation conditions." While it is true that different types of soil and vegetation may or may not be particularly fragile in terms of OHV use, it is true that any change to a type of soil may affect animal and vegetative life.

Mr. C. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director July 19, 1972 Page 2-2-2
Therefore, the document should delete the word "special" in line 4.
4. Page 3-#2  "Designating all lands for ORV use as open (with controls) or closed." Considering the unknown consequences to the eco-balance which can occur within the context of this statement, the "red light approach" should be utilized when there is doubt as to the major consequences of ORV use. As you know, past decisions have been made with a bias toward project development or utilization of space even though consequences were unknown.
5. Page 3-#2  The phrase "restrictions or controls may be developed, when necessary," is used. We find this phrase too ambiguous and susceptable to interpretation. The phrase should read: restrictions or controls shall be developed in every case with regard to area and types of venicles utilized.
6. Page 14-#2- Special mention should be made regarding exhause systems. Funes from exhaust emmissions can have negative affects on water quality.
7. Page 15 - Noise may be a factor in plan life cycles as well as being detrimental to animal habitation and breeding.
8. Page 23 - Use of special soils is referred to again. Please see #3 above.
9. Page 23  In many cases, land reclamation in terms of Lines 14 returning the landscape to its original and 15 appearance and the capability of the land to its original use is not very workable. The major problem appears to be that reclamation often seriously lags behind use-over-use mis-use and scarring of the landscape.
10. Page 22 - We agree with the statement that operating Last four criteria and registration requirements for lines ORV should conform to State Laws.
Thank you for the opportunity of responding to your draft statement.
Jun P. indurus Physical Planner
Sincerely yours,
