conditional.entity: Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
conditional.quote: The document represents a comprehensive statement setting forth criteria for protection of natural resources on Federal lands. If the criteria are conscientiously followed and agencies carry out their mission responsibilities, adverse environmental effects should be minimized.
conditional.summary: The Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife conditionally supports the draft environmental statement, finding it a comprehensive document that, if conscientiously followed, should minimize adverse environmental effects. However, the Bureau raises specific concerns, including the inconsistency of permitting ORV racing on public lands with its wildlife protection mission, requesting explicit exclusion of National Wildlife Refuges from such activities, and calling for clearer noise standards, better enforcement mechanisms, and more consistent open/closed policies across bureaus. The Bureau also requests rewording of the section describing its mission to better reflect its primary responsibility for fish and wildlife protection.
conditional.statementText:
United States Department of the Interior
FISH AND WILDLIFE SERVICE BUREAU OF SPORT FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE WASHINGTON; D.C. 20240
AUG 1 1 1972
Memorand m
To:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Acting Deputy
From:
Director, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
Subject: Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order
11644, pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the
Public Lands (DES 72-62)
This Bureau appreciates the opportunity to review and comment on the subject draft statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on public lands. The document represents a comprehensive statement setting forth criteria for protection of natural resources on Federal lands. If the criteria are conscientiously followed and agencies carry out their mission responsibilities, adverse environmental effects should be minimized.
Our specific comments are as follows:
1. The proposal description should include all of the definitions as given in Section 2 of Executive Order 11644, unless a copy of the document is to be attached to the environmental statement. Of particular interest to the public would be the definitions of "off-road vehicles" and "public lands." Additionally, the statement does not mention ORV use on public lands which are open to mineral and mining entry and to established mining claims. The Executive order is not clear on this point; it is recommended that it be clarified in the statement.
2. The proposal to permit ORV racing, rallies, endurance contests, etc., on public lands is inconsistent with existing land management policies of this Bureau. It is recognized that the multiple-use concept is promoted when consistent with wise resource management. The broad authorization given to this proposal which will admittedly adversely affect the natural resources of this Bureau, in particular the National Wildlife Refuge System, is not responsible

management. Concessions such as this should be beyond the expectations of any user group. It is recommended that this Bureau be specifically excluded from participation in this activity by means of the draft environmental statement.
3. It is suggested that the paragraph concerning this Bureau (page 9) be reworded to read as follows: "The mission of the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife is to assure maximum opportunity for the American people to benefit from fish and wildlife resources as part of their natural environment. The Bureau is responsible for the management and operation of a nationwide system of national wildlife refuges and waterfowl production areas comprising 30 million acres of land, including wilderness areas, 90 national fish hatcheries and 6 research stations along with associated lands. A significant portion of Bureau lands have been specifically designated as protected habitat for rare and endangered species of wildlife. Travel in or use of any motorized vehicle, including land, water, ice, snow, and aircraft types, is prohibited on areas administered by the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, except on specific routes of travel or in designated areas posted for public use. In accordance with paragraph 3(a)(4) of Executive Order 11644, areas and trails will be established only if the Bureau head determines that ORV use on Bureau lands will not adversely affect the natural, aesthetic, or scenic values. Because of the Bureau's primary responsibility for the protection and perpetuation of fish and wildlife resources, with wildlifeoriented public use as a secondary objective, administration of the ORV program must necessarily be more restrictive than other bureaus or agencies."
4. On page 17 it is stated that the Upper Great Lakes Regional Commission reported snowmobiling was worth $212,180,000 to the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan in 1970-71. The Bureau feels it inappropriate to use this gross, or net figure without some follow-up discussion of associated impacts in terms of environmental degradation or possible human benefits received. Use of such an isolated figure as a beneficial impact only is misleading to the reader. Nuch of the description of economic impacts is inappropriate and unnecessary.
5. The last paragraph of page 17 is suggested for rewording as follows: "Controlled use, adequately administered, would have a minor alverse impact on the economic effects of ORVs. An enhancement of vacation land and home values is a possibility, but as yet is unproven. Environmental degradation could detract from previously established vacation land uses during the same or other seasons, and real estate values could actually decrease because of ORV intrusions and disturbances: Past off-season tourist periods could be eliminated or reduced. In individual areas where ORV use is prohibited, a negative impact would result."

6. While the Executive order and introductory statement of the draft refer to visually designating only those trails and areas open to ORV use, it should be readily recognized that posting only the open areas would pose enforcement problems. This is acknowledged in the environmental statement on page 20, line 13, which reads "...adequate posting must be improved to permit enforcement of any restrictions." In essence, this means areas not open should be posted. This may not be possible to do in some areas, and will require an expanded effort in communication, designation of areas, and enforcement.
7. We believe that completed studies on noise pollution contain enough information for definite acceptable noise levels to be spelled out (in decibels) for the different types of ORVs and outdoor public use areas. Included in the acceptable levels of noise must be the cumulative effect of several ORVs even though they are operating at their individual acceptable level. This determination must be made before adequate administrative controls can be developed—spice zoning, time zoning, restricted areas, etc. A general statement referring to "unusual or excessive" noise will not suffice because interpretation by individual land managers will vary and this will ultimately mean problems in administration.
8. Although we are aware of the problems that exist we feel there will be many problems regarding the open or closed policies of each of the Bureaus. They should be consistent.
It is hoped that the above will be helpful in preparation of the final document.

conditional.summary: Stan Elmer, on behalf of Utah's Environmental Impact Evaluation Committee, supports ORV use on public lands but argues the draft environmental statement takes an overly negative tone and undervalues the role of management, design, and planning in mitigating environmental impacts. MEMORANDUM
TO:
GORDON E. HARMSTON
FROM:
STAN ELMER, CHAIRMAN,
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT EVALUATION COMMITTEE
SUBJECT:
DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT - USE OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES
ON PUBLIC LANDS (IMPLEMENTATION OF EXECUTIVE ORDER 11644)
K 14
Utah is just completing its first year of implementation of a comprehensive Recreation Vehicle Act (attached) governing all off-road vehicle use on public land in Utah. The proposed program discussed in the ORV Environmental Statement is either identical or compatible with the Utah regulation in most respects.
1. Under "operating criteria," item (1). Since there is no evidence that operators under 16 years of age contribute disproportionately to accidents or other problems in the use of boats or ORV's, and they represent a significant portion of these family recreational pursuits, we can find no just reason to require a highway operators license or supervision by someone who is at least 21 years old. This is the kind of requirement which is designed more to stifle the use than to promote safety; and it would be contradictory if it recognized the responsibility of a 16 year old with a license but would not accept his ability to supervise those under 16. There should be general supervision of those under 16; but it could surely be by someone who is at least 16 who is experienced with the equipment.
2. In the section requiring permits for competitive events, the requirement for bonds and the provision for rehabilitating the use areas are good, but should not be used to discourage or prohibit activity by setting the costs unrealistically high.
90

3. The frequent use of the phrase "can" or "may have irreversible and irretrievable harmful effect on" throughout the report definitely encourages a negative frame of mind in the consideration of ORV programs. Much of the theory which is represented in the proposal was apparently developed by non-users and those without a great deal of expertise with ORV use. We, therefore, encourage an accelerated feeling of responsibility by all public land administering agencies to provide developed areas and trails in as many places as possible. In some of the areas with "excessive erosion or siltation characteristics," a properly developed and managed trail may be a better solution than closure.
4. The Utah Division of Parks and Recreation has enjoyed an excellent working relationship with BLM and other Federal agencies in implementation of our program, and the identification of legitimate use areas throughout Utah.
The following sections of the enclosed State Law (most of which encompass the Federal proposals) are now being enforced by Division officers and county sheriffs on public land in Utah:
Section 3 - Registration.
Section 10 - (3) (a) Mufflers, (b) lights, (c) brakes, (4) (a) reckless and negligent operation, (b) posted speeds, (c) buddy system (d) operator under 16.
Section 12 - (2) Operating in closed areas.
Section 13 - Vandalism, harrassment of animals, burglaries, damage to environment.
Section 14 - Operating under the influence.
Section 15 - Permission to hold competitive events.
Our Division of Water Resources has pointed out its reliance on ORV's in constructing and servicing many water transfer facilities, etc., which are generally inaccessible except by some type of ORV.
The State's need to construct, service and maintain these projects is echoed by the Utah Division of Oil and Gas Conservation which uses ORV's to reach isolated oil rigs. The needs of many other official government and private concerns to manage their resources and operations are dependent on some types of off-road vehicles.
It would appear from experience that the best alternative to the proposed action would be that action, but with a much greater emphasis on management, supervision and planning than indicated in the Secretarial memorandum of May 5, 1972.
90 Specific comments on the draft environmental statement follow:
Page 1: We question the use of the word "frequently" when disclosing ORV conflicts with wise resource management, etc.

Pages 2 and 3: We agree with the positive attitude expressed in most of these statements. We especially endorse the requirement for research and studies regarding the environmental impact of ORV's. We would add the need for research on management and design practices which can help reduce or eliminate detrimental environmental impacts of ORV use.
Page 7: We suspect that the wide range of resources available for ORV use, and the wide range of design and management practices available in the use of each different environmental form, gives the Department of the Interior the opportunity to provide for ORV use in a variety of ways as well as in a variety of areas.
Page 8: The "state-of-the-art" of eco-management is the real key to ORV use, as it is with traditional uses of the public lands.
Pages 9 and 10: While public use on the National Wildlife Refuge System is secondary to the primary responsibility of wildlife protection and perpetuation, it is safe to say there would be much less public use without the traditional pressures from the states for public use areas. These compromise practices have not been detrimental to wildlife, but have allowed greater use of the resource.
Page 10: We applaud the Bureau of Land Management's planning system and its management of land under multiple use principles. We urge that the approach taken to ORV use be one of "open unless closed" rather than "closed unless open." To confine ORV use as indicated may concentrate the use so greatly in too small an area as to destroy that area and thereby justify further closure.
Page 11: We agree that areas and trails should be selected on lands having vehicle use capability and having low erosion and siltation potentials. We do not think areas of low vegetative production are necessarily suitable, however. If an attitude prevailed based on management of the use, an area which could more quickly revegetate or recover from use might be a much better area than one which takes longer to respond. This entire impact statement seems to leave out the options created by intelligent planning, design, maintenance and management.
The consistent use of the word "control" rather than "manage" reflects an unfortunate negative attitude. Limiting use to areas too small to handle the growing demand will only concentrate the impact. A policy of dispursed, yet managed use will offer more recreation opportunity and create less environmental impact.
Page 12: We agree with all statements except the last paragraph. The word "some" reflects reality much better than "many."
Page 13: We agree that data is needed on both the use and environmental impact side of the question; but feel it is needed also on the design and management side. Additional monies are needed by all agencies involved to provide the opportunities for ORV use while managing that use and the resource itself.

We question again the negative attitude toward ORV use displayed in the writing of this environmental statement. The fact is that "no area of public lands is free from potential damage by . . ." almost any use. To suggest that all sand dune areas and all snow fields are "fragile and susceptible land forms" is to not understand that the next breeze or the next snowfall can completely mitigate the environmental impact of ORV tracks on sand or snow.
We agree with the use of soil erodibility appraisals in helping to identify areas for appropriate ORV use; but suggest that they are needed also in defining areas for many other traditional uses such as grazing, mining and timber. Again, the answer is not so much "open" or "close," but "manage."
Pages 15 and 16: The discussion of biological impacts sounds like all populations and species of wildlife have had a run-in with ORV's. We suspect that the discussion applies more realistically to isolated instances, as with other uses of the public lands. The writers and readers of such impact statements need to be reminded that even the revered backpackers can "disturb" wildlife.
Page 17: We see no reason to assume that properly managed use of ORV's would have a "minor adverse impact on the economic effects of outdoor recreation." To the contrary, safe and sane provision of ORV opportunities could increase the positive economic effect because of the increased interest and use which would be attracted by well-managed areas. As the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation should know, most ORV users are responsible individuals looking for protection of their "investment" as well.
Page 18: We question the use of the phrase "often at high speeds" when referring to exploring of areas. Anyone familiar with most ORV use would know that most exploring is at a leisurely pace and that the racing event, which is usually held at an appropriate site and under appropriate regulations, is at high speed; but is far from "exploring," and is not the kind of activity pursued by the average ORV user.
Page 19: We agree that the time when any user can use the public lands whenever and wherever he wishes is long gone. All must accept the idea that their use of public lands will of necessity be managed.
We wonder why trails, parking areas, rest stops and other developments are "unsightly" when associated with ORV use, but not an unmanageable problem when associated with camping, picnicking or backpacking use.
Page 20: We question the idea that concentrating vehicles and people in designated areas will help the situation. It could cause more environmental damage unless there are enough such areas, and they are large enough in terms of their capacity.
We think that ORV designated areas should be rated similar to ski runs: (1) beginning, (2) intermediate, (3) advanced, etc, so users can match their degree of skill with the terrain.

The public lands are also reservoirs of our recreation and leisure heritage, and, as they later state, the Department of the Interior also has a charge to provide outdoor recreation opportunities.
Page 21: We agree that implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memorandum will impose a substantial impact upon the Department of the Interior (and the Department of Agriculture) and that additional financial resources must be forthcoming if even the public's minimum needs are to be met.
Page 22: We agree that the needs of the users and the needs of the public lands themselves must be balanced. It is our impression, however, that the tone and attitude expressed in the Executive Order, the Secretarial memorandum and the environmental statement, are psychologically "heavy" on the side of resource protection; do not adequately consider the middle-ground options offered by good design and adequate management; and generally reflect a lack of appreciation for the recreation experience offered by ORV use.
As indicated above, we have attached a copy of Utah's ORV regulations which indicate operating criteria and registration requirements.
Page 23: Since Utah has actively attempted to regulate ORV use on public lands, and since more than 75% of Utah is either Federal or State land, we respectfully request State review of all proposed manual releases, regulations and administrative guidelines.
Page 24 and 26: The use of the word "will" instead of "may" in talking about detrimental effects of ORV use, again does not consider that management and design could prevent detrimental impact. Environmental impacts will occur. "Detrimental" environmental impacts may occur if ORV use areas are not properly located and managed. Good location and design could also prevent changes or destruction to historical and archaeological structures. To suggest, as is done, that these effects "cannot be avoided" is to admit that they do not rely on their professional landscape architects; that they do not intend to survey proposed ORV use areas for potential conflicts; and that they do not have the expertise to lay out an ORV use area or trail. We know that this is not the case, because we work with land management field personnel and they are capable of avoiding these kinds of impacts.
In addition to the Department of Interior responsibilities listed, we would add "... plus a responsibility to provide for man's needs through the wise use of these resources." This would cover such traditional uses as mining, timber harvesting, grazing, and pursuit of recreation activities.
Page 25: We agree that short term needs of the present should not preclude future management options; but we do not agree that backpacking and other wilderness or "natural" kinds of activities, as intimated, are the only compatible future uses.
To even suggest that "the current intensifying use of ORV may represent a temporary novelty . . ." is to clearly indicate a lack of

understanding and appreciation for this phenomena which does "represent the beginnings of a long-lasting mode of outdoor recreation."
Page 26: We recommend adding to the last sentence, "...in some areas which cannot withstand the pressure, or which are not being maintained during use and rehabilitated after use."
Page 27: We recommend adding to the last sentence " . . . and in providing for legitimate outdoor recreation use of those lands."
Page 28: To suggest that ORV use is the only one which can disturb animals and plants on public land areas is to ignore the impacts of other traditional uses.
We also recommend adding the following sentence to this discussion:
"It would also decrease the amount of enjoyment the ORV users could derive from using their vehicles, from appreciating the wonders of the public lands by ORV and from getting into otherwise distant areas in a relatively shorter amount of time."
Page 29: We agree that ORV use is a primary source of enjoyment to a significant number of recreationists. As an illustration, in Utah it is the 5th highest activity in terms of recreation days participated in, and 7th in terms of participant occasions.
Although we do not advocate opening <u>all</u> public lands to ORV use, a movement in that direction would certainly spread out the impact, and, if the use were managed, it could lessen the overall environmental impact.
The "widespread damage" discussed is exaggerated if Utah's experience is a just measurement. Much of this depends on management, which in turn depends on personnel, well-planned areas, and public (or user) education.
As you can tell, our main point is that proper planning, design, maintenance and regulation of ORV use can give many more options for management of the public lands to meet the legitimate needs of the public.

conditional.quote: The Department of Legal Affairs suggests that a test program to control off-road vehicles be instituted on a limited bas s; the Department offers comments on several other portions of the statement which should be considered.
conditional.summary: The Florida Department of Legal Affairs (through Attorney General Robert L. Shevin) argues that the draft environmental impact statement inadequately evaluates the alternative of prohibiting off-road vehicle use on public lands, and that the policy choice to permit such use is questionable given acknowledged irreversible environmental harms. Rather than implementing a nationwide program of controlled ORV use, the Department recommends initiating a limited test program to allow for monitoring and data collection, with ORV use restricted to established roadways in the meantime. The letter also expresses concern that public lands should serve as a retreat from urban noise and annoyance, and that ORV use would undermine that purpose.
conditional.statementText:
TALLAHASSUE, PLOUIDA, 3290-1
August 7, 1972
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
State Planning and Development Clearinghouse
Department of Administration
725 South Bronough Street
Tallahassee, Florida 32304
Re: U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Outdoor Recreation: Draft Environmental Impact Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands (K14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
Dear Mr. Still:
The following are comments on the draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The general approach to the regulation of off-road vehicles on
public lands, as delineated in the proposed Impact Statement, appears
to be adequate and comprehensive, assuming that one agrees with the\nunderlying policy.
The President's Executive Order 11644 and the Memorandum from Interior Secretary Morton to various assistant secretaries appear to assume that off-road vehicles will be permitted to use public lands off established roadways. The entire draft statement addresses itself to minimizing the damage or conflict caused by the use of these vehicles off established roadways. It assumes that there should be allowed certain damage or conflict with the present activities that exist on these lands.
As a result of this policy choice, the draft statement attempts to make a case for the use of such vehicles, rather than fully evaluating the alternative of prohibiting such use. For example, on page 28 of the draft there is a statement that prohibiting

completely the use of these off-road vehicles on public lands would result in "effects on economic sectors which are presently influenced by current demand for and production of off-road vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near bepartment lands where off-road vehicle use takes place."

The would seem that the more important consideration here should be the tagnitude of impact on the economic sector as opposed to the rare presence of an effect. The amount of the economic effect is not ordinanted in the draft, and so one cannot evaluate the significance of any negative economic effect. On page 29 of the draft statement, there is a statement that
closing all Department of Interior lands to ORY use would constitute an action inconsistent with the Department's responsibility to maintain certain of its lands for the enjoyment and inspiration of the general public. It would, likewise, not be consistent with the Department's mandate to encourage the broadest possible mix of compatible multiple uses on certain of its lands— multiple uses which include recreation among the primary potentials and ORV use being a primary sounce of enjoyment to significant numbers of recreationists.
The draft does not discuss the bases for these conclusions. A policy or maintaining certain lands for the enjoyment and inspir tion of the general public hardly requires the use of areas off established roadways by off-road vehicles. Certainly, the Department does not allow all desired uses of its lands which may be sujoye le to certain members of the public. The necessity of evaluating competing uses of the land and determining acceptable uses must often come before the Department. The proposal to permit off-road vehicle use of public lands would seem to be one of those instances requiring an evaluation of competing and conflicting uses. The draft statement does not adequately treat this fundamental question.
In regard to the alternative of allowing off-road vehicle use of public lands, it seems highly questionable from comments in the draft statement that such use is a wise one. At page 12 of the draft, it is stated that whether operated properly or improperly, ORV can cause irreversible and irretrievable harm to man and the environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates that 0 W use will have an adverse effect on wildlife. The adverse effects of encessive noise from ORV on humans and wildlife are outlined at page 19.

Page 3
Part V of the draft statement, at page 24, states that
Even though the net effect of implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memoraneum would be a reduction in the adverse impact on human and natural values, there are certain continued unavoidable adverse effects.
* * *
Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Noise levels will be discomforting to some users of public lands.
Historical and archeological structures may be changed or destroyed by ORV use.
These conclusions are reiterated at page 26 in part VII, of the draft entitled "Tracversible and Irretrievable Commitments of Resources Which Would be Involved in the Proposel Action Should It be Implemented".
In addition to the above concerns and effects, the draft statement observes, at page 13, that there is less than satisfactory data available in regard to the impact of ORV on the lands in question. Therefore, I would suggest that instead of instituting a program of controlled ORV use throughout the Nation's public lands system, it would be more prudent to initiate a test program on a very limited basis. Such a program would facilitate monitoring and data collection, would not require the commitment and expenditure of large sums of money for additional policy and enforcement (see page 21 of draft statement), and would enhance the ability of the Department of Interior to fully evaluate ORV use on public lands. During the operation of such a test program, ORV use of public lands should be limited to established readways.
With the increase in the metropolitan style of living and all the attendant noise and pressure associated with that life, it seems that the public lands are playing an increasing role in providing

Page 4
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
the public with a retreat from the type of noise and annoyance associated with ORV. We should be reluctant to facilitate the intrusion onto those lands by urban sources of noise and annoyance, and so should scrutinize carefully any proposal for CRV use of public lands.
Sincerely
ROBERT L. SHEVIN Attorney General
RLS/DW

conditional.entity: New Mexico State Park and Recreation Commission
conditional.quote: The operations of motorcycles within the State Park system shall be permitted on improved, main roads only and shall be properly muffled.
conditional.summary: The New Mexico State Park and Recreation Commission issued Regulation No. 18, which conditionally permits motorcycles, dune buggies, and all-terrain vehicles within the State Park system under specific restrictions. Motorcycles are limited to improved main roads and must be properly muffled, while dune buggies and ATVs are confined to designated areas only, with recreational use areas and beaches off-limits. All such vehicles are prohibited during nighttime hours.
conditional.statementText:
STATE PARK
AND RECREATION COMMISSION
REGULATION NO. 18 STATE PARK REGULATIONS
18. Motorcycles, Dune Buggies and All-Terrain Vehicles.
The operations of motorcycles within the State Park system shall be permitted on improved, main roads only and shall be properly muffled.
The operations of dune buggies and all-terrain vehicles within the State Park system shall be permitted in designated areas only. All recreational use areas and beaches are off limits. Check with park personnel in each respective park prior to operations.
The use of motorcycles, dune buggies and all-terrain vehicles is prohibited between the hours of 9:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. during daylight savings time and 7:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. during standard time.
Adopted by the New Mexico State Park and Recreation Commission the 18th day of July, 1972.

OREGON STATE HIGHWAY DIVISION
SALEM, OREGON HIGHWAY BUILDING 97310

Mr. James G. Watt Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D. C. 20240

neutral.role: Assistant Secretary for Environment and Urban Systems (Designate), Office of the Secretary of Transportation
neutral.quote: Our primary concern is with the sections covering regulation of noise emitted by these vehicles.
neutral.summary: Hirten, writing on behalf of the Office of the Secretary of Transportation, reviewed the proposed regulations and draft EIS on off-road vehicle use on public lands. His primary concern was with the noise regulation sections, suggesting that the final regulations should include a statement on the need to develop appropriate noise standards since state regulations may be non-existent or inadequate. He also recommended that the final regulations address public hearings for area designations, preparation of environmental impact statements in advance of such hearings, and the establishment of a mechanism for handling complaints related to noise, pollution, or destruction caused by ORV operators.
neutral.statementText:
OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20590
JUL 26 1072
Honorable W. W. Lyons
Assistant Secretary
U.S. Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Lyons:
This office has reviewed the proposed regulations and the draft environmental impact statement concerning the use of off-road vehicles on public lands managed by bureaus of the Department of the Interior.
Our primary concern is with the sections covering regulation of noise emitted by these vehicles. It is stated that a vehicle which produces unusual or excessive noise or other pollutants shall not be permitted to operate on public lands. A statement on the need to develop appropriate noise standards would strengthen this section, as State regulations may be either non-existent or inadequate in some instances.
We suggest that the final regulations include discussion of the opportunity for public hearings with respect to designation of areas and trails for the use of off-road vehicles. If such hearings are anticipated, are environmental impact statements to be prepared in advance of these hearings in order to evaluate the environmental effects of off-road vehicles? Is there currently a mechanism set up for handling complaints because of noise, pollution, or other destruction to public lands or wildlife on the part of vehicles or their operators?

We hope these comments will be of some assistance to you, and we look forward to receiving the Department of the Interior's final regulations and the final environmental impact statement on the operation of off-road vehicles on public lands.
Sincerely yours,
John E. Hirten
Assistant Secretary for
XIATINE
Environment and Urban Systems
(Designate)

Mark found the draft environmental statement to be quite thorough overall, but raised a concern about the minimum operator age of 21, suggesting it might be lowered to 18 or 20 given that Hawaii's age of majority is 18. He also noted the importance of preparing and publicly circulating maps designating ORV-permitted and prohibited areas within national parks, and acknowledged limited information about ORV problems on Hawaii's federal public lands.
neutral.statementText:
DEPARTMENT OF PLANNING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
P. O. BOX 2359 . HONOLULU, HAWAII 96804
JOHN A. BURNS Governor
SHELLEY M. MARK
Director
EDWARD J. GREANEY, JR. Deputy Director
STATE OF HAWAII
July 7, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
28
Your Reference: K14
Dear Mr. Watt:
This is in response to your letter dated June 1, 1972, which we did not receive until July 3, 1972, transmitting a draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
We have studied the draft statement and find it to be quite thorough in its discussion of the subject matter. On page 5, under Operating Criteria, we note that 21 years is the minimum age limit set for operators unless they have a learner's permit or they are accompanied by a person 21 years of age or older if they are under licensing age for their state of residence. The licensing age in most states is under 21; likewise they can now vote at the age of 18; and in Hawaii they reach the age of majority at 18. You may want to give this age limit matter some more thought to decide if it should be lowered to 20 or 18 years. Otherwise, the operating criteria seem reasonable.
Our other area of concern was to visualize how control of CRV's would actually be implemented. We would assume that each national park would have to prepare some maps indicating areas in the park which would permit CRV's and other areas where ORV's would be prohibited. Such maps should be prepared in draft form and be circulated and made available to the public before they are finally adopted. There could be a variety of arguments about the boundaries of such area designations.
Actually, we do not have any information about the ORV problem on public lands in Hawaii. Most of the Federal public lands in Hawaii are either military lands or the two National parks. I am sure the military commands can keep the problem under control on their bases. We have not heard of complaints of this nature in the two National parks. However, this is not to say they do not exist, or that ORV's are not causing damage; it is probable that such complaints would not be directed to our office.

We are forwarding one copy of your draft environmental statement to the Governor's Office of Environmental Quality Control. It is the agency in our State which reviews and processes all required Federal and State environmental statements. It also makes the statements available to other governmental agencies and the general public. Should further comments be forthcoming, we have asked that office to forward them to you. Our copy of the statement shall also be made available for public review. Thank you for the opportunity of reviewing your statement.
Sincerely,
Shellev M. Mark

STATE OF WASHINGTON
Office of the Governor
PLANNING AND COMMUNITY AFFAIRS AGENCY
OLYMPIA, WASHINGTON 98504
July 18, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr.
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
United States Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
RE: K-14
Pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, following are my comments relating to your draft Environmental Impact Statement on off-road vehicles (ORV) on public lands.
From a state perspective, I recommend that copies of this draft be circulated among primary state land management and regulatory agencies. These would include the Departments of Highways, Natural Resources, Fisheries, Game, Ecology, Parks and Recreation, and Social and Health Services.
It appears that the main consideration regarding ORV use is a flexible use criteria, (pages 2-31). According to the draft, this will be the responsibility of each respective land manager at the federal level to assure that the scenic, natural and aesthetic order is maintained. I realize the difficulty of uniform regulations for the entire Department of Interior because of the many variables one must consider for lands that range from mountains to desert to wetlands.
In the course of policy development, I suggest coordination with local units of governments, particularly at the county level (county commissioners) in order to apprise them of your efforts. This could precipitate ORV policies at the county level.
These are my primary comments at this time. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Sincerely yours,
Richard H. Slavin
Director

opposed.quote: We find the draft statement to be totally inadequate. It does not comply with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, Executive Order 11644, or other laws which define Interior Department responsibilities in managing the public lands.
opposed.summary: The Natural Resources Defense Council found the draft Environmental Impact Statement totally inadequate, arguing it failed to comply with NEPA, Executive Order 11644, and other laws governing Interior Department responsibilities for public lands. They contended that the draft statement accommodated ORV use rather than protecting environmental values, and demanded that both the draft statement and the Secretary's May 16 memorandum be withdrawn so that implementation of E.O. 11644 could begin anew. Their attached detailed comments further argued that ORVs should be banned from national parks and wildlife refuges, and that environmental values must be given the highest priority in any revised policy.
opposed.statementText:
Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
1600 TWENTIETH STREET, N.W. WASHINGTON, D.C. 20009
147
202 387-2855
July 17, 1972
New York Office 36 WEST 44TH STREET NEW YORK, N.Y. 10036 212 986-8310
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Enclosed are the comments of the Natural Resources Defense Council on the Draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
We find the draft statement to be totally inadequate. It does not comply with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, Executive Order 11644, or other laws which define Interior Department responsibilities in managing the public lands. Instead, it militates against the clear duty imposed by these directives to identify and protect environmental values. It indicates that the policy of the Department is not to insure that the use of off-road vehicles is "controlled and directed so as to protect resources on [the public] lands," as required by E.O. 11644, but rather to accommodate all demands for ORV use. For these reasons we believe that the draft statement must be withdrawn.
Furthermore, the Secretary's memorandum of May 16 is an inadequate attempt to implement E.O. 11644. It fails to take account of Interior's legal responsibilities to identify environmental values, and fails to propose concrete policies for the regulation of ORV use. It is useful neither as a proposal for action, nor as a guide to substantive policy. Therefore, we believe that the memorandum must be withdrawn along with the draft statement, and the entire process of implementation of E.O. 11644 must begin again.

We are shocked that Interior, as the agency charged with the protection of natural resources on over 60% of Federal lands, should reject the opportunity to declare its commitment to the protection of environmental values and choose instead to accommodate an environmentally-destructive activity. The effect of this choice is to seriously weaken and misdirect the implementation of laws which are intended to promote environmental quality. In its revised implementation of E.O. 11644, Interior must change its policy on ORV use to give environmental values the highest priority. Only in this way can the Department properly fulfill its responsibilities.
Sincerely yours,
Thomas B. Stad, Jr.
Thomas B. Stoel, Jr.
Grey & Studen
Greg E. Studen

    Council on Environmental Quality

opposed.quote: We seriously challenge and question the environmental wisdom in conceding to the thought that ORV's really belong, in almost any setting, on Federal Lands.
opposed.summary: The Milwaukee Audubon Society, through its president David Tillotson, strongly opposes ORV use on federal public lands, arguing that the Draft Impact Statement improperly institutionalizes and legitimizes motorized recreational vehicles rather than questioning whether they belong on public lands at all. The Society contends that ORVs cause documented ecological damage, destroy wilderness solitude and mood, threaten endangered species, and that the multiple-use concept cannot reconcile wilderness values with ORV use. They call for a phasing out of motors from public lands, with ORV activity redirected to private lands, and criticize the draft statement for being conciliatory toward ORV manufacturers and users rather than taking a firm environmental stance.
opposed.statementText:
14 Mar 1973
Mr. Nathaniel Reed US Department of Interior Washington, D.C. 20340
Dear Mr. Reed,
Attached is a position paper of the Milwaukee Audubon Society dealing with the subject of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land.
It is our understanding that public reaction was invited to a draft statement on ORV use issued by one of Interior's subagencies - the Eureau of Outdoor Recreation.
We trust that you will see that our position on the ORV matter gets to the proper agency in time for the hearing on this matter.
Sincerely
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society
12259 Underwood Fkwy
Wauwatosa, Wis 53226
CC: Cynthia Wilson (Natl Audubon)
CC: Ed Brigham (Natl Midwest Audubon Rep)
114
3/27/1

Position Paper
Milwaukee Audubon Society
regarding
The Use of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land
prepared by
David Tillotson
President
Milwaukee Audubon Society
12 March 1973
In our assessment of the Draft Impact Statement on Off The Road Recreational Vehicles (prepared by the Department of Interior to implement Presidential Executive Order #11644) we believe that one serious weakness immediately presents itself. This is the fact that the Department of Interior Draft Statement helps institutionalize motorized recreational vehicles on the public lands and waters. It appears to make proper and acceptable what we in the Audubon Society believe is improper and un-acceptable. Before we as a Nation decide on THERE to use the ORV's schould we not decide THETHER to use them?
We seriously challenge and question the environmental wisdom in conceding to the thought that ORV's really belong, in almost any setting, on Federal Lands.

In a time of fast diminishing recreational space, is it wise to give any Governmental help (by an ORV policy statement) to ORV's, that simply by their existance and normal method of operation shrink recreational space at a disproportionately rapid rate. One can hear the motors for miles. The outdoor atmosphere is spoiled and diluted. ORV's swallow up land in minutes that would take a hiker hours to traverse. The new recreational vehicles are simply sophisticated ways for exploiting untouched nature more rapidly. Their growing use and popularity fits neatly, we will admit, into our current environmental milieu which is quite frankly hedonistic and materialistic.
The draft statement by implying that since the vehicles are here and are now using Public Lands, that it is proper for such use to continue without challenge.
Our second objection is that the statement as it stands is conciliatory and even not neutral in that it more or less takes the position of the ORV manufacturer and user by saying that this or that use MAY harm the soil, MIGHT damage lakes, etc, etc. In point of fact there are numerous documented instances where lakes, forests, waters, lands and wildlife are actually being harmed.
To mention just a few:
1. Trout spawning area spoiled by motorcycles in Sequoia Natl Forest (Calif) Documented Audubon Mag Jan '72
114. Coyotes run over by snowmobilers in Grand Teton Park (Wyo) Documented Audubon Mag Jan 172 
3. Snow compaction (in Canada) injures microenvironment of small mammals shrinking food chains Aud Mag Jan '72

4. Motorized outdoorsman can cause 200 times more damage to landscapes than the walker Audubon Mag Jan 172
5. Elk & Deer harassment by snowmobiles in S.E. Idaho "drains these animals of as much energy as a week's normal winter existance."

Aud Mag Jan '72
6. A Federal Game manager says that "snowmobiles can harm wild animals by driving them from protective cover & food supplies".

documented Milwaukee Journal Feb 6 '72
7. In Humbolt Natl Forest (Nev) jeeps and ORV's caused $50,000 damage to soil and vegetation. Aud Mag Jan 172
8. In one BLM study area in the west, trail bikers stripped away 60% of the vegetation in a 1500 acre area Aud Mag Jan 172
We question the unsubstantiated statement in the draft that a snowmobile or other ORV's are a boost to family ties. Considering what the car is generally known to have done to the American home and family life - 
_{\rm We}
 challenge the idea that ORV's are going to "Cement family relationships".
It will be argued that tens of thousands of individuals already own ORV's, that it is too late to outlaw on public lands; we can only regulate. We do not concele this point. On private lands, where motors are operated in such fashion that they do not infringe on the legitimate rights of contiguous property owners, we have no argument.
But we do question whether the larger, long term interests of today's and tomorrow's citizens (and ecosystems?) are best served by opening government lands to general use by ORV's.
We believe that the multiple use concept is deformed and abused 114 by asking that it stretch far enough to blanket, simultaneously, wilderness values and values pursued by ORV users.

We question the wisdom of permitting the great wilderness and wildlife sanctuaries (whether "official" or unofficial) to be overwhelmed by ORV activity. We believe the chief value of much undesignated federal land is that it furnishes a valuable staging area, a resting area, a cosmic mood, a wilderness retreat (incidentally for man and primarily for wildlife) and that non-use is healthful and recharges the intricate (not totally known) mechanisms of the various ecosystems. "Unused" wilderness, for example, is responsible for clean water coming out of mountain country as clean as it is.
Stricter controls, stricter enforcement is needed, with the focus on THE SPECIAL KIND OF HARM done to nature by ORV activity. Beyond the obvious damage to plants, lands, and animals and waterways, there is a loss of mood, a loss of authentic outdoor atmosphere which may be far more significant than all other kinds of damage combined.
The "differentness" of the land - the land undominated by ORV's is why we believe a vast majority of outdoor oriented citizens like the out of doors. These are the citizens, many now deceased, who have helped see to it that one third of the land of the United States has remained in public hands and in one sense, still "whole".
We of Audubon feel about all landscapes as Theodore Roosevenlt felt about one landscape, the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. The ages have been at work upon it - let it be.
114 Historian Will Lurant has written that Mations are born stoic and die epicurian. Are the CRV's an example of a mechanized epicurianism? A squandering of all the untouched land in America? Land that has not thus far been defiled by the joyous fact that it is remote?

ORV
ORV's don't give citizens who want to escape into nature the opportunity to do just that. The ORV catches the eye, it dominates the scene with motion, it kills solitude and stunts the growth and development of outdoor aesthetics. Its root is commercial, not esthetic; hedonistic and pagan, not frugal, disciplined, and sacrificial. In other words, the kinds of philosophies that are pre-requisites to the conservation movement are really not yet understood to the ORV user and manufacturer.
Because of the nature of the ORV itself, we must put restraints on it we will not put on other kinds of recreational devices; sail boats, kayaks, canoes, rowboats, bicycles, skis, snowshoes, ice boats. We believe that ORV's (land, water, air) pose very serious threats to several of our endangered species. By means of the ORV we visualize an ever growing number of ill-informed hunters having access to timber wolves, condors, eagles, antelope, prairie dogs, mountain lions. The consequences, for wildlife, of access by way of ORV use, is ominous for the future of many species.
People are coming into nature hopeful of finding enough quality in the way of the environment to save them the extra expense and time of driving a thousand miles more to a place—like a National Fark where severe restrictions have curtailed ORV activity. Much public land, all over the nation, should be free of the blight of the machine.

114 Vast, intact acreages, not subdued by ORV activity, ought to be available to those who are gentler users of the land.

To sum up, we do not believe that certain conflicting uses on ' public lands can be reconciled and no amount of cosmetic rhetoric should be allowed to conceal this fact.
The draft statement, as written, is, in a sense, a commentary on the permissive temper of our times. Rather than ever say NO to anybody, be it the Army Corps of Engineers, the Highways builders, the stream channelizers, the rioters on the campus, or group X,Y, or Z that has siezed a park or a building or a National Forest and then demands that we negotiate. We can't seem to consider the social and environmental imperative of using the simple word, NO!
Merely because Federal managers have thus far (apparently in lieu of directives from anyone) failed to halt the mushrooming encroachments by ORV's on Federal lands, is no reason to assume that the presence of these vehicles is proper or that it should be allowed to continue.
In the absence of a directive, we believe managers should have held the Line and not accommodated the ORV user.
The assumption by Federal land managers that ORV's do BELONG is far more pernicious than one would think. For it leads to institutionalization of the idea that the ORV on Federal land is here to stay.
The land managers are put in a position of accomodating themselves to the CRV and being on the defensive from the beginning.
114 We are convinced that the long suffering but concerned silent majority of the American public gets a great feeling of solace from merely contemplating the fact that vast chunks of Federal land are as yet unspoiled by the Users and producers of ORV's.

And further, that these lands are going to be protected by Federal managers for all time to come, regardless of the talk (and money) of the advocates of motorized exploitation.
In World War II when gas rationing and the war effort cut the visits to the National Forests, there was a 50% drop in the losses due to forest fire. Natural (lightning) fires tend to start high on the mountain while man caused fires (9 out of 10 forest fires are still man caused) start at a lower level and can do much more damage. Thy does the draft statement emphasize the potential of the ORV in preventing fire, when there is historical evidence from World War II and the National Forests, that human access to the forest, especially the remote forests, will increase the number of fires. Come studies that have delved into the psychological make-up of the ORV user indicates that they have a significantly higher accident rate that the non-user. The ORV buff turns out to be a "risk taker" and thus has a higher accident rate. This risk taker is going to pose amever greater threat by fire in the forest and on the grasslands - and game law violators are going to be next to impossible to stop because the ORV will provide opportunity to go anywhere.
114 On most public lands, in such places as the National Parks and monuments, in State Parks, in nearly all the Mational and State Forests, and on the vast tracts controlled by the Bureau of Land Management, we believe motors are a mistake. The evidence of ecological damage and impairment of the natural mood is going to increase, not decrease.

Therefore we believe that a phasing out of the motors from various "established" places should begin at once. We believe that conservation authorities should not develop or promote trails as these trails lead to "locking in" a kind of outdoor use that must eventually be phased out. Also trails are merely "way stations" on the road to ever greater development.
When Congress created the Park System in 1916 it stated that "Above all, the mood of naturalness should prevail."
Except for emergency rescue work, law enforcement activity, and necessary patrols of one kind or another, we believe that concept should eventually govern ORV activity on all public land. Private holdings, private lands, vasts tracts furnished by the manufacturers of the ORV's themselves (two thirds of this Nation's land mass is private) - this is where ORV activity can legitimately be expanded.
Respectfully submitted
David Tillotson

opposed.summary: The American Petroleum Institute's Committee on Exploration argues that the draft environmental statement and implementing memorandum focus almost exclusively on recreational ORV use while failing to adequately consider legitimate mineral and energy resource development on public lands. They contend that geological, geophysical, and other vehicles essential to oil, gas, and mineral exploration are vital to the nation's energy needs and should not be restricted by Executive Order 11644. They strongly urge that such vehicular equipment be explicitly exempted in any revised memorandum, impact statement, and implementing regulations.
opposed.statementText:
AMERICAN PETROLEUM
1801 K STREET, NORTHWEST
(202) 833-5722
WILSON M. LAIRD, Director Committee on Exploration
July 10, 1972
Hon. Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
The attention of the Committee on Exploration of the American Petroleum Institute has been called to Executive Order 11644, "Use of Off-road Vehicles on Public Lands." Your May 5 memorandum directing the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources in implementing this Order and the Draft Environmental Statement prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation on May 26, 1972, have been reviewed, and the following comments are offered:
Neither the memorandum nor the impact statement suggest that the entire spectrum of public land use has been considered. Emphasis is almost entirely on recreational use. Other uses, such as oil, natural gas, mineral and geothermal development, forestry and grazing, are not given adequate consideration, indeed, it appears that the mineral resources area of your own department has been bypassed.
Exploration and development of oil and natural gas resources require the use of wheeled and tracked vehicles, and the statement should reflect legitimate uses of such vehicles. An example of primary importance to exploration is the use of off-road vehicles for geological and geophysical work. Should substantial quantities of oil or gas be discovered as a result of exploratory work, other vehicles, such as trucks, drilling rigs and other auxiliary vehicles, would be needed to develop the deposits and make them available for use.
That the development of such resources is vitally needed for the nation's welfare is beyond question in view of the energy crises expected in the near future. Inasmuch as public lands account for approximately one-third of the land surface of the United States, it is obvious that these areas are likely to contain much of the country's oil and gas potential.

In view of the danger that undue and unnecessary restrictions on legitimate exploration and development of oil and gas, as well as other minerals, on public lands may ensue under the definitions and terms of this order, it is strongly urged that geological, geophysical, and other vehicular equipment necessary to mineral development be exempted in a revised memorandum and impact statement and in the regulations being prepared to implement Executive Order 11644 in order to assure that there can be no misunderstanding and that such vehicular equipment is not intended to be included in the terms of the order.
Sincerely,
Stilson m. Land
33
Wilson M. Laird Director
Committee on Exploration American Petroleum Institute

SUBJECT: Relation of Energy Crisis to Encouragement of Off-Road Vehicle Use
Dear Sir:
These comments are submitted in response to the Draft Environmental Impact Statement of the Department of the Interior, dated May 27, 1972, published June 2, 1972, with regard to Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands.
Apart from the normal environmental considerations, not enough attention has been paid in the draft statement to the growing energy crisis, as it has been termed, and the effect upon the domestic economy and transit generally of increasing reliance on imports to meet our growing fuel and energy needs.
In light of this, FCWC questions, as a matter of national policy, the encouragement of recreational use, through the opening of public lands to snowmobiles and off-road vehicles, with the consequent increasing demand upon ever-shrinking petroleum and energy supplies.
This would indicate, on the basis of national policy, the wisdom of adoption of the alternative as referred to in Item "4" of the Draft Statement, to close all Interior lands to ORV use (except for emergency purposes, of course). Eventually, we may simply find that priorities in use of scarce petroleum resources require further limitations on use thereof by recreational vehicles.
The Department of the Interior, as a matter of environmental responsibility, must take this into consideration in establishing its current land use policy on land administered by the Department.

top.quote: I strongly urge that you amend your instructions to the Assistant Secretaries to except geological and geophysical survey equipment, while being used exclusively for their designed purposes, from the general category of off-road vehicle to which the proposed regulations will apply.
top.summary: The Society of Exploration Geophysicists, through its President Carl H. Savit, argues that geological and geophysical survey vehicles should be exempted from the proposed ORV regulations, just as farm tractors, construction equipment, and forestry vehicles are exempted. The Society contends that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground impact and serve vital national interests related to energy and mineral resource discovery. They urge the Secretary of the Interior to amend his instructions to exclude such survey equipment from the recreational ORV regulatory framework.
top.statementText:
Dear Sir:
Members of the Society of Exploration Geophysicists have called to my attention Executive Order 11644 and your consequent memorandum of May 5, 1972 to the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish and Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources.
Our members are deeply concerned by the text of that memorandum which fails to take account of the special nature of off-road vehicles used in geological and geophysical surveys throughout the public lands of the United States. In particular, they feel that recognition of the exceptional nature of such vehicles should be included among the exceptions listed in the third paragraph of the subject memorandum. Vehicles for geophysical or geological surveying, when used exclusively for their designed purposes, should logically fall into the same broad category as farm tractors, self-propelled agricultural equipment, equipment for harvesting and transporting forest products, and earth moving and construction equipment when such vehicles are used for their designed purposes. It should be noted that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground loading consistent with their survey purposes and are therefore inherently far less likely to leave permanent imprints on the ground than are self-mobile construction and excavation devices or forest product transporters, vehicles which carry heavy loads and, of necessity, create large local ground loading.
Geological and geophysical surveys of the public lands are undertaken, in conformity with statutory requirements, for the purposes of discovering or assessing mineral, fuel, or thermal resources of the United States or for scientific and educational purposes. As such, the continuation of such surveys is of vital interest to the people of the United States in view of the present energy crisis and of the critical shortages of many of our mineral resources. To impose upon such surveys the requirement to conform to regulations designed for the control of recreational vehicles rather than to
11
* . · · · · · · ·

The Honorable the Secretary of the Interior June 30, 1972
Page 2
include such surveys along with agricultural, forestry, and construction operations would appear unjustified on any reasonable basis.
Our nearly 8000 members would be adversely and vitally affected in their activities on the public lands of the United States by being required to adhere to regulations designed for recreational activities. On behalf of our membership, I strongly urge that you amend your instructions to the Assistant Secretaries to except geological and geophysical survey equipment, while being used exclusively for their designed purposes, from the general category of off-road vehicle to which the proposed regulations will apply.
Sincerely,
Carl H. Savit
President

top.quote: I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business.
top.summary: Stewart R. Wallace, president of Mine Finders, Inc., expresses alarm that proposed ORV restrictions—particularly a four-month advance notice requirement for permits—would severely hamper mineral exploration activities that depend on flexible, unplanned off-road vehicle use. He argues there is a meaningful distinction between recreational 'joy-riding' and professional use of ORVs for making a living, and urges the Bureau to develop a licensing arrangement that allows exploration geologists to work without undue restriction. While he shares concern about environmental degradation from indiscriminate ORV use, he contends that the proposed regulations as written would jeopardize mineral discovery efforts critical to the nation's raw material supply.
top.statementText:
MINE FINDERS, INC.
8700 WEST 14TH AVENUE LAKEWOOD, COLORADO 80215 (303) 233-0585
July 12, 1972
44
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Sir:
I am writing to express my concern for legislation or regulation which may come about as a result of executive order 11644 regarding the use of off-road vehicles — Draft Environmental Statement, Int DES 72 - 62, May 26, 1972, notice of which I understand appeared in the Federal Register June 2.
I am a professional geologist with two graduate degrees and have worked in the field for about 24 years. I was employed by the U.S. Geological Survey on both full-time and part-time bases from 1948 to 1955 and worked in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. For the last 17 years I have been a mining and exploration geologist and was fortunate enough, while in the employee of the Climax Molybdenum Company, to participate in two major mineral discoveries. For the last two and one-half years I have been working for a small company, of which I am the president, engaged in contract exploration in western North America for a major raw material company. We now have a staff of seven full-time geologists plus supporting personnel, and hope to add one or two more people during the next eighteen months.
As a geologist and one who enjoys and appreciates nature, I share your concern for the degradation of our remaining "wild lands" by the indiscriminate use or over use by off-road vehicles. On the other hand I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business. I am not familiar with all of the proposed regulations but understand that a four month advance notice would be required for the application of a permit for an off-road vehicle event. It is literally impossible for us to predict four months in advance a specific or, in many cases, even a general off-road vehicle usage. Thus, I am fearful that such restrictions rigidly enforced would greatly reduce our chances of success in making a mineral discovery and in properly locating it according to existing laws governing the location of mineral claims. I might add that mineral exploration is a particularly hazardous business at best and that the odds are great against making a significant find.

lfl
Since the end of World War II, the American mining companies (and others, too) have spent a great deal of time, effort and money here and abroad in the exploration for, and development of, new material resources. Now, for the first time in the last thirty years, the world has finally caught up with itself in that the supply of basic earth materials is sufficient to meet the immediate demand. This situation, however, will not long continue. If the U.S. is to maintain a competitive position (in any field) among the community of nations, it must have access to an assured supply of raw materials at reasonable prices. I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
I do not know what ethical or moral problems there may be in denying use to some while allowing others freedom from such restrictions. I do contend, however, that there is a real difference between simple "joy-riding" and travel for the purpose of making a living. I also maintain that the exploration geologist does perform useful and necessary work, not only for himself and his company, but for the country.
Sincerely yours,
Stewart R. Wallace
Situan IR (1 milenne.

top.quote: We find the draft statement to be totally inadequate. It does not comply with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, Executive Order 11644, or other laws which define Interior Department responsibilities in managing the public lands.
top.summary: The Natural Resources Defense Council found the draft Environmental Impact Statement totally inadequate, arguing it failed to comply with NEPA, Executive Order 11644, and other laws governing Interior Department responsibilities for public lands. They contended that the draft statement accommodated ORV use rather than protecting environmental values, and demanded that both the draft statement and the Secretary's May 16 memorandum be withdrawn so that implementation of E.O. 11644 could begin anew. Their attached detailed comments further argued that ORVs should be banned from national parks and wildlife refuges, and that environmental values must be given the highest priority in any revised policy.
top.statementText:
Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
1600 TWENTIETH STREET, N.W. WASHINGTON, D.C. 20009
147
202 387-2855
July 17, 1972
New York Office 36 WEST 44TH STREET NEW YORK, N.Y. 10036 212 986-8310
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Enclosed are the comments of the Natural Resources Defense Council on the Draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
We find the draft statement to be totally inadequate. It does not comply with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, Executive Order 11644, or other laws which define Interior Department responsibilities in managing the public lands. Instead, it militates against the clear duty imposed by these directives to identify and protect environmental values. It indicates that the policy of the Department is not to insure that the use of off-road vehicles is "controlled and directed so as to protect resources on [the public] lands," as required by E.O. 11644, but rather to accommodate all demands for ORV use. For these reasons we believe that the draft statement must be withdrawn.
Furthermore, the Secretary's memorandum of May 16 is an inadequate attempt to implement E.O. 11644. It fails to take account of Interior's legal responsibilities to identify environmental values, and fails to propose concrete policies for the regulation of ORV use. It is useful neither as a proposal for action, nor as a guide to substantive policy. Therefore, we believe that the memorandum must be withdrawn along with the draft statement, and the entire process of implementation of E.O. 11644 must begin again.

We are shocked that Interior, as the agency charged with the protection of natural resources on over 60% of Federal lands, should reject the opportunity to declare its commitment to the protection of environmental values and choose instead to accommodate an environmentally-destructive activity. The effect of this choice is to seriously weaken and misdirect the implementation of laws which are intended to promote environmental quality. In its revised implementation of E.O. 11644, Interior must change its policy on ORV use to give environmental values the highest priority. Only in this way can the Department properly fulfill its responsibilities.
Sincerely yours,
Thomas B. Stad, Jr.
Thomas B. Stoel, Jr.
Grey & Studen
Greg E. Studen
